blocks.h: 1. The Convention's definition of pollution, and what makes it unusually wide

blocks.p: UNCLOS article 1(1)(4) defines "pollution of the marine environment" as the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as: harm to living resources and marine life; hazards to human health; hindrance to marine activities, including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea; impairment of quality for use of sea water; and reduction of amenities.
Five features of that wording earn marks, and each should be stated as a point:

ol: "By man" - a natural seep or a volcanic discharge is not pollution under the Convention, however damaging.
"Directly or indirectly" - a river carrying industrial waste to the sea is caught, so the polluting act need not happen at sea at all.
"Substances or energy" - heat, noise and radiation are pollution. This is the element most candidates omit and it is the one that makes the definition modern.
"Results or is likely to result" - no damage need have occurred. Likelihood is enough, which is what allows preventive regulation.
"Reduction of amenities" - purely aesthetic and recreational harm counts. Oil on a beach is pollution even where nothing is killed.

blocks.p: Note finally that the definition is source-neutral. Nothing in it mentions ships. Ships are one source among land-based sources, dumping, seabed activities and the atmosphere, and that is why the coastal State's obligations are structured source by source.

blocks.h: 2. The general obligation, and why it is not confined to any zone

blocks.p: Article 192 states the whole of Part XII in one sentence: States have the obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment. It is free-standing and not zone-limited - the rest of the Convention allocates rights zone by zone, but this imposes a duty across all of them, including the high seas.

Article 193 then makes the balance explicit: States have the sovereign right to exploit their natural resources pursuant to their environmental policies and in accordance with their duty to protect and preserve the marine environment. Development is permitted; it is not unconditioned.
Article 194 is the operative obligation:

ul: 194(1) - all measures necessary to prevent, reduce and control pollution from any source, using the best practicable means at their disposal and in accordance with their capabilities, endeavouring to harmonize policies. Note that the standard is expressly capability-relative.
194(2) - activities under a State's jurisdiction or control must not cause damage by pollution to other States, and pollution from incidents under its control must not spread beyond its zones.

194(3)(b) - for vessels specifically: preventing accidents, dealing with emergencies, ensuring safety of operations, preventing intentional and unintentional discharges, and regulating design, construction, equipment, operation and manning.
194(5) - measures to protect rare or fragile ecosystems and the habitat of depleted, threatened or endangered species.

blocks.p: Two short articles complete the frame and are easy marks. Article 195 forbids a State, in taking measures, from transferring damage or hazards from one area to another, or transforming one type of pollution into another - so scrubbing a stack emission into the sea is not compliance. Article 196 covers harmful technologies and the introduction of alien or new species, which is the treaty root of ballast water and biofouling control.

blocks.h: 3. The coastal State's obligations - rule-making

blocks.p: Part XII deals with pollution source by source, and the coastal State's freedom of action differs sharply between them:

headers: What the coastal State must do
rows: Adopt national laws and regulations, taking into account internationally agreed rules and standards
National law; and dumping within the territorial sea, EEZ or on the continental shelf requires the express prior approval of the coastal State
Wide, and a positive control power
Act through the competent international organization; national law must have at least the same effect as the generally accepted international standard
Narrow - the tightest constraint in Part XII
Laws for airspace under sovereignty and for ships of its flag

blocks.p: Article 211 is the one that matters for ships, and its internal structure is the answer to "key features":

ul: 211(1) - rules and standards are established through the competent international organization, that is the IMO, and are re-examined from time to time.
211(2) - a flag State's own laws must have at least the same effect as those international standards. Stricter for your own ships, yes; laxer, no.
211(4) - in the territorial sea a coastal State may legislate for foreign vessels including those in innocent passage, but such laws shall not hamper innocent passage.
211(5) - in the exclusive economic zone it may legislate only conforming to and giving effect to generally accepted international rules. It cannot invent its own standard.

211(6) - the one escape route: for a particular, clearly defined area of its EEZ where the international rules are inadequate, it may submit scientific and technical evidence to the IMO; the IMO determines within 12 months; the measures bind foreign vessels only 15 months after submission; and they may never impose design, construction, manning or equipment standards other than the generally accepted international ones.

blocks.p: That last prohibition is the single most quotable limit in Part XII. It is why a coastal State can impose a discharge or routeing requirement but cannot demand a different hull, and it is the legal basis on which Special Areas and Particularly Sensitive Sea Areas are created through the IMO rather than declared unilaterally.

blocks.h: 4. The coastal State's obligations - enforcement, and its limits

blocks.p: Rule-making and enforcement are separately allocated, and confusing them is the commonest error on this question.

ul: Article 217 - the flag State. The primary enforcement duty: compliance by ships of its flag wherever the violation occurs.

Article 218 - the port State. Where a ship is voluntarily in port, proceedings may be taken for a discharge outside that State's own waters - a jurisdiction that exists nowhere else in the Convention.

Article 220 - the coastal State, and its powers are deliberately graded: proceedings where the ship is voluntarily in port for a violation in its territorial sea or EEZ (220(1)); on clear grounds for a territorial-sea violation, physical inspection and, where the evidence warrants, proceedings including detention (220(2)); and for an EEZ violation, first only the power to require information - identity, port of registry, last and next port of call (220(3)) - escalating to inspection and then to detention as the evidence and the gravity of the discharge increase.

Article 221 - after a maritime casualty, the right to take and enforce measures beyond the territorial sea, proportionate to the actual or threatened damage, to protect the coastline and related interests including fishing, where major harmful consequences may reasonably be expected. The article carries its own definition of maritime casualty.
Article 235 - States are responsible for fulfilling their international obligations and must ensure recourse for prompt and adequate compensation for pollution damage.

blocks.p: The safeguards in section 7 of Part XII then constrain how all of this is exercised. The shape of the coastal State's position is therefore: a duty everywhere, rule-making power that narrows as you move seaward, and enforcement power that is graded by evidence and by seriousness. And article 235 is the bridge to the second limb - the compensation regime exists because UNCLOS requires that recourse.

blocks.h: 5. Why the oil pollution compensation regime has three tiers

blocks.p: Before listing the tiers, say why there are tiers. A major tanker spill can cost more than any shipowner or his insurer could reasonably carry. Unlimited liability would have made tankers uninsurable; leaving victims uncompensated was politically and legally unacceptable. The compromise reached was that the shipowner is liable strictly but with a limit, and the balance is placed on the cargo interest - those who receive the oil.
The defining idea of the regime is therefore that the cost of an oil spill is shared between the ship and the cargo. Every feature below follows from it.

blocks.h: 6. Tier one - the shipowner and his insurer

rows: The registered owner of the ship, strictly - no fault need be proved. Liability is channelled to him, so claims may not be brought against the master, crew, pilot, charterer, manager, operator or salvor acting as such
The shipping side - the owner and, in practice, his P&I club under the compulsory insurance

A certificate of insurance or other financial security, issued or certified by the flag State (or by a State Party where the ship is not registered in one), carried on board, for ships carrying persistent oil in bulk as cargo. It is issued against a 'blue card' from the insurer

ul: There is a right of direct action against the insurer, so the victim is not defeated by the owner's insolvency.
The owner may limit his liability by reference to the tonnage of the ship. No figure is given here - the limits are amended over time and every figure carries a date.
He loses the right to limit if the damage resulted from his personal act or omission, committed with intent to cause damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result.

The exceptions are narrow: act of war; a wholly exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by a third party's intentional act; or the negligence of an authority responsible for navigational aids.

blocks.h: 7. Tiers two and three - the Funds, and who actually provides the money

rows: Where tier one gives no compensation, or is financially inadequate to meet the established claims
Where tier two is insufficient to meet the established claims
The 1992 International Oil Pollution Compensation Fund, an intergovernmental body
Levies on receivers of contributing oil - crude oil and heavy fuel oil received by sea above a threshold quantity in a State Party
The same - contributions from receivers of contributing oil in States that have opted into the Protocol
NONE. The ship carries no Fund certificate; the ship's document is the CLC certificate alone

blocks.p: Three points here separate a good answer from a list:

ol: The cargo interest pays for tiers two and three - not the shipowner and not governments. The Funds are financed by the oil receivers in the member States. This is the fact most candidates get wrong.
The tiers are cumulative and sequential, each with its own overall ceiling for any one incident, and each tier is reached only when the one below it is exhausted or unavailable.

Tier three is optional. A State must already be a member of the 1992 Fund and must separately accede to the 2003 Protocol. So the compensation available for the same casualty depends on where it happens.

blocks.p: Note the answer to "certification required by ship under each tier" precisely: only tier one produces a certificate carried by the ship. Saying so, and explaining why - the Funds are financed ashore, not by the ship - is worth more than inventing two more certificates.

blocks.h: 8. What the three tiers do NOT cover - and the trap

ul: The regime is about persistent oil carried in bulk as cargo - in substance, the laden or residue-carrying tanker case. It is not a general marine pollution compensation scheme.

Bunker oil spilled from a non-tanker is the Bunkers Convention 2001: strict liability on a wider group of owners, compulsory insurance and a certificate, but a single tier with no fund behind it. A candidate who offers Bunkers as one of the three tiers has misread the question.
Hazardous and noxious substances have their own convention, which is not in force at this sitting. It cannot be cited as a tier or as current law.
Geography matters. The tiers respond only in States party, and the third only where that State has opted in.
In India, domestic effect to the civil liability and fund regimes is given through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

blocks.p: Close by joining the two limbs, because the examiner printed them together: UNCLOS article 235 obliges States to ensure recourse for prompt and adequate compensation for pollution damage, and the three tiers are how that obligation is discharged for oil. The first limb states the duty; the second shows the machinery.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two limbs, no printed marks, and a very wide subject. The risk is not ignorance - most candidates know something about UNCLOS and something about CLC - it is drift: writing a general essay on marine pollution and never answering either printed instruction. The route defends against that by anchoring each limb on the words the examiner actually used.

Limb A prints two demands - "define" and "discuss the key features of obligations of coastal states". Definition is a quotation task: reproduce article 1(1)(4) as closely as you can and then dissect it, because every element of it is a scoring proposition. Obligations is a structure task: the marks are in showing that the Convention allocates rule-making and enforcement separately, and that the coastal State's freedom narrows as it moves seaward.

Limb B prints three demands and they are easy to leave one out: who pays, the source of funds, and the certification required by the ship, in each case. Three demands times three tiers is nine propositions, and they are best written as a table. Step 5 - why there are tiers at all - is what turns the table from a memorised list into an explanation, and step 8 is where the examiner separates candidates by asking, in effect, what the regime is not.

blocks.h: The definition is worth learning word for word

blocks.p: Very few provisions repay verbatim memory as well as article 1(1)(4), because the marks are distributed across its clauses. If you can write "the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as..." you have earned several propositions before you have explained anything.

The five deleterious effects are: harm to living resources and marine life; hazards to human health; hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea; impairment of quality for use of sea water; and reduction of amenities. Reduction of amenities and or energy are the two most frequently omitted, and both are distinctive enough to be noticed.

blocks.h: Rule-making and enforcement are different questions

blocks.p: Candidates routinely answer "what are the coastal State's obligations" by listing enforcement powers. The Convention separates them, and saying so is itself a scoring point. Rule-making runs 207 land-based, 210 dumping, 211 vessels, 212 atmosphere - and the coastal State's discretion is widest for land-based sources and narrowest for ships. Enforcement runs 217 flag, 218 port, 220 coastal, 221 casualties - and the coastal State's power is graded rather than absolute.

The reason for the asymmetry is worth one sentence: a State may regulate its own territory as it likes, but a ship is a moving object subject to another State's flag, so uniform international standards are the only workable basis. That is why article 211 keeps referring back to the competent international organization.

blocks.h: The 12 and 15 month periods in article 211(6)

blocks.p: If you can carry two numbers into this answer, carry these. Where a coastal State wants special mandatory measures for a clearly defined area of its EEZ, it communicates to the IMO with scientific and technical evidence; the IMO determines within 12 months; and the laws become applicable to foreign vessels only 15 months after the submission. They may never impose design, construction, manning or equipment standards beyond the generally accepted international ones. That paragraph is the legal skeleton of the Special Area and PSSA machinery, and quoting the two periods proves the Convention was opened.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Paraphrasing the definition loosely and losing "or energy", "indirectly", "is likely to result" and "reduction of amenities" - four separate propositions gone.
Answering limb A entirely with enforcement powers and never mentioning the rule-making obligations.
Treating article 192 as applying only inside national zones. It is not zone-limited.
Offering the Bunkers Convention 2001 as one of the three tiers. It is a separate, single-tier regime for bunkers from non-tankers.
Offering the HNS Convention as a tier, or describing it as in force. It is not in force at this sitting.
Saying the Funds are financed by shipowners or by governments. They are financed by receivers of contributing oil.
Inventing a Fund certificate or a Supplementary Fund certificate carried by the ship. Only tier one produces a ship's certificate.
Quoting SDR limits from memory. They are amended over time and a stale figure is worse than none.
Writing that the coastal State may impose its own construction standards on foreign ships in its EEZ. Article 211(6) expressly forbids it.
Forgetting that the owner loses the right to limit for his own intentional or reckless conduct with knowledge.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Is noise pollution?" Yes - the definition says substances or energy. So is waste heat.
"Must damage have occurred?" No - 'results or is likely to result'.

"Can a coastal State demand a double hull in its EEZ?" No. Article 211(6) permits special measures for a defined area but not design, construction, manning or equipment standards beyond the generally accepted international ones.
"Who may be sued under CLC 92?" The registered owner, and liability is channelled to him - not the manager, charterer, crew, pilot or salvor.
"Who pays for tiers two and three?" Receivers of contributing oil. Say cargo, not ship.
"What does the ship carry for tier two?" Nothing. Only the CLC certificate is a ship's document.
"Is the third tier available everywhere?" No - it is optional, and requires 1992 Fund membership first.
"What links the two limbs?" Article 235 - the duty to ensure recourse for prompt and adequate compensation.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Define pollution under UNCLOS. Give the article. Article 1(1)(4).
Which article states the general obligation? 192. And what qualifies the right to exploit resources? 193.
Which article deals with pollution from vessels? 211. What standard must national law meet? At least the same effect as the generally accepted international rules.
What can a coastal State do about a suspected discharge in its EEZ? Require information first; inspect on clear grounds; detain only where the evidence and the gravity warrant it - article 220.
What may a State do after a casualty outside its territorial sea? Measures proportionate to the actual or threatened damage - article 221.
Name the three tiers. CLC 1992, the 1992 Fund, the Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003.
Who is strictly liable under tier one and can he limit? The registered owner; yes, by tonnage, unless the damage resulted from his personal intentional or reckless act with knowledge.

What certificate does the ship carry, and who issues it? A certificate of insurance or other financial security under CLC 92, issued or certified by the State, on the strength of the insurer's blue card.
Is the Bunkers Convention one of the tiers? No - separate regime, one tier, no fund.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: For limb A, DEFINE - DUTY - RULES - ENFORCE. Inside the definition, MAN, INDIRECT, ENERGY, LIKELY, AMENITIES - the five words that carry the marks. Inside rule-making, walk seaward: LAND (207) - DUMP (210) - SHIPS (211) - AIR (212), discretion shrinking as you go. Inside enforcement, FLAG - PORT - COASTAL - CASUALTY, that is 217, 218, 220, 221.

For limb B, SHIP - CARGO - CARGO. Tier one is the ship and its insurer; tiers two and three are both the cargo receivers. Then the three demands in every row: WHO PAYS - WHERE FROM - WHAT PAPER. And remember the answer to the third column is certificate, none, none.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: Limb A rests on UNCLOS read verbatim at source. The Convention entered into force on 16 November 1994 and is unamended, so the text MIW holds is the June 2023 text. There is no edition question and no reversal to perform. That is the strongest evidential position on this paper, and it belongs to this limb alone. Articles 207, 210, 212, 217, 218 and 235 are cited by identity, with their substance carried from MIW's own verification record for the September 2023 sitting of a related question; the section 7 safeguards are referred to only in general terms.

Limb B is deliberately weaker and says so. MIW holds no text of CLC 1992, the Fund Convention 1992 or the Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003 - the corpus classifies them as citation and index only with verified status facts. Accordingly no monetary or Special Drawing Right figure is asserted anywhere: not a CLC tonnage-band limit, not either Fund ceiling, not the contributing-oil threshold. Those limits are amended by tacit acceptance, so every figure carries a date, and a figure recalled from a textbook is likely to be a superseded one. No article number of any of the three instruments is asserted and no text of any of them is quoted. What the question asks for - who pays, from what source, against what certificate - is answered in full without any of that.

One currency instruction for a later editor: do not add SDR figures to this object without sourcing them and without confirming they are the position at or before June 2023. If figures are wanted, they must be dated.

notes: LIMB A IS THE IDEAL EVIDENTIAL CASE AND IT IS UNIQUE ON THIS PAPER. UNCLOS entered into force on 16 November 1994 and is UNAMENDED. The text MIW holds IS the June 2023 text. There is no later edition, no consolidation and no amendment to reverse. Article 1(1)(4) and articles 192 to 196, 211, 220 and 221 were read verbatim at source in this session, so the core of the answer rests on the reading rather than on a record of a reading.

THE DONOR RUNS THE RIGHT WAY FOR ONCE, AND THIS IS THE FIRST SUCH CASE ON THE PAPER. QP2303-Q1 is March 2023 - THREE MONTHS EARLIER than this sitting and inside the same regime. Both sittings stand after the 1 January 2023 entry into force of EEXI and CII and before MEPC 80 of 3 to 7 July 2023. Nothing in the donor's regulatory position required reversing. This is noted precisely because the standing batch warning is the opposite, and a warning applied mechanically where it does not bite is its own error.

THE ONE TEMPORAL FACT THE DONOR COULD NOT CARRY, AND IT FALLS INSIDE THE SITTING MONTH. The Agreement under UNCLOS on the conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity of areas beyond national jurisdiction - the BBNJ or 'High Seas' Agreement - was ADOPTED ON 19 JUNE 2023. That is INSIDE this paper's printed sitting month. The paper prints JUNE 2023 with NO DAY, so it cannot be established whether the examination fell before or after 19 June, and NO CLAIM IN THIS ANSWER DEPENDS ON THE ANSWER. This follows the standing rule against week-granularity reasoning from a month-only sitting. At the March 2023 sitting the donor could state flatly that the Agreement was future; here that statement is unavailable, and the honest position is silence rather than a guess.

NOTHING TURNS ON IT IN ANY EVENT, AND THE REASON IS RECORDED SO THAT A LATER EDITOR DOES NOT 'FIX' THE OMISSION. The BBNJ Agreement is an implementing agreement under UNCLOS; it DOES NOT AMEND the Convention, and it does not touch article 1(1)(4), Part XII rule-making or Part XII enforcement. It was not open for signature until September 2023 and was not in force at this sitting on any reading. The stem asks about UNCLOS itself. It is therefore correctly absent from the answer, and its absence is a decision rather than an oversight.

LIMB B'S INSTRUMENTS WERE ALL LONG IN FORCE. CLC 1992, the Fund Convention 1992 and the Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003 were all operative years before June 2023. There is no in-force question to resolve on any of the three tiers.

THE LIVE TEMPORAL RISK ON LIMB B IS MONETARY, AND IT IS CLOSED BY ASSERTING NOTHING. CLC tonnage-band limits and the two Fund ceilings are amended by TACIT ACCEPTANCE over time, so every figure carries a date and a figure carried from a donor or a textbook is likely to be a superseded one. NO MONETARY OR SPECIAL DRAWING RIGHT FIGURE IS ASSERTED ANYWHERE IN THIS ANSWER, and no article number of any of the three instruments is asserted.

THE HNS CONVENTION IS CORRECTLY DESCRIBED AS NOT IN FORCE AT THIS SITTING. Its entry-into-force conditions were not met until 2026 and it enters into force in 2027 - years after this examination. It is named only to mark the boundary of the three-tier regime and is not offered as a tier.

A SECOND DAY-DEPENDENT EVENT INSIDE THE SITTING MONTH WAS CHECKED AND IS NOT ENGAGED. The Hong Kong Convention reached its entry-into-force conditions on 26 June 2023, fixing entry into force for 26 June 2025. It is not in force at this sitting on any reading of the day and no claim in this answer touches ship recycling.

MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 IS THE INDIAN STATUTE at this sitting. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 - thirty-three months after this examination - and does not appear anywhere in this answer.

steps.title: The Convention's definition of pollution, and what makes it unusually wide
points: article 1(1)(4) - introduction BY MAN, DIRECTLY OR INDIRECTLY, of SUBSTANCES OR ENERGY into the marine environment, INCLUDING ESTUARIES
which RESULTS OR IS LIKELY TO RESULT in deleterious effects
'by man' excludes a natural seep; 'indirectly' catches a river carrying waste to the sea
'or energy' - heat, noise and radiation are pollution
'or is likely to result' - no damage need have occurred
five effects: harm to living resources and marine life; hazards to human health; hindrance to marine activities including fishing; impairment of quality for use of sea water; REDUCTION OF AMENITIES
the definition is SOURCE-NEUTRAL - nothing in it is about ships

steps.title: The general obligation, and why it is not confined to any zone
points: article 192 - States have the obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment
free-standing and NOT zone-limited; the zones allocate rights, this imposes a duty across all of them
article 193 - the sovereign right to exploit resources is expressly subject to that duty
article 194(1) - all measures necessary, from ANY source, by the BEST PRACTICABLE MEANS and IN ACCORDANCE WITH CAPABILITIES
194(2) - activities under jurisdiction or control must not cause damage by pollution to other States
194(3)(b) - for vessels: accidents, emergencies, discharges, and design, construction, equipment, operation and manning
194(5) - rare or fragile ecosystems and the habitat of threatened species
article 195 no transferring damage or transforming pollution; article 196 technologies and alien species

steps.title: The coastal State's obligations - rule-making
points: the Convention deals with pollution SOURCE BY SOURCE
article 207 land-based - national law TAKING INTO ACCOUNT international rules. Wide discretion
article 210 dumping - national law, and EXPRESS PRIOR APPROVAL of the coastal State within its zones
article 211 vessels - act THROUGH IMO; national law must have AT LEAST THE SAME EFFECT
article 212 from or through the atmosphere
211(4) territorial sea - may legislate for foreign vessels but SHALL NOT HAMPER INNOCENT PASSAGE
211(5) EEZ - only CONFORMING TO AND GIVING EFFECT TO generally accepted international rules
211(6) special measures for a clearly defined area - IMO determines in 12 months, binds foreign vessels 15 months after submission, and NEVER design, construction, manning or equipment standards

steps.title: The coastal State's obligations - enforcement, and its limits
points: article 217 FLAG STATE - compliance by its own ships wherever the violation occurs. The primary duty
article 218 PORT STATE - where the ship is VOLUNTARILY in port, proceedings for discharges OUTSIDE its own waters
article 220 COASTAL STATE - violations in the territorial sea or EEZ, powers GRADED by seriousness and evidence
220(3) information first, then physical inspection on clear grounds, then detention where the evidence warrants
article 221 - measures BEYOND the territorial sea after a MARITIME CASUALTY, proportionate to the damage threatened
article 235 - responsibility, liability, and RECOURSE FOR PROMPT AND ADEQUATE COMPENSATION
the Part XII section 7 safeguards constrain how the powers may be exercised
article 235 is the bridge to limb B

steps.title: Why the oil pollution compensation regime has three tiers
points: a major spill can cost more than any owner or insurer could reasonably carry
unlimited liability would have made tankers uninsurable; leaving victims uncompensated was unacceptable
the compromise: the owner is STRICTLY BUT LIMITEDLY liable
and the balance is placed on the CARGO INTEREST - those who receive the oil
the regime SHARES THE COST BETWEEN SHIP AND CARGO, which is its defining idea

steps.title: Tier one - the shipowner and his insurer
points: CLC 1992. The REGISTERED OWNER is STRICTLY liable - no fault need be proved
liability is CHANNELLED to him - not master, crew, pilot, charterer, manager, operator or salvor
COMPULSORY INSURANCE for ships carrying persistent oil in bulk, evidenced by a CERTIFICATE CARRIED ON BOARD, issued against the insurer's blue card
RIGHT OF DIRECT ACTION against the insurer
source of funds: THE SHIPPING SIDE - the owner and his P&I club
he may LIMIT by reference to tonnage. NO FIGURE IS GIVEN - the limits are amended over time
the limit is LOST for his personal act or omission with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge
narrow exceptions: war, exceptional natural phenomenon, wholly a third party's intentional act, negligence of a navigational-aids authority

steps.title: Tiers two and three - the Funds, and who actually provides the money
points: TIER TWO - the 1992 IOPC Fund, where tier one gives nothing or is financially inadequate
TIER THREE - the Supplementary Fund under the 2003 Protocol, where tier two is insufficient
source for BOTH: contributions levied on RECEIVERS OF CONTRIBUTING OIL - crude and heavy fuel oil received by sea above a threshold quantity
THE CARGO INTEREST PAYS, not the shipowner and not governments - the point most candidates miss
NO CERTIFICATE IS CARRIED BY THE SHIP for either Fund tier; only tier one produces a ship's document
the tiers are CUMULATIVE AND SEQUENTIAL, each with its own overall ceiling
TIER THREE IS OPTIONAL and requires membership of the 1992 Fund first
so the compensation available for the same casualty depends on WHERE IT HAPPENS

steps.title: What the three tiers do NOT cover - and the trap
points: the regime is about PERSISTENT OIL CARRIED IN BULK AS CARGO - the tanker case
BUNKER OIL FROM A NON-TANKER is the Bunkers Convention 2001 - a SINGLE TIER WITH NO FUND behind it
HAZARDOUS AND NOXIOUS SUBSTANCES have their own convention, NOT IN FORCE at this sitting
GEOGRAPHY MATTERS - the tiers respond only in States party, and the third only where opted into
in India, domestic effect is given through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958
closing: the three tiers exist because UNCLOS article 235 requires recourse for prompt and adequate compensation

questions.understand_first: Strip the two limbs down and they are one idea seen twice. The first asks what the law of the sea means by pollution and what it therefore requires of the State whose coastline is at risk; the second asks who actually pays when the pollution happens anyway. The definition is deliberately enormous - anything a person puts into the sea, whether a substance or merely energy such as heat or noise, that is likely to do harm, even if no harm has yet occurred. Because it is that wide, the duty it creates has to be split up, and the way the Convention splits it is the real content of the first limb: a State has almost a free hand over what it does on its own land, and almost none over what it demands of a foreign ship, because a ship moves and belongs to somebody else. So the rules for ships are made through the international organisation, and the coastal State's power to enforce them grows as the evidence and the seriousness grow. The second limb follows from the last piece of the first: having imposed a duty, the Convention also requires that victims can actually recover. For oil that recovery is built in layers, and the reason it is layered is that no single shipowner could carry the cost of a bad spill and no insurer would write unlimited cover. So the cost is shared between the ship and the cargo - the owner pays first, strictly but only up to a limit, and beyond that the people who receive the oil pay through funds they finance. Once you see that the whole scheme is ship-then-cargo, the details stop being a list to memorise.
questions.memory_cue: Limb A walks outward: DEFINE (1) - DUTY (2) - RULES (3) - ENFORCE (4). Inside the definition, the five earning words: MAN, INDIRECT, ENERGY, LIKELY, AMENITIES (1). Inside rule-making, go seaward and watch the discretion shrink: LAND, DUMP, SHIPS, AIR (3). Inside enforcement: FLAG, PORT, COASTAL, CASUALTY (4). Limb B is SHIP, CARGO, CARGO (6, 7) - and in every row answer the same three columns, WHO PAYS, WHERE FROM, WHAT PAPER (7), whose third answer is certificate, none, none. Finish on what it is not: BUNKERS IS NOT A TIER (8).

quick_revision.critical_regulation: UNCLOS article 1(1)(4) defines pollution of the marine environment as the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as harm to living resources and marine life, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea, impairment of quality for use of sea water and reduction of amenities. Article 192 imposes the general obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment, and article 211 requires that rules for vessel-source pollution be established through the competent international organization, with national law having at least the same effect.
quick_revision.major_trap: Two traps, one in each limb. In limb A, answering "the obligations of coastal states" with a list of enforcement powers and never mentioning the rule-making obligations under articles 207 to 212 - and in particular missing that the coastal State's discretion is widest for land-based sources and narrowest for ships, and that article 211(6) forbids it from imposing design, construction, manning or equipment standards on foreign ships even in a special area. In limb B, offering the Bunkers Convention 2001 as one of the three tiers, saying the Funds are financed by shipowners or governments rather than by receivers of contributing oil, and inventing Fund certificates carried by the ship - only tier one produces a ship's certificate. And quote no SDR figure: the limits are amended over time and a remembered number is probably a superseded one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the UNCLOS pollution and three-tiers question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The definition and what makes it wide. 2 The general obligation, not zone-limited. 3 Coastal State rule-making, source by source. 4 Coastal State enforcement, graded. 5 Why there are three tiers at all. 6 Tier one, the shipowner. 7 Tiers two and three, the Funds. 8 What the tiers do not cover.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 5 and 8 are what lift limb B out of a memorised list; step 3 is where most candidates lose limb A.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define pollution of the marine environment under UNCLOS, and give the article.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 1(1)(4): the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the marine environment, including estuaries, which results or is likely to result in such deleterious effects as harm to living resources and marine life, hazards to human health, hindrance to marine activities including fishing and other legitimate uses of the sea, impairment of quality for use of sea water, and reduction of amenities.
retrieval_cards.why: The marks are distributed across the clauses, so a loose paraphrase loses several propositions at once.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which four elements of the UNCLOS definition are most often omitted, and why does each matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: 'By man' - a natural seep is not pollution. 'Indirectly' - a river carrying waste to the sea is caught. 'Or energy' - heat, noise and radiation are pollution. 'Is likely to result' - no damage need have occurred, which is what permits preventive regulation. A fifth, 'reduction of amenities', makes purely aesthetic harm count.
retrieval_cards.why: Each is a separate scoring proposition and each is distinctive enough for an examiner to notice its absence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the coastal State's rule-making obligations from its enforcement powers under Part XII.
retrieval_cards.answer: Rule-making runs source by source - article 207 land-based, 210 dumping, 211 vessels, 212 atmosphere - and the coastal State's discretion is widest for land-based sources and narrowest for ships, where it must act through the IMO and legislate only to at least the same effect. Enforcement is separately allocated - 217 flag, 218 port, 220 coastal, 221 after a casualty - and the coastal State's power is graded by evidence and gravity.
retrieval_cards.why: Answering 'obligations' with enforcement alone is the commonest way to lose half of limb A.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does article 211(6) allow a coastal State to do in its EEZ, on what timetable, and what does it forbid?
retrieval_cards.answer: For a particular, clearly defined area where the international rules are inadequate, it may communicate to the IMO with supporting scientific and technical evidence; the IMO determines within 12 months; the resulting laws apply to foreign vessels only 15 months after submission. It may never impose design, construction, manning or equipment standards other than generally accepted international ones.
retrieval_cards.why: The two periods prove the Convention was opened, and the prohibition is the legal skeleton of Special Areas and PSSAs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How are a coastal State's enforcement powers graded under article 220?
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the ship is voluntarily in port, proceedings may be instituted for a violation in the territorial sea or EEZ. For a territorial-sea violation, on clear grounds, physical inspection and, where the evidence warrants, proceedings including detention. For an EEZ violation, on clear grounds, first only a power to require information - identity, port of registry, last and next port of call - escalating to inspection and then detention as the evidence and the seriousness of the discharge increase.
retrieval_cards.why: The grading is the point of the article; describing it as a single power to detain misstates the Convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three tiers of oil pollution compensation, and say who is responsible for payment in each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Tier one, CLC 1992 - the registered owner of the ship, strictly, with liability channelled to him. Tier two, the Fund Convention 1992 - the 1992 IOPC Fund. Tier three, the Supplementary Fund Protocol 2003 - the Supplementary Fund. The tiers are cumulative and sequential, each reached only when the one below is exhausted or unavailable.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks 'in each case' who is responsible, so all three must be named separately.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does the money for tiers two and three actually come from?
retrieval_cards.answer: From levies on receivers of contributing oil - crude oil and heavy fuel oil received by sea above a threshold quantity in a State Party. The cargo interest funds both Funds, not the shipowner and not governments. Tier three additionally requires that the State has opted into the 2003 Protocol, having first joined the 1992 Fund.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the single most commonly wrong statement on the question, and it is also the idea that explains the whole regime.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What certification does the ship carry under each of the three tiers?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only under tier one. A certificate of insurance or other financial security under CLC 1992, issued or certified by the State on the strength of the insurer's blue card, carried on board by ships carrying persistent oil in bulk as cargo. Neither Fund tier produces a ship's certificate, because the Funds are financed ashore by cargo receivers rather than by the ship.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks specifically about certification per tier, and the correct answer is certificate, none, none - with the reason.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the Bunkers Convention 2001 one of the three tiers?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It is a separate regime for pollution by bunker oil from ships other than tankers carrying persistent oil as cargo - strict liability, compulsory insurance and a certificate, but a single tier with no fund behind it. The HNS Convention is likewise not a tier, and is not in force at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: Offering Bunkers as a tier is the classic misread, and naming the boundary correctly is itself worth marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What connects the two printed limbs of this question?
retrieval_cards.answer: UNCLOS article 235. Having imposed the duty to protect and preserve the marine environment, the Convention also requires States to ensure that recourse is available for prompt and adequate compensation for pollution damage. The three tiers are the machinery by which that obligation is discharged for oil.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner printed the two limbs together; saying why converts two half-answers into one argument.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why should you quote no SDR figure in this answer?

blocks.h: 1. The origin - from a 1948 conference to the Organization of today

ul: The United Nations Maritime Conference met in Geneva and, on 6 March 1948, adopted a convention establishing the Inter-Governmental Maritime Consultative Organization (IMCO). It was the first international body devoted exclusively to maritime affairs.

The convention did not enter into force until 17 March 1958 - a delay of ten years, because it needed ratification by a set number of States including several with substantial tonnage. That delay is itself the best illustration of the ratification process the same limb asks about.
The first Assembly met in January 1959, and the Organization's first task was the 1960 SOLAS Convention.

The name was changed to the International Maritime Organization with effect from 22 May 1982. The word "Consultative" was dropped, and its removal marks the Organization's shift from an advisory forum to the body that makes the international rules for shipping.
It is a specialized agency of the United Nations, with its headquarters in London.

blocks.h: 2. The authority vested in IMO - and the decisive limitation

blocks.p: The Convention gives the Organization four purposes, and they define the whole of its authority:

ol: to provide machinery for cooperation among Governments in governmental regulation and practices relating to technical matters of all kinds affecting shipping engaged in international trade;

to encourage and facilitate the general adoption of the highest practicable standards in matters of maritime safety, efficiency of navigation, and the prevention and control of marine pollution from ships;
to deal with the related administrative and legal matters; and
to encourage the removal of discriminatory action and unnecessary restrictions affecting international shipping.

blocks.p: Now the point that separates a good answer from a recital. The authority vested in IMO is legislative in form and wholly indirect in effect. The Organization:

ul: adopts conventions, protocols, codes, guidelines and resolutions;
cannot enforce any of them against any ship. It has no inspectors, no ships, no power of detention and no power to prosecute;
regulates States, not vessels. An IMO instrument binds a State when that State accepts it, and it reaches a ship only through that State's own legislation and administration;

so enforcement rests with the flag State, the port State and the coastal State - which is exactly the allocation UNCLOS Part XII makes, and it is why UNCLOS repeatedly says that rules for ships shall be established "through the competent international organization".

blocks.p: That is why the audit scheme in the second limb exists at all: if the Organization cannot enforce, the only thing it can usefully examine is whether the State is discharging what it accepted.

blocks.h: 3. The organs through which the authority is exercised

rows: All Member States; regular session every two years
The governing body. Approves the work programme and the budget, elects the Council, and adopts Assembly resolutions (the A. series)

Forty Members elected by the Assembly, in three categories - the largest providers of international shipping services; the largest interested in seaborne trade; and States with special interests, elected to secure geographical representation
The executive organ. Supervises the work of the Organization between Assemblies, and appoints the Secretary-General subject to Assembly approval
MSC maritime safety; MEPC marine environment protection; Legal; Technical Cooperation; Facilitation. The MSC and MEPC are where the technical amendments are adopted
Report to the MSC and MEPC

Do the detailed technical work - carriage of cargoes and containers, ship design and construction, ship systems and equipment, navigation and communications, human element and training, pollution prevention and response, and implementation of IMO instruments
Administration, depositary functions, and circulation of instruments

blocks.p: One current point worth a mark at this examination: amendments to the Convention that would enlarge the Council from 40 to 52 Members were adopted by the Assembly in December 2021, but they require acceptance by two thirds of Members and have not entered into force. Adopted is not in force - which is precisely the distinction the third part of this limb is testing.

blocks.h: 4. The ratification process - briefly, as the question asks

ol: Adoption. The text is adopted either by the relevant IMO organ - the MSC or MEPC for the technical conventions - or by a diplomatic conference convened for the purpose. Adoption creates no obligation on anybody.

Consent to be bound. A State expresses consent either by signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval - a two-stage route, where signature indicates intent and the later instrument gives consent - or, where the convention is already closed for signature, by a single act of accession. Ratification and accession have identical legal effect; they differ only in whether the State signed first.
Deposit. The instrument is deposited with the Secretary-General of IMO as depositary, who notifies all States.

Entry into force. Every convention states its own conditions. For a convention of an important technical nature these are deliberately demanding and are set on two axes at once: a minimum number of Contracting States, and a minimum share of world merchant tonnage - and often a further period, typically twelve months, after both are met.
Application. The State then gives the convention effect in national law and administers it. Until that happens the convention binds the State internationally but reaches no ship.

blocks.p: The tonnage condition is the feature to explain rather than merely state: a convention on ship construction is worthless if it binds only States with no ships. Requiring a tonnage share ensures that when the convention enters into force it governs a real proportion of the world fleet. The price is delay - as the Organization's own constitution showed, taking ten years to enter into force.

blocks.h: 5. Keeping a convention current - tacit acceptance

blocks.p: Amendment by the same explicit process proved unworkably slow; some early amendments never gathered enough acceptances to enter into force at all. The technical conventions therefore use tacit acceptance: an amendment adopted by the committee is deemed accepted on a stated date and enters into force on a second stated date, unless objections are received from a specified number of Contracting Governments before the first date.

The burden is reversed - silence is consent. This is why SOLAS and MARPOL can be kept current, and it is also why an engineer must always check which amendment set was in force at a given date rather than relying on an edition on the shelf.

blocks.h: 6. Short note - the Casualty Investigation Code

ul: Full title, the Code of the International Standards and Recommended Practices for a Safety Investigation into a Marine Casualty or Marine Incident. Adopted by resolution MSC.255(84) on 16 May 2008.

It is mandatory, and the route is worth stating because it is the pattern described in limb a): the Code is not binding of itself - SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 requires each Administration to conduct investigations in accordance with the Code, and that made Parts I and II mandatory from 1 January 2010. The underlying duties to investigate are older still - SOLAS regulation I/21, MARPOL Article 12 and UNCLOS Article 94(7).
Structure: Part I general provisions and definitions; Part II mandatory standards; Part III recommended practices.

The obligation. A marine safety investigation must be conducted into every very serious marine casualty, and into other casualties and incidents where the flag State judges an investigation likely to provide information that could prevent recurrence.
A very serious marine casualty is one involving the total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment. That definition is worth carrying verbatim.

The defining principle. The sole objective is the prevention of future casualties. A marine safety investigation is separate and independent from, and must not prejudice, any investigation for the purpose of apportioning blame or determining liability - and it is not to be conducted with that purpose. Evidence given is protected accordingly.

Who investigates. The flag State is the marine safety investigating State, with provision for a substantially interested State to participate and for States to agree which shall lead. The report is submitted to the Organization.

blocks.h: 7. Short note - the IMO Member State Audit Scheme

ul: It audits the Member State, not the ship and not the company. That is what makes it unlike every other instrument on this paper, and it follows directly from the limitation described in step 2: since IMO cannot enforce against ships, the only thing it can examine is whether the State is capable of doing so.

It began as a voluntary scheme and became mandatory from 1 January 2016, by amendments to the instruments themselves - SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines 1966 and its 1988 Protocol, Tonnage 1969 and COLREG 1972. Every Member State is now subject to audit as a condition of membership of those conventions.
The audit standard is the III Code - the IMO Instruments Implementation Code, resolution A.1070(28) of 4 December 2013. The audit does not invent criteria; it measures the State against that Code.

What the III Code requires of a State: an overall strategy for discharging its responsibilities, with a methodology to monitor and assess that the strategy is delivering; national legislation giving full and complete effect to the instruments it has accepted; adequate enforcement and administrative arrangements; and a periodic evaluation of its own performance against performance indicators. The Code is organised into the three State roles - flag, coastal and port.
What the audit examines is therefore the State's law, its administration, its resourcing, its oversight of any recognized organizations it has delegated to, and its own performance measurement.

Outcome. The audit produces findings and observations, against which the audited State prepares a corrective action plan. The Organization uses the aggregated results to identify systemic weaknesses and to direct technical cooperation and capacity building - so the Scheme feeds back into the work programme rather than functioning as a penalty.

A supporting instrument at this examination is the Assembly's non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the III Code, which identifies the auditable areas. The list in force at this sitting is resolution A.1157(32).

blocks.h: 8. What the two short notes have in common

blocks.p: Do not leave them as two disconnected paragraphs. Both are oversight mechanisms that answer the same structural weakness identified in the first limb - IMO makes rules it cannot enforce - and they attack it from opposite ends:

rows: Backwards, at a casualty that has happened
Forwards, at whether the State can prevent one
Amendments to SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG, from 1 January 2016

blocks.p: And both illustrate the pattern of limb a) exactly: a resolution of the Organization acquires binding force not from its own words but from the convention that points at it.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: This is four questions inside one, and the commonest failure is not ignorance but budgeting. Limb a) prints three separate demands - trace the origin, elaborate on authority, explain briefly the ratification process - and limb B prints two short notes. That is five deliverables against sixteen marks, so nothing can be written at length and nothing can be omitted. A candidate who writes four beautiful pages on the ratification process and two lines on the audit scheme will score less than one who writes five adequate sections.

Note the printed command in each part. "Trace" invites a short chronology, so give dates. "Elaborate" is the heaviest verb on the question and is attached to authority, so that is where the argument belongs. "Briefly" is printed against ratification, and it is an instruction - obey it. "Short notes" means bullet-form substance, not essays.

The route also does one thing a list cannot: it makes step 2 - what IMO may and may not do - carry both limbs. The audit scheme in limb B exists because of that limitation, and saying so at step 8 turns five fragments into one answer.

blocks.h: The one idea that unlocks the whole question

blocks.p: IMO regulates States, never ships. It has no inspectors, no power of detention, no power to prosecute. Everything else follows: the ratification process exists because a State must accept an instrument before it binds anything; tacit acceptance exists because that process is too slow for technical amendment; the audit scheme exists because the State is the only thing the Organization can examine; and the Casualty Investigation Code binds only because SOLAS points at it.
If you can state that sentence and then show four consequences of it, you have answered a question most candidates answer as five disconnected recitals.

blocks.h: Dates that are worth carrying

ul: 6 March 1948 - convention adopted at Geneva, creating IMCO
17 March 1958 - entry into force, ten years later. Use this as your worked example of why ratification matters
January 1959 - first Assembly
22 May 1982 - renamed International Maritime Organization
16 May 2008 - MSC.255(84) adopts the Casualty Investigation Code
1 January 2010 - the Code becomes mandatory through SOLAS XI-1/6
4 December 2013 - A.1070(28) adopts the III Code
1 January 2016 - the audit scheme becomes mandatory

blocks.h: Adopted, in force, and mandatory are three different things

blocks.p: This question rewards precision about status more than almost any other on the paper, and it offers a live example at this sitting. The amendments enlarging the IMO Council from 40 to 52 Members were adopted in December 2021 and require acceptance by two thirds of Members. At this examination they are not in force, so the Council is forty. Writing 52 is a factual error at this date; writing 40 and adding that the enlargement is adopted but awaiting acceptance is worth an extra mark and demonstrates the very distinction the ratification limb is testing.

The same discipline applies to the audit limb. The Assembly's non-exhaustive list of obligations at this sitting is A.1157(32). It was replaced by A.1187(33) on 6 December 2023 - six months after this examination. A candidate revising from a later paper would carry the wrong number. The III Code itself, A.1070(28), is unaffected: it was the lists that were replaced, not the Code.

blocks.h: The one line that must appear in the casualty note

blocks.p: That a marine safety investigation is separate and independent from, and must not prejudice, any investigation for the purpose of apportioning blame or determining liability. Its sole object is prevention. Examiners ask this because it is counter-intuitive to anyone who thinks of an investigation as finding fault, and because it explains why evidence given to a safety investigation is protected. If you carry only one sentence from the Code, carry that one - and pair it with the definition of a very serious marine casualty: total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Answering "authority vested in IMO" by listing the organs. Structure is not authority; the organs are how the authority is exercised.
Saying or implying that IMO enforces its conventions, inspects ships or detains them. It does none of these.
Writing that the Council has 52 Members. The enlargement was adopted in December 2021 and is not in force at this sitting.
Confusing ratification with accession - or treating them as legally different in effect. They differ only in whether the State signed first.
Saying entry into force depends only on a number of States. For a technical convention it also depends on a share of world tonnage.
Describing tacit acceptance as applying to the entry into force of a convention. It is the amendment procedure.
Writing the two short notes at essay length and running out of time before limb a) is finished - or the reverse.
Saying the audit scheme audits ships or companies. It audits the Member State.
Saying the audit scheme is still voluntary. It has been mandatory since 1 January 2016.
Citing A.1187(33) for the list of obligations. That is six months future at this sitting; the list here is A.1157(32).
Presenting the Casualty Investigation Code as a blame-finding instrument.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "What did the C in IMCO stand for, and why was it dropped?" Consultative. Its removal in 1982 marks the shift from advisory forum to rule-making body.
"Can IMO detain a ship?" No. It has no enforcement power over any ship whatever.

"Why did the IMO Convention take ten years to enter into force?" Because it had to be ratified by a set number of States including several with substantial tonnage - the same mechanism the limb asks you to explain.
"Difference between ratification and accession?" Only whether the State signed first. Legal effect is identical.
"Who is the depositary?" The Secretary-General of IMO.
"Under tacit acceptance, what does silence mean?" Consent. The burden is reversed.
"What is the audit standard?" The III Code, A.1070(28) - not the conventions themselves.

"Is a safety investigation report admissible to establish liability?" The investigation is separate and independent from any liability proceeding and must not prejudice it; that separation is the Code's governing principle.
"Which State investigates?" The flag State as marine safety investigating State, with provision for substantially interested States to participate.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: When and where was IMO founded, and when did the convention enter into force? Geneva, 6 March 1948; in force 17 March 1958.
What was it originally called and when did the name change? IMCO; renamed 22 May 1982.

State two purposes of the Organization. Machinery for cooperation on technical matters affecting international shipping; adoption of the highest practicable standards for safety, efficiency of navigation and prevention of pollution from ships.
How many Members has the Council and in what categories? Forty, in three categories; the enlargement to 52 is adopted and not in force.
Name the five main committees. MSC, MEPC, Legal, Technical Cooperation, Facilitation.
How does a State become bound? Signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, or accession; instrument deposited with the Secretary-General.
On what two axes are entry-into-force conditions set for a technical convention? Number of States and share of world merchant tonnage.
What is the Casualty Investigation Code and how is it mandatory? MSC.255(84) of 16 May 2008, made mandatory by SOLAS XI-1/6 from 1 January 2010.
Define a very serious marine casualty. Total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment.
What does the Member State Audit Scheme audit, and against what? The Member State's implementation of the instruments it is party to, against the III Code, A.1070(28); mandatory since 1 January 2016.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb a) is three beats: BORN - POWERS - BINDING. Born gives you 1948, 1958, 1982. Powers gives you the one sentence that carries the question - the Organization makes rules for States and cannot touch a ship. Binding gives you adopt, consent, deposit, enter into force, legislate.
For the ratification chain itself: ADOPT - ACCEPT - DEPOSIT - FORCE - LAW. For the entry-into-force test, COUNT AND TONNAGE. For amendment, SILENCE IS CONSENT.

For limb B, remember the two notes as a pair pulling in opposite directions: BACK versus FORWARD - the Code looks back at a casualty on a ship, the Scheme looks forward at the capability of a State. And each is mandatory only because a convention points at it.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: The two short notes rest on the stronger evidence. The Casualty Investigation Code was consulted in the held resolution MSC.255(84), and the SOLAS, MARPOL and UNCLOS bases and the Code's definitions come from MIW's own verification record for a question where they were read. The III Code, A.1070(28), and the whole mandating chain come from MIW verification records for two sittings of the III Code question, one of them August 2023, two months after this examination and therefore in the same regulatory position.

Limb a) is weaker and says so. MIW holds no copy of the Convention on the International Maritime Organization. The 1948 adoption, the 1958 entry into force, the 1982 renaming, the purposes of the Organization and the composition of the organs are stated from authoritative secondary description. No article of the IMO Convention is cited by number and no text of it is quoted. Likewise MIW holds no resolution setting out the Framework and Procedures for the Audit Scheme, so the Scheme is described from what is verified - the III Code as its standard and the mandating chain - and no resolution number is asserted for the Framework, and no audit periodicity is claimed.

Two currency instructions for a later editor. Do not update the Council to 52 Members unless it is established that the A.1152(32) amendments had entered into force by June 2023 - they had not. And do not replace A.1157(32) with A.1187(33): the later list was adopted on 6 December 2023, six months after this sitting. Note carefully that only the lists were replaced; the III Code itself is unaffected, and an editor who reverses the Code's own number has misunderstood the change.

notes: TWO REVERSALS, BOTH ON THE 33RD ASSEMBLY BOUNDARY, AND BOTH SIT ON THE AUDIT LIMB. The 33rd Assembly adopted its resolutions on 6 DECEMBER 2023 - SIX MONTHS AFTER this examination. The non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the III Code is therefore A.1157(32) at this sitting and NOT A.1187(33). Where the answer needed a worked example of an Assembly resolution it used A.1155(32), the 2021 PSC Procedures, and not A.1185(33). Any donor object written for a 2024 sitting or later carries the 33rd Assembly numbers and they are not inherited.

THE III CODE ITSELF IS NOT AFFECTED AND THE DISTINCTION IS KEPT EXPLICITLY. A.1070(28) of 4 December 2013 stands unrevoked and mandatory from 1 January 2016. IT WAS THE LISTS THAT WERE REPLACED, NOT THE CODE. This is recorded in the answer itself because an editor who reverses the Code's own number has misunderstood the reversal in the opposite direction.

A LIVE ADOPTED-BUT-NOT-IN-FORCE ITEM SITS INSIDE LIMB A, AND IT IS THE BEST TEACHING EXAMPLE ON THE QUESTION. Resolution A.1152(32) of December 2021 adopted amendments to the IMO Convention enlarging the Council from 40 to 52 Members. They require acceptance by TWO THIRDS of Members and HAD NOT ENTERED INTO FORCE at this sitting. The Council is therefore stated as FORTY, with the enlargement described as adopted and awaiting acceptance. This is checked rather than recalled, and it is verified against MIW's record for the SEPTEMBER 2023 sitting of the IMO-structure question - three months after this one and therefore in the same position.

THE CASUALTY LIMB CARRIES NO TEMPORAL RISK. MSC.255(84) was adopted 16 May 2008 and the Code has been mandatory through SOLAS XI-1/6 since 1 JANUARY 2010 - THIRTEEN YEARS before this sitting. SOLAS I/21, MARPOL Article 12 and UNCLOS Article 94(7) are older still. Nothing here entered force after this sitting and nothing could be carried back.

THE MANDATING CHAIN IS TEMPORALLY STABLE AND NEEDS NO REVERSAL. A.1083(28), A.1084(28), A.1085(28), MSC.366(93), MSC.373(93), MSC.374(93), MSC.375(93), MEPC.246(66) and MEPC.247(66) all pre-date this sitting by years, and the audit scheme's mandatory application from 1 January 2016 is seven years old at this examination.

THE ORIGIN MATERIAL IS TEMPORALLY INERT. 1948, 1958, 1959 and 1982 are historical facts that no later instrument moves. This is the one part of the question a donor from any sitting could have supplied unchanged - and no donor holds it.
THE JANUARY 2023 LIMB DONOR RUNS THE RIGHT WAY. QP2301-Q7 is five months earlier in the same year, inside the same regime, and required no reversal on the casualty material.

NO CLAIM DEPENDS ON THE EXAMINATION DAY WITHIN JUNE 2023. Nothing on this question moved during the sitting month. The two day-dependent June 2023 events recorded in the paper anchor - the BBNJ adoption of 19 June and the Hong Kong Convention accessions of 26 June - touch nothing here.
MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 governs at this sitting and the 2025 Act is thirty-three months future. Neither is load-bearing on this question, which is entirely international.

DONOR CONTAMINATION SWEEP: CLEAN, AND THE PRINCIPAL RISK WAS SCALE RATHER THAN LAW. The January 2023 casualty question devotes an entire 16-mark question to material that is a QUARTER of one limb here. The donor was deliberately compressed rather than reproduced; carrying it across in full would have starved the other four deliverables. The entry-into-force family was compressed for the same reason, against the printed word 'briefly'.

questions.understand_first: The question hides one idea behind four tasks. That idea is that the body which writes the world's shipping rules cannot enforce a single one of them. It was set up after the war as a forum where governments could agree technical standards for ships trading internationally, and for its first three decades even its name said it was only there to consult. What it does is produce texts. Those texts do nothing until a government decides to be bound by one, tells the depositary so, and then writes it into its own law and polices it. Everything else in the question is a consequence of that. The long formal process by which a State accepts a text exists because acceptance is the only thing that makes the text law. A shortcut had to be invented for keeping those texts up to date, because the full process was so slow that improvements were arriving years after the accidents that prompted them; so the rule was reversed, and a proposed change now takes effect unless enough governments object. And because the organisation can only ever look at governments, its two oversight tools both point at government rather than at industry: one examines what went wrong after a ship is lost, on the strict understanding that it is looking for causes and not for someone to punish, and the other examines whether a government is actually equipped to do what it promised when it accepted the texts in the first place. Hold that single thread and the four parts stop being four things to remember.
questions.memory_cue: Limb a) is three beats - BORN (1), POWERS (2), BINDING (4) - with the organs slotted between as the machinery (3) and tacit acceptance as the shortcut (5). Born is 48, 58, 82. Powers is one sentence: rules for States, never for ships. Binding is ADOPT, ACCEPT, DEPOSIT, FORCE, LAW (4), and the test is COUNT AND TONNAGE (4). Amendment is SILENCE IS CONSENT (5). Limb B is a pair pulling opposite ways - BACK (6) versus FORWARD (7), ship versus State - and they meet at (8).
