quick_revision.critical_regulation: The Casualty Investigation Code, resolution MSC.255(84) of 16 May 2008, is made mandatory by SOLAS regulation XI-1/6, which requires each Administration to conduct investigations of marine casualties and marine incidents in accordance with the Code, with effect from 1 January 2010. The IMO Member State Audit Scheme became mandatory on 1 January 2016 through amendments to SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, the Load Lines Convention and its 1988 Protocol, the Tonnage Convention and COLREG, and applies the IMO Instruments Implementation Code, resolution A.1070(28) of 4 December 2013, as its audit standard.
quick_revision.major_trap: Budgeting. Five printed deliverables against sixteen marks - trace the origin, elaborate on authority, explain the ratification process briefly, and two short notes - and the usual failure is writing two of them well and running out of time. The substantive traps are: answering "authority" with a description of the organs, when the answer is that IMO regulates States and cannot enforce anything against a ship; writing the Council as 52 Members, when the enlargement adopted in December 2021 is not in force at this sitting; saying the audit scheme is voluntary or that it audits ships, when it has audited States compulsorily since 1 January 2016 against the III Code; citing A.1187(33) for the list of obligations, which is six months future here - the list is A.1157(32); and presenting the Casualty Investigation Code as a blame-finding instrument when its governing principle is that it is separate from and must not prejudice any liability proceeding.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the IMO origin, authority, ratification and two short notes question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The origin, 1948 to 1982. 2 The authority, and the limitation that IMO cannot enforce against ships. 3 The organs. 4 The ratification process, briefly. 5 Tacit acceptance. 6 Short note: Casualty Investigation Code. 7 Short note: Member State Audit Scheme. 8 What the two notes have in common.
retrieval_cards.why: Five printed deliverables; the route exists to stop one of them eating the others.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Trace the origin of IMO in four dates.
retrieval_cards.answer: 6 March 1948 - the convention establishing IMCO is adopted at the UN Maritime Conference in Geneva. 17 March 1958 - it enters into force, ten years later. January 1959 - the first Assembly meets. 22 May 1982 - the Organization is renamed the International Maritime Organization.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Trace' invites a chronology, and the ten-year gap is the worked example the ratification limb needs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What authority is actually vested in IMO?
retrieval_cards.answer: Authority to provide machinery for cooperation among Governments on technical matters affecting international shipping, and to encourage and facilitate the adoption of the highest practicable standards for maritime safety, efficiency of navigation and prevention of pollution from ships, with the related administrative and legal matters. It is legislative in form and wholly indirect in effect: IMO adopts instruments but cannot enforce any of them against any ship. It regulates States, and enforcement rests with flag, port and coastal States.
retrieval_cards.why: Answering this with a list of organs is the commonest way to lose the heaviest command verb on the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many Members does the IMO Council have at this sitting, and what is the trap?
retrieval_cards.answer: Forty, elected in three categories. Resolution A.1152(32) of December 2021 adopted amendments enlarging it to 52, but they require acceptance by two thirds of Members and had not entered into force at this examination. Adopted is not in force.
retrieval_cards.why: It is a factual error at this date and it is also the exact distinction the ratification limb is testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain the ratification process from adoption to application.
retrieval_cards.answer: The text is adopted by the relevant IMO organ or by a diplomatic conference, which binds nobody. A State then consents to be bound by signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, or by accession where signature is closed - both have identical legal effect. The instrument is deposited with the Secretary-General. The convention enters into force on its own conditions, which for a technical convention require both a number of Contracting States and a share of world merchant tonnage. The State then legislates.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem prints 'briefly', so this is the whole of it - five beats, no more.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why do technical conventions set an entry-into-force condition on tonnage as well as on the number of States?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a convention regulating ship construction or operation is worthless if it binds only States with few or no ships. Requiring a share of world merchant tonnage ensures that when it enters into force it governs a real proportion of the world fleet. The price is delay - the IMO Convention itself took ten years.
retrieval_cards.why: Explaining the reason rather than reciting the condition is what lifts this limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is tacit acceptance and why was it introduced?
retrieval_cards.answer: An amendment adopted by the committee is deemed accepted on a stated date and enters into force on a second stated date, unless objections are received from a specified number of Contracting Governments before the first. It was introduced because explicit amendment was so slow that some amendments never gathered enough acceptances to enter into force at all. The burden is reversed - silence is consent.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the mechanism that keeps SOLAS and MARPOL current, and it explains why the amendment set in force at a date must always be checked.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Casualty Investigation Code and how did it become mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Code of the International Standards and Recommended Practices for a Safety Investigation into a Marine Casualty or Marine Incident, adopted by resolution MSC.255(84) on 16 May 2008. It is not binding of itself: SOLAS regulation XI-1/6 requires each Administration to conduct investigations in accordance with it, which made Parts I and II mandatory from 1 January 2010. The older underlying duties are SOLAS I/21, MARPOL Article 12 and UNCLOS Article 94(7).
retrieval_cards.why: It is the worked example of the pattern in limb a) - a resolution binds because a convention points at it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the governing principle of a marine safety investigation, and how is a very serious marine casualty defined?
retrieval_cards.answer: Its sole objective is the prevention of future casualties. It is separate and independent from, and must not prejudice, any investigation for the purpose of apportioning blame or determining liability, and it is not conducted for that purpose. A very serious marine casualty is one involving the total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment.
retrieval_cards.why: Counter-intuitive to anyone who thinks an investigation finds fault, and it explains why evidence to a safety investigation is protected.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the IMO Member State Audit Scheme audit, against what standard, and since when has it been compulsory?
retrieval_cards.answer: It audits the Member State - its law, administration, resourcing, oversight of recognized organizations and its own performance measurement - and not ships or companies. The standard applied is the IMO Instruments Implementation Code, resolution A.1070(28) of 4 December 2013. It began voluntary and became mandatory on 1 January 2016 through amendments to SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines and its 1988 Protocol, Tonnage and COLREG.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying it audits ships, or that it is still voluntary, are the two standard errors.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Assembly resolution lists the auditable obligations at a June 2023 sitting, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: A.1157(32). The later list, A.1187(33), was adopted on 6 December 2023 - six months after this examination - and must not be cited here. Note that only the lists were replaced: the III Code itself, A.1070(28), stands unrevoked, so reversing the Code's own number is an error in the opposite direction.
retrieval_cards.why: Material revised from a 2024 or later paper carries the 33rd Assembly numbers throughout.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do the Casualty Investigation Code and the Member State Audit Scheme have in common?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both are oversight mechanisms answering the same weakness - IMO makes rules it cannot enforce. The Code looks backwards at a casualty on a ship, for prevention and never for blame; the Scheme looks forwards at whether a State is capable of preventing one, and produces corrective action. Both are mandatory only because conventions point at them.
retrieval_cards.why: It converts two disconnected short notes into a single argument and ties limb B back to limb a).

reverify_before_publication.claim: The IMO Council has forty Members at this sitting; the enlargement to 52 under A.1152(32) is adopted and NOT in force
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT ADVANCE THIS. The amendments were adopted in December 2021 and require acceptance by two thirds of Members. An editor working from a later source may find the Council described as 52 and would introduce a factual error at this date. Equally, if it is ever established that the amendments entered into force before June 2023, this must be corrected - but only on evidence, not on the currency of a later document.

reverify_before_publication.why: The 33rd Assembly adopted its resolutions on 6 December 2023, six months after this examination. Any donor or revision source from 2024 onward carries the 33rd Assembly numbers. Note the asymmetry: the LISTS were replaced, the III CODE was not, so A.1070(28) must not be reversed in the other direction.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The Member State Audit Scheme has been mandatory since 1 January 2016 and applies the III Code as its audit standard
reverify_before_publication.why: Stable and seven years old at this sitting, but recorded because the pre-2016 voluntary description is still in circulation in older textbooks and an editor working from one would reintroduce it.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The origin, purposes and organ composition of IMO
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW holds no copy of the Convention on the International Maritime Organization. blocks.h: 1. Where these two clauses live, and why the question pairs them

blocks.p: The two are not the same kind of thing, and saying so is the opening mark.

ul: The Running Down Clause (RDC) is a clause in a hull and machinery policy. In the Institute Time Clauses - Hulls it appears under the heading "3/4ths Collision Liability"; "Running Down Clause" is the older market name for the same provision. They are the same clause.

General average is not a policy clause at all. It is a rule of maritime law, given effect in practice by the York-Antwerp Rules, which are a contractual code incorporated by the contract of affreightment. The policy then decides how much of the resulting liability the insurer pays.

blocks.p: The examiner pairs them because both are places where the hull policy stops and the P&I club begins. The question "how are claims treated by H&M as well as P&I" is therefore one question asked twice, and the answer in each case is about where the line falls.

blocks.h: 2. The Running Down Clause - what the hull policy covers

blocks.p: The hull policy is primarily a property policy on the assured's own ship. The collision liability clause is the one place where it also takes on liability to a third party. Where the insured vessel comes into collision with another vessel and the assured becomes liable in damages, underwriters indemnify him for three fourths of the sums paid in respect of:

ol: loss of or damage to the other vessel or property on board her;
delay to or loss of use of that other vessel or her property;
general average, salvage, or salvage under contract of that other vessel or her property.

blocks.p: Four features are worth stating explicitly because each carries a mark:

ul: It responds in addition to any claim for damage to the insured vessel herself - the two are separate recoveries under one policy.
The clause is limited by reference to the insured value; it is not open-ended.
It ordinarily also covers the assured's legal costs of contesting liability, with underwriters' consent.

Adjustment is normally on the cross-liabilities principle - each ship's liability to the other is calculated in full and then set off - rather than on the single balance actually paid. The exception is where one or both owners are entitled to limit liability, when the single-liability basis applies.

blocks.p: One historical point explains the fraction. Underwriters deliberately left one quarter uninsured so that the shipowner retained a real financial interest in defending the claim and in navigating prudently. It is the classic co-insurance device.

blocks.h: 3. What the Running Down Clause excludes, and where the rest goes

blocks.p: This is the heart of the printed question, because the exclusions are, almost item for item, the P&I book.

rows: Damage to the other vessel and property on board her
Loss of use / delay of the other vessel
General average and salvage of the other vessel
Removal of obstructions or wreck, and the wreck of the other ship
Damage to fixed and floating objects - piers, jetties, buoys, cables, moorings - and to any property other than the other vessel
Cargo or other property on the insured vessel, and the assured's own engagements
Loss of life, personal injury or illness
Pollution or contamination of any kind, other than damage to the other vessel or the property on her

blocks.p: Two consequences the examiner is looking for:

ol: A ship that strikes a jetty has no claim at all under the collision liability clause, however large the damage, because the clause responds only to collision with another vessel. The whole liability is the club's. This is the single most common misunderstanding of the RDC.

The P&I club therefore performs two distinct functions here: it insures the one fourth the hull policy does not, and it insures the excluded heads in full. Saying both is worth more than saying either.

blocks.p: Note also that some modern hull forms - and many owners by special agreement - provide four fourths collision liability, in which case the club's first function disappears but the second remains. The policy wording governs.

blocks.h: 4. General Average Expenses - what they are

blocks.p: The stem does not ask for a definition of general average, so state it compactly and move to the treatment. Under Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules there is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety, for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.

ul: A general average sacrifice is property given up - cargo jettisoned, machinery damaged in refloating, fire-fighting damage to sound cargo.

General average expenditure, which is what this question names, is money spent - salvage or towage engaged for the common safety, and above all port of refuge expenses: the cost of putting in, discharging, storing and reloading cargo, wages and maintenance of crew and fuel and stores consumed during the detention.

The loss is then shared rateably between ship, cargo and freight at risk, in proportion to contributory values ascertained by an average adjuster at the termination of the adventure. No formula or figure is given here - contributory values are case-specific.
The critical contrast is with particular average: accidental, uncompensated partial loss that lies where it falls, borne by the owner of the property damaged and by his own insurer alone.

blocks.p: Which edition of the York-Antwerp Rules applies - 1994, 2004 or 2016 - is a matter of the contract of affreightment, not of the date. All three are in use, and an answer that asserts one universally is wrong.

blocks.h: 5. How H&M and P&I each treat a general average claim

rows: General average sacrifice of the ship - machinery damaged in refloating, structure damaged fighting a fire
Paid in full as damage to the insured property, without waiting for the adjustment
The ship's proportion of general average contribution, and of salvage charges
Paid, under the general average and salvage clause of the hull policy
The ship is under-insured - the insured value is less than the contributory value
Pays only the proportion the insured value bears to the contributory value. The balance is the owner's
Some clubs cover the shortfall by rule or by special cover; it is not automatic
Cargo's proportion cannot be recovered because the owner is in breach of the contract of carriage - typically unseaworthiness - so cargo successfully resists contribution
Not engaged. The hull policy insures the ship's share, not the owner's failure to recover others'
This is the club's classic exposure - unrecoverable general average, together with the owner's liability for the cargo damage that produced the breach
Cargo's proportion of a sacrifice of cargo
Cargo's own underwriters, through the adjustment

blocks.p: The organising sentence, and it is the answer to the printed question: the hull underwriter pays the ship's own share of general average; the club pays where the general average machinery fails the owner - because he cannot enforce contribution, or because his own breach of contract has destroyed the right to it. Rule D preserves the right to contribution notwithstanding fault, but expressly leaves intact any remedy against the party at fault, which is exactly the gap the club fills.

blocks.h: 6. Damage found in dry dock a year later - is it admissible?

blocks.p: Yes, in principle - provided the assured can prove it. The governing point is a distinction the question is built to test:

ul: A claim attaches to the policy that was on risk when the damage was SUSTAINED, not to the policy in force when it was DISCOVERED. A marine policy responds to a fortuity occurring during its currency; late discovery does not defeat the claim. So the claim lies against the underwriters on risk at the date of the incident, even though that policy year has since closed.

The burden of proof is on the assured, and it is a real burden at this remove. He must show, on the balance of probabilities, that the damage was caused by an insured peril and that it occurred during that policy period. After a year, and after a further year's trading, both are harder to establish - which is a practical answer worth giving.

Evidence. The dry-dock survey report, photographs, the deck and engine log entries and any incident report for the original casualty, the previous dry-docking or in-water survey showing the area sound, and class records. The best evidence is a documented incident already notified.

Notice. Hull policies require prompt notice so that underwriters may appoint their own surveyor before repairs are put in hand. Where notice is not given in time to allow that survey, the clauses provide for a reduction from the ascertained claim. This is where a late-discovered claim is most often prejudiced - not by admissibility but by the deduction and by the loss of the underwriter's opportunity to survey.

Time. A claim identified a year after the incident will ordinarily be well within any applicable limitation or contractual suit-time period, but the assured must check both the policy and the applicable limitation law.
Deductible. The policy deductible applies to each accident or occurrence, so the claim is only worth pursuing if the damage exceeds it.

blocks.p: So the answer to the first part of limb b) is: admissible against the policy on risk at the time of the incident, subject to proof of an insured peril within that period, and subject to any deduction for want of notice.

blocks.h: 7. The unrepaired damage claim, and how its value is ascertained

blocks.p: The owner now elects not to repair, because Class is unaffected. He may still claim. An indemnity policy does not require the assured to spend the money before he is indemnified - it requires him to have suffered a loss.

The measure is statutory and is restated in the hull clauses. Under the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, section 69 - and the identically worded section of the Marine Insurance Act 1906 from which the Indian Act is drawn:

ul: where the ship has been repaired, the assured recovers the reasonable cost of repairs, less the customary deductions;
where she has been partially repaired, the cost of those repairs plus depreciation for the unrepaired part;

where she has NOT been repaired and has not been sold in her damaged state during the risk, the assured is entitled to be indemnified for the REASONABLE DEPRECIATION arising from the unrepaired damage, BUT NOT EXCEEDING the reasonable cost of repairing such damage.

blocks.p: The Unrepaired Damage clause of the hull policy restates this and adds two limits:

ol: the measure is the reasonable depreciation in the market value of the vessel at the time the insurance terminates, capped at the reasonable cost of repairs;

underwriters are not liable for unrepaired damage at all in the event of a subsequent TOTAL LOSS - whether or not that total loss is covered - sustained during the period of the insurance or any extension of it; and liability is in any event capped at the insured value.

blocks.p: How the value is ascertained in practice:

ol: Establish the repair cost first. Obtain repair specifications and yard quotations for the damage as surveyed. This fixes the ceiling on the claim and is the figure the adjuster starts from.

Then establish depreciation, which is the actual measure. This is a valuation exercise, not an engineering one: the vessel is valued in her sound condition and again with the damage disclosed, at the same date, by an independent valuer or broker with reference to comparable sales in the market for that type, age and trade. The difference is the depreciation.

Test it against a purchaser's view. The question is what a willing buyer would deduct knowing the damage exists - which is why unaffected Class status matters so much to the answer: if Class is unaffected and the damage does not impair earning capacity, a buyer may deduct little or nothing, and the depreciation - and therefore the claim - may be small or even nil.
Apply the caps. The recovery is the depreciation, but never more than the reasonable cost of repair and never more than the insured value.

Settle by agreement or by adjustment. In practice underwriters and the owner very often compromise on an agreed figure, or the owner elects to repair at the next scheduled docking and claim the repair cost instead.

blocks.p: Two warnings to close on, because they are what makes this a decision rather than a formality. If the vessel becomes a total loss within the same policy period the unrepaired damage claim is lost entirely - so deferring the repair transfers a real risk to the owner. And if the damage is left and later worsens, the additional deterioration is not an insured peril; underwriters answer for the damage as it stood at the casualty, not for the consequences of the owner's decision to live with it.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: This is one of the few questions on the paper that prints its own mark split - (8) and (8) - so the budget is fixed and there is no excuse for spending twelve marks' worth of writing on general average. Limb a) contains three demands: define the Running Down Clause, define general average expenses, and say how claims under each are treated by H&M as well as P&I. The third demand is the one that carries the marks, and it is the one most candidates answer in a single sentence after two long definitions.

The route therefore front-loads the definitions to a minimum and gives two tables to the allocation - one for collision liability, one for general average. A table is the right form because the examiner's question is a mapping question: for each head of loss, which market pays? Prose obscures that; a table makes every row a countable proposition.

Limb b) is two legal questions wearing one paragraph, and separating them is the whole skill. First, is it admissible - which turns on when the damage was sustained, not when it was found. Second, what is the measure of indemnity if it is not repaired - which turns on the depreciation rule. A candidate who runs them together answers only the second and loses half the limb.

blocks.h: The name is the trap

blocks.p: Many candidates have learned the modern clause heading, 3/4ths Collision Liability, and have never met the older market name. Others know "Running Down Clause" from an oral and do not recognise it in a policy. They are the same provision. Say so in your first line; it costs six words and it tells the examiner immediately that you know what you are describing.

blocks.h: The exclusion that decides the question

blocks.p: The collision liability clause responds only to collision with ANOTHER VESSEL. Strike a jetty, a buoy, a submarine cable, a mooring dolphin or a rig, and the hull policy's collision clause does not respond at all - not three quarters of it, none of it. The entire liability is the club's, under fixed and floating object cover.

Learn the exclusions as a list, because between them they are almost the whole P&I book: wreck removal · fixed and floating objects and any property other than the other vessel · cargo and property on your own ship · loss of life, injury and illness · pollution. Then state the club's two roles: it insures the missing quarter, and it insures the excluded heads in full.

blocks.h: Why three quarters?

blocks.p: Because underwriters deliberately left the shipowner uninsured for a quarter so that he retained a genuine financial stake in defending the claim and in careful navigation. It is co-insurance in its purest form, and giving the reason rather than the fraction alone is what turns a remembered number into an understood one. Add that some modern forms provide four fourths, so the fraction is a market convention and not a rule of law.

blocks.h: The one distinction limb b) is really testing

blocks.p: SUSTAINED versus DISCOVERED. A marine policy answers for a fortuity occurring during its currency. Damage caused by an insured peril in year one and found in dry dock in year two is a claim on year one's policy, not year two's. Late discovery does not defeat the claim - it makes it harder to prove and it exposes the assured to the deduction for want of notice.

That last point is where the real prejudice lies, and examiners like it: the problem with a late claim is usually not admissibility but that underwriters were denied the chance to survey before repairs, and the clauses provide for a reduction from the ascertained claim in consequence.

blocks.h: The unrepaired damage rule, in one line

blocks.p: Reasonable depreciation arising from the unrepaired damage, not exceeding the reasonable cost of repairing it. That is section 69(3) of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, and the hull clause restates it as depreciation in market value at the time the insurance terminates, capped at repair cost and at the insured value.

Then the two conditions that make it a commercial decision rather than a formality: no recovery for unrepaired damage if the vessel becomes a total loss within the same policy period - whether or not that loss is covered - and no cover for subsequent deterioration, because underwriters answer for the damage as it stood at the casualty. Deferring the repair moves real risk onto the owner.

blocks.h: Why 'Class unaffected' is in the question

blocks.p: It is not decoration. Depreciation is measured by what a willing buyer would deduct knowing the damage exists. If Class is unaffected and earning capacity is unimpaired, a buyer may deduct very little - so the depreciation, and therefore the claim, may be small or even nil, even though the repair would cost a great deal. Saying that explicitly shows you understand that the measure is a market measure and not an engineering one, and it is the most discriminating single sentence available on this limb.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Not recognising that the Running Down Clause and the 3/4ths Collision Liability clause are the same provision.
Saying the collision clause covers striking a jetty, buoy or cable. It responds only to collision with another vessel.
Saying P&I covers only the missing quarter. It also covers the excluded heads in full.
Treating general average as a policy clause. It is a rule of maritime law given effect by a contractual code.
Asserting that a particular York-Antwerp edition applies. 1994, 2004 and 2016 are all current and the contract selects.
Confusing general average expenditure with sacrifice, or general with particular average.
Saying the hull underwriter pays general average in full regardless of value. If the vessel is under-insured he pays only the proportion the insured value bears to the contributory value.
Missing unrecoverable general average - the club's classic general average exposure, arising where the owner's own breach of the contract of carriage defeats his right to contribution.
In limb b), answering that the claim fails because it was discovered late. It attaches to the policy on risk when the damage was sustained.
Answering limb b) with the cost of repair. Unrepaired, the measure is depreciation, capped at repair cost.
Omitting the subsequent total loss rule, which is what makes the decision not to repair a risk.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Your ship damages a berth. What does the collision clause pay?" Nothing. Not a vessel.
"Why three quarters?" Deliberate co-insurance to keep the owner interested in the defence and in prudent navigation.
"Cross-liabilities or single liability?" Cross-liabilities normally; single liability where one or both owners limit.
"Does the collision clause come out of the sum insured for hull damage?" No - it responds in addition, subject to its own limit.

"Who pays cargo's share of general average if cargo successfully resists because the ship was unseaworthy?" Nobody recovers it from cargo; the owner bears it and looks to his club for unrecoverable general average.
"The ship is insured for less than her contributory value. What does the hull policy pay on general average?" Only the proportion the insured value bears to the contributory value.
"Damage found two years later - which policy?" The one on risk when the damage was sustained.
"You do not repair. How much do you get?" The reasonable depreciation, not exceeding the reasonable cost of repair.

"The ship is then lost in the same policy year. What happens to the unrepaired damage claim?" It is lost - underwriters are not liable for unrepaired damage where a subsequent total loss is sustained in the period.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: What is the Running Down Clause and what is it called in the Institute clauses? The collision liability clause; 3/4ths Collision Liability.
Name three heads it indemnifies. Damage to the other vessel and property on her; loss of use or delay of that vessel; general average, salvage or salvage under contract of that vessel.
Name three heads it excludes. Wreck removal; fixed and floating objects and any property other than the other vessel; loss of life and personal injury; pollution; cargo on your own ship.

Define a general average act. An extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety, to preserve from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
Give three examples of general average expenditure. Salvage or towage engaged for the common safety; port of refuge expenses; crew wages and maintenance and fuel during the detention.
Who prepares the adjustment and on what basis? An average adjuster, on contributory values at the termination of the adventure.

What is unrecoverable general average? The proportion the owner cannot recover from cargo because his own breach of the contract of carriage - typically unseaworthiness - defeats the right to contribution. It falls to the club.
Damage discovered a year later - is it covered? Yes, against the policy on risk when it was sustained, if he can prove an insured peril in that period; subject to any deduction for late notice.

How is an unrepaired damage claim valued? Reasonable depreciation in market value, established by valuation of the vessel sound and damaged, capped at the reasonable cost of repair and at the insured value.
What defeats it entirely? A subsequent total loss during the same policy period, whether or not covered.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: For limb a) hold two lines and two lists. Line one: RDC is a policy clause; general average is a rule of law. Line two: both are where the hull policy stops and the club begins.

For the collision clause, remember what it pays as DAMAGE, DELAY, SALVAGE - of the OTHER SHIP, and what it does not as WRECK, OBJECTS, OWN CARGO, PEOPLE, POLLUTION. For general average, SHIP'S SHARE to the hull; SHORTFALL and UNRECOVERABLE to the club.

For limb b), two questions in order: WHEN WAS IT SUSTAINED, then WHAT IS IT WORTH UNREPAIRED. And for the measure, one sentence: depreciation, capped at repair cost - with the killer condition, no total loss in the period.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: This question carries the weakest evidential position on the paper and the answer says so rather than disguising it. The True Source corpus consumed for this paper holds no marine insurance material whatever - no Institute Time Clauses or any other hull clause set, no York-Antwerp Rules text, no Marine Insurance Act 1963 and no adjusting practice material. That is the same position recorded for the April 2023 sitting of the general average question.

Three consequences were applied deliberately. No clause wording is quoted anywhere - every provision is described by effect. Clause numbering is given as the standard Institute Time Clauses - Hulls numbering and is flagged as varying between forms, so that no candidate memorises a number his own policy does not use. And no figure is asserted - no deductible, no contributory-value formula, no percentage for the notice-of-claim reduction, and no limitation period in years - with the single exception of the three-quarters and one-quarter proportions, which are the defining characteristic of the very clause the question names, and which are themselves qualified by the note that some modern forms give four fourths.

Two positions are stated as contract-selected rather than date-selected, and that is a finding rather than an evasion: which York-Antwerp edition applies, and which hull clause set applies. Both depend on the contract in the particular case, and an answer asserting one universally would be wrong at this sitting as at any other.

notes: NOTHING ON THIS QUESTION MOVED AT OR NEAR THIS SITTING, AND THAT WAS ESTABLISHED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 was in force sixty years before this examination. The Institute Time Clauses - Hulls sets of 1983 and 1995 and the International Hull Clauses 2003 all long pre-date it. The York-Antwerp Rules editions of 1994, 2004 and 2016 all pre-date it. No instrument relied on here entered force, was amended or was superseded during 2023.

THE APPLICABLE YORK-ANTWERP EDITION IS CONTRACT-SELECTED, NOT DATE-SELECTED, AND THIS IS THE ONE TEMPORAL FINDING WORTH RECORDING. A sitting date does NOT determine which edition governs; the contract of affreightment does. The answer states that position rather than asserting one edition. This is inherited as a verified finding from the APRIL 2023 sitting of the general average question, two months before this one, whose December 2023 same-year cross-check settled the same point for the year.

THE APPLICABLE HULL CLAUSE SET IS LIKEWISE CONTRACT-SELECTED. The 1983 and 1995 Institute Time Clauses and the International Hull Clauses 2003 are all in use at this sitting. The answer identifies each provision by FUNCTION and flags the numbering as varying between forms, which is the only defensible position where MIW holds no clause set.

THE LATER DONOR REQUIRED NO REVERSAL, AND THAT WAS CHECKED. QP2407-Q8 is JULY 2024, thirteen months AFTER this sitting. Its collision-clause material rests on market practice and clause structure that did not change between the two dates, and it asserts no dated instrument that would need reversing. The general average family runs from April 2023 to March 2026 and is similarly stable.

THE APRIL 2023 GENERAL AVERAGE DONOR RUNS THE RIGHT WAY. QP2304-Q3 is two months EARLIER than this sitting, in the same year and the same regime. Its verification record is the closest available authority for the 2023 position and required no adjustment.

NO CLAIM DEPENDS ON THE EXAMINATION DAY WITHIN JUNE 2023. Nothing on this question moved during the sitting month, and neither of the two day-dependent June 2023 events recorded in the paper anchor touches marine insurance.

MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 governs at this sitting; the 2025 Act commenced 15 March 2026, thirty-three months later. Neither is load-bearing here - the applicable Indian statute on this question is the MARINE INSURANCE ACT, 1963, which is a separate enactment and is unaffected by the Merchant Shipping Act change. That distinction is recorded because a sweep keyed to 'Indian statute' would otherwise flag it.

DONOR CONTAMINATION SWEEP: CLEAN. The risk here was not temporal but definitional - importing the general average family's full treatment of what general average IS, when this stem asks only how a claim under it is TREATED. The family was deliberately compressed to Rule A and the sacrifice/expenditure distinction, and the space given to allocation instead.

questions.understand_first: Both halves of this question are really about one boundary: where the cover on the ship herself ends and the cover on the owner's liabilities to other people begins. A hull policy is fundamentally a policy on a piece of property. It makes one deliberate exception, taking on the owner's liability when his ship hits another ship - and even then it pays only three quarters of it, because the underwriters wanted the owner to keep some of his own money at stake so he would fight the claim properly. Everything the clause leaves out - striking a pier rather than a ship, wreck removal, injury to people, oil in the water, the cargo in his own holds - belongs to the mutual association that covers the residue of his liabilities. General average is a different animal that ends up at the same boundary: an old rule that when something is deliberately given up or spent to save everybody's property from a common danger, everybody whose property was saved shares the cost. The hull policy pays the ship's own share of that; the club steps in where the sharing breaks down, typically because the owner's own failings have given the cargo owners a good reason not to pay. The second half then asks a question about time and about what a loss is actually worth. Damage belongs to the year it happened in, not the year somebody noticed it. And if the owner decides to live with it because nothing important is affected, he is not paid what the repair would have cost - he is paid what the damage has knocked off the value of the ship, which may be very much less, and which may be nothing at all if a buyer would not care.
questions.memory_cue: Two lines carry limb a): a policy clause versus a rule of law, and both mark WHERE HULL STOPS AND CLUB BEGINS (1). The clause pays DAMAGE, DELAY, SALVAGE - OF THE OTHER SHIP (2); it refuses WRECK, OBJECTS, OWN CARGO, PEOPLE, POLLUTION (3). General average is SACRIFICE versus EXPENDITURE (4), and the split is SHIP'S SHARE to hull, SHORTFALL and UNRECOVERABLE to club (5). Limb b) is two questions in order: SUSTAINED NOT DISCOVERED (6), then DEPRECIATION CAPPED AT REPAIR COST (7) - and the killer, NO TOTAL LOSS IN THE PERIOD (7).

Responds in addition to hull damage; limited by insured value; covers legal costs with consent; adjusted on cross-liabilities (single liability where limitation applies). The 1/4 is left uninsured deliberately - co-insurance. EXCLUDED (and therefore P&I in full): wreck removal · FIXED AND FLOATING OBJECTS and any property other than the other vessel · cargo on your OWN ship · loss of life, injury, illness · pollution. Strike a jetty and the clause pays NOTHING - not a vessel. Club's two roles: the missing quarter, and the excluded heads in full. Some forms give 4/4. Expenditure = salvage/towage for common safety, and above all port of refuge expenses (in, discharge, store, reload, crew wages and maintenance, fuel). Shared on contributory values by an average adjuster. TREATMENT: H&M pays GA sacrifice of the ship in full, and the ship's proportion of GA contribution and salvage - but if under-insured, only the proportion insured value bears to contributory value. P&I pays the 1/4 collision, the excluded heads, and UNRECOVERABLE GENERAL AVERAGE - the share the owner cannot get from cargo because his own breach of the contract of carriage (unseaworthiness) defeated it. Rule D keeps the right to contribution but leaves remedies against the party at fault intact. LIMB B. Admissible? YES - the claim attaches to the policy on risk when the damage was SUSTAINED, not DISCOVERED. Burden on the assured: insured peril, within that period. Evidence: dock survey, photos, logs, incident report, previous docking, class records. Notice must be prompt so underwriters can survey - failure attracts a reduction from the ascertained claim. Deductible per occurrence. Unrepaired? He may still claim. MIA 1963 s.69(3): reasonable DEPRECIATION arising from the unrepaired damage, NOT EXCEEDING the reasonable cost of repairing it. Hull clause: depreciation in market value at termination of the insurance, capped at repair cost and insured value. NO liability if a SUBSEQUENT TOTAL LOSS occurs in the period, covered or not. Ascertained by: repair quotations (the ceiling) → independent valuation sound vs damaged at the same date → what a willing buyer would deduct - Class unaffected means the deduction may be small or nil → apply caps → agree, or repair at the next docking and claim the cost.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: Marine Insurance Act, 1963 section 69(3), reproducing section 69(3) of the Marine Insurance Act 1906: where the ship has not been repaired and has not been sold in her damaged state during the risk, the assured is entitled to be indemnified for the reasonable depreciation arising from the unrepaired damage, but not exceeding the reasonable cost of repairing such damage. The Unrepaired Damage clause of the hull policy restates this as the reasonable depreciation in market value at the time the insurance terminates, capped at the reasonable cost of repairs and at the insured value, and excludes liability altogether where a subsequent total loss is sustained during the period of the insurance.
quick_revision.major_trap: In limb a), treating the Running Down Clause as covering collision with anything. It responds only to collision with another VESSEL - a ship that strikes a jetty, buoy, cable or rig recovers nothing under it and the whole liability is the club's. The related trap is answering "how are claims treated by H&M as well as P&I" with a single sentence after two long definitions, when the allocation IS the question. In limb b), two traps: concluding that a claim discovered a year later fails, when it attaches to the policy on risk at the date the damage was sustained; and answering the valuation with the cost of repair, when the measure for unrepaired damage is the reasonable depreciation, merely capped at repair cost - and is lost entirely if the ship becomes a total loss within the same policy period.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Running Down Clause, general average and unrepaired damage question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Where the two sit - policy clause versus rule of law, both at the hull/club boundary. 2 What the collision clause pays. 3 What it excludes, and the club's two roles. 4 General average expenditure, compactly. 5 How H&M and P&I each treat a GA claim. 6 Is late-discovered damage admissible? 7 The unrepaired damage measure and how it is ascertained.
retrieval_cards.why: The paper prints 8 and 8, so the budget is fixed; steps 3 and 5 are where limb a)'s marks actually are.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Running Down Clause, and what is it called in a modern hull policy?
retrieval_cards.answer: The collision liability clause of a hull and machinery policy - the one place a hull policy takes on liability to a third party. In the Institute Time Clauses - Hulls it appears as the 3/4ths Collision Liability clause. Running Down Clause is the older market name for the same provision.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates often know one name and not the other, and stating the identity immediately shows you know what you are describing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What three heads of liability does the collision liability clause indemnify, and in what proportion?
retrieval_cards.answer: Three fourths of sums paid for loss of or damage to the other vessel or property on board her; delay to or loss of use of that other vessel or her property; and general average, salvage or salvage under contract of that other vessel. It responds in addition to any claim for damage to the insured vessel, and is limited by reference to the insured value.
retrieval_cards.why: Delay and the other ship's general average are the two heads most often omitted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship damages a jetty. What does the collision liability clause pay?
retrieval_cards.answer: Nothing. The clause responds only to collision with another vessel. Damage to fixed and floating objects - piers, jetties, buoys, cables, moorings - falls entirely to the P&I club under fixed and floating object cover.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the single most common misunderstanding of the clause, and it is the fastest way to show the exclusions are understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the collision clause exclude, and what are the P&I club's two roles?
retrieval_cards.answer: Excluded: wreck and obstruction removal; fixed and floating objects and any property other than the other vessel; cargo or property on the insured vessel; loss of life, personal injury and illness; and pollution or contamination. The club therefore does two things - it insures the remaining one fourth of the covered heads, and it insures the excluded heads in full.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying only 'the club covers the quarter' answers half the printed question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a general average act, and distinguish expenditure from sacrifice.
retrieval_cards.answer: Under Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules there is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety, for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure. Sacrifice is property given up - jettison, machinery damaged refloating, fire-fighting damage. Expenditure is money spent - salvage or towage for the common safety, and port of refuge expenses.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem names 'General Average Expenses', so the expenditure half must be the one worked out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the hull policy respond to general average, and what reduces it?
retrieval_cards.answer: It pays a general average sacrifice of the ship in full as damage to the insured property, and it pays the ship's proportion of general average contribution and of salvage charges. If the vessel is under-insured - the insured value being less than the contributory value - underwriters pay only the proportion the insured value bears to the contributory value, and the balance falls on the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: The under-insurance proportion is the detail that separates a real answer from a general one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is unrecoverable general average and why does it fall to the club?
retrieval_cards.answer: The proportion of general average that the shipowner cannot recover from cargo or other contributing interests because his own breach of the contract of carriage - typically unseaworthiness - gives them a defence to contribution. Rule D preserves the right to contribution notwithstanding fault but expressly leaves intact remedies against the party at fault, and that gap is the club's classic general average exposure.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the clearest illustration of the answer's organising idea - the club pays where the general average machinery fails the owner.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Damage from an insured peril is found in dry dock a year later. Which policy responds?
retrieval_cards.answer: The policy on risk when the damage was sustained, not the one in force when it was discovered. Late discovery does not defeat the claim, but the assured bears the burden of proving that an insured peril caused it within that policy period, and failure to give prompt notice so underwriters could survey attracts a reduction from the ascertained claim.
retrieval_cards.why: Sustained versus discovered is the distinction the scenario is built to test.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The owner elects not to repair. Can he claim, and what is the measure?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Under section 69(3) of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, where the ship has not been repaired and has not been sold in her damaged state during the risk, the assured is indemnified for the reasonable depreciation arising from the unrepaired damage, but not exceeding the reasonable cost of repairing such damage. The hull clause restates this as depreciation in market value at the time the insurance terminates, capped at repair cost and at the insured value.
retrieval_cards.why: Answering with the repair cost is the standard error; repair cost is only the ceiling.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is the value of an unrepaired damage claim actually ascertained?
retrieval_cards.answer: Obtain repair specifications and yard quotations, which fix the ceiling. Then value the vessel in sound condition and with the damage disclosed, at the same date, by an independent valuer or broker against comparable sales for that type, age and trade; the difference is the depreciation. Test it by what a willing buyer would deduct knowing the damage exists. Apply the caps, then settle by agreement - or repair at the next docking and claim the cost instead.
retrieval_cards.why: It is a valuation exercise, not an engineering one, and the question asks specifically how the value is ascertained.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does it matter that Class is unaffected, and what destroys the claim entirely?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because depreciation is measured by what a buyer would deduct. If Class is unaffected and earning capacity unimpaired, the deduction may be small or nil even though the repair would be expensive. The claim is destroyed altogether if the vessel becomes a total loss during the same policy period, whether or not that loss is covered; and subsequent deterioration is not an insured peril.
retrieval_cards.why: The 'Class unaffected' clue is in the stem for a reason, and the total-loss rule is what makes deferring the repair a real risk.

(16)

NO LEGAL ADVICE IS GIVEN ON WHAT MAY OR MAY NOT BE SAID TO THE MEDIA OR TO RELATIVES. The answer states that legal and insurer advice must be taken and that admissions of liability are not made; it does not attempt to state the law of any jurisdiction on defamation, privilege or data protection.

blocks.h: 1. Where the printed words come from, and what is actually being asked

blocks.p: The opening sentence of the question is ISM Code paragraph 8.3, almost word for word. Say so - it costs one line and it frames everything that follows. Section 8, Emergency Preparedness, has three paragraphs and they are short enough to carry:

ol: 8.1 - the Company should identify potential emergency shipboard situations, and establish procedures to respond to them;
8.2 - the Company should establish programmes for drills and exercises to prepare for emergency actions;
8.3 - the SMS should provide for measures ensuring that the Company's organization can respond AT ANY TIME to hazards, accidents and emergency situations involving its ships.

blocks.p: Two words in 8.3 do the work. "The Company's organization" - not the ship. And "at any time" - not in office hours. The paragraph is about the shore organisation being reachable and capable round the clock, which is precisely why the question then asks about the office, the equipment, the press and the families.

The stem prints two demands and both must be answered: underline the importance of communication in emergency preparedness, and state what measures are required for four named items. The first is an argument; the second is four lists.

blocks.h: 2. Why communication is the load-bearing element of emergency preparedness

blocks.p: Communication is not one item in the emergency plan alongside fire-fighting and damage control. It is the medium through which every other element operates. Set out the argument in steps:

ul: An emergency plan that cannot be activated is not a plan. Procedures under 8.1 exist on paper until somebody transmits the alarm, so the first act of any response is a communication.

The ship cannot resolve a serious casualty alone. Salvage, technical support, class, charterers, cargo interests, flag State, coastal State, P&I and the family of an injured man are all reached through the office. The ship's only route to all of them is the link to shore.
Delay is the cost. Almost every escalation from incident to disaster contains an interval in which the right information had not reached the person who could act.

Information degrades as it is relayed. Under stress, with an unfamiliar vocabulary and often a second language, detail is lost and inference is added. This is why the ISM Code requires under section 6 that personnel be able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties and receive SMS information in a working language they understand.

Bad external communication creates a second emergency. A well-handled casualty can still destroy a company commercially if the press and the families are handled badly - and unlike the fire, that damage is entirely self-inflicted.
Communication failure is a recurring causal factor in casualties and near misses, which is why it is treated as a safety system requirement and not as a courtesy.

blocks.p: Hence the ISM formula: the SMS must ensure the organisation can respond at any time. Availability, not intention, is what is required.

blocks.h: 3. The ISM framework that supports emergency communication

blocks.p: Element 8 does not stand alone, and citing the supporting sections shows the Code is understood as a system:

headers: What it contributes to emergency communication
rows: Responsibility, authority and interrelation of all personnel defined and documented, with adequate resources and shore-based support. In an emergency this is what tells everyone who decides and who reports to whom

The link between the Company and those on board, with direct access to the highest level of management. The DP is the reason a Master can reach a decision-maker at 0300 without going through a commercial chain of command

The SMS must contain a clear statement of the Master's overriding authority to make decisions for safety and pollution prevention and to request the Company's assistance as may be necessary. The right to ask for help is written into the Code
Personnel able to communicate effectively in their SMS duties, and SMS information supplied in a working language they understand
The only mechanism that tests whether any of the above actually works before it is needed
A communication failure in a drill or an incident is a non-conformity, reported, analysed and corrected - so the system improves rather than merely being exercised

blocks.h: 4. Item (i) - contact between ship and the office

ul: A written emergency contact procedure carried on board and ashore, forming part of the SMS, stating who is called, in what order, by what means and with what information.

A 24-hour emergency contact number that is answered by a person, not by a machine - this is the direct expression of "at any time" in 8.3 - backed by a duty roster and a call-out list naming a first contact and at least one alternate for every role, with all numbers.
The Designated Person as the primary route, with authority to escalate immediately to senior management, and with the emergency response team convened on a defined trigger.

A standard initial report format so that nothing essential is forgotten under stress: ship, position, time, nature of the incident, casualties, pollution, damage and stability, weather, immediate action taken, assistance required, and who is calling.

An agreed reporting interval - regular situation reports thereafter, so the office is not obliged to keep interrupting the Master, and so silence is recognised as a signal rather than assumed to be good news.
Multiple independent means - satellite voice, e-mail, mobile and the radio installation - with the order of preference stated, so that a single failure does not sever the link.

One point of contact each way. The Master, or an officer he nominates, speaks for the ship; a single duty person speaks for the office. Multiple simultaneous conversations produce contradictory instructions and consume the Master's time when he has least of it.
A written log of every communication, timed, kept both on board and ashore. It supports the later safety investigation and is the only reliable record of what was known when.
The Master's overriding authority is respected. The office supports and advises; it does not navigate the ship or fight the fire from the shore.

A shore contact list maintained current for flag State, coastal State and port authorities, class, salvors, P&I correspondents, charterers and technical support - because in an emergency there is no time to look for a number.

blocks.h: 5. Item (ii) - communication equipment

ul: Equipment appropriate to the ship's trading area, maintained in working order and available at all times, covering the GMDSS functions - distress alerting, search and rescue coordinating communications, on-scene communications, locating signals, maritime safety information and general communications.

Emergency power and independence. The installation must work when main power is lost - a dedicated reserve source of energy, charged batteries, and equipment sited so that a fire or flood in one space does not remove every means at once.

Portable equipment for on-scene use - intrinsically safe portable radios for fire and enclosed-space teams, portable VHF for survival craft, EPIRB and SART - with a defined allocation of sets to teams so that nobody is searching for a radio while mustering.

Routine testing and record. Scheduled testing of all distress and safety equipment with results recorded, batteries tested and dated, and the whole installation covered by the ship's planned maintenance system.

Defect reporting and redundancy. A defective set is a reportable defect, not something to be fixed at the next port. The procedure must state what alternative arrangements apply while equipment is out of service and whom to inform.

Qualified operators, and enough of them. Certificated radio operators, and enough people who can actually use the equipment that the response does not depend on one individual who may be the casualty.

Clear, unambiguous operating instructions posted at the station, with distress procedures displayed at the position from which they would be transmitted - because under stress people follow what is in front of them.

Internal communications matter as much as external. Public address and general alarm, telephones between bridge, engine room and steering gear, sound-powered or otherwise independent of main power, and portable sets for teams. Most emergencies are lost internally, not externally.

Compatibility with rescue services. Equipment and procedures must allow direct working with rescue coordination centres, assisting ships and helicopters, including the on-scene frequencies and the language to be used.

blocks.h: 6. Item (iii) - dealing with the media

blocks.p: This is a company function, not a shipboard one, and the first measure is to say so.

ul: A single authorised spokesperson, named in the plan, is the only person who speaks publicly. All other personnel, ashore and afloat, are instructed to make no statement and to refer every enquiry to that person. This is not secrecy; it is the only way to prevent contradictory accounts.

The Master and crew do not speak to the press. They are fully occupied, they have partial information, and anything said will be treated as the company's position. The plan must say this explicitly, because a reporter will reach the ship.

A prepared holding statement, drafted in advance and issued quickly, confirming only that an incident has occurred, that the company is responding, that the safety of those on board is the priority and that further information will follow. Speed matters more than completeness: a vacuum is filled by speculation and by others' accounts.

Facts only, and only confirmed facts. No speculation as to cause, no estimate of damage or quantity spilled before it is established, and no admission or attribution of liability. Legal and P&I advice is taken before anything of substance is released.
Names are never released before the next of kin have been informed. This is an absolute rule and it links items (iii) and (iv).
Media training for the spokesperson, and a single controlled channel of release - a company statement and a monitored press contact - rather than answering individual approaches ad hoc.

Monitor what is being published, including social media, and correct significant factual errors promptly through the same channel. Assume crew members' own posts and photographs will appear, and cover that in the plan and in crew briefing.

Coordinate with the other parties - flag State, coastal State, salvors, charterers, class and P&I - so that statements do not conflict, and remember that a marine safety investigation is being conducted separately and must not be prejudiced.
Keep the crew and the office informed too. An organisation that learns about its own casualty from a news bulletin loses confidence in its management at exactly the moment it needs it.

blocks.h: 7. Item (iv) - dealing with the next of kin

blocks.p: One principle governs everything here: the family must hear it from the company first, from a person, and accurately.

ul: Accurate, current next-of-kin records for every person on board - name, relationship, address, telephone, language - maintained by the crewing department, reviewed at every crew change, and immediately retrievable out of hours. A plan that depends on files nobody can open at 0300 has failed.

Named, trained personnel to make contact. This is done by designated and briefed people - never by the switchboard, never by the person who happens to answer - and where possible by someone who can speak the family's own language.

Contact is made as soon as the facts are verified. Verified, but fast: the family must not learn of it from the news or from another seafarer's family. Verify the identity of the person you are speaking to before disclosing anything.

Say only what is known. Do not speculate, do not minimise, and do not give assurances that may prove false. Where information is not yet available, say so, and say when you will call again - and then call.
A single named point of contact for each family, with a direct number, so that they are not passed between departments and so that the company hears their questions consistently.

Practical and welfare support: travel and accommodation, assistance with documents and visas, help with the repatriation of an injured or deceased person, interpreters, and access to counselling. Say clearly what the company will do rather than leaving it to be asked for.

Clear, prompt information on entitlements - wages, contractual compensation, insurance and any statutory entitlement - handled with the P&I club, without pressing anyone to sign anything while in shock.
Protect the family from the press. Do not release names before they are informed, advise them that they may be approached, and offer the company's assistance in handling it.

Keep contact up. Communication does not end with the first call - the family needs updates during the response, during any investigation and afterwards, and the plan should say who is responsible for maintaining that contact.

Do not make admissions. Compassion and liability are separate; the plan should make clear that being humane costs nothing legally, but that statements about cause and fault are not for this conversation.

blocks.p: Close by tying it back. The ISM Code requires that the Company's organisation can respond at any time. Items (i) and (ii) are how the response is delivered; items (iii) and (iv) are how it is judged. A company that fights the fire well and handles the families badly will still be remembered for the second - and only element 8.2, the programme of drills and exercises, tests whether any of it works before the day it is needed.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks are printed on the question and the four items carry no split, so the paper is silent on weighting and the candidate must decide it. The stem prints two demands: "underline the Importance of communication in emergency preparedness" and "what measures are required for the following". A candidate who answers only the second has answered perhaps three quarters of the question; one who writes a general essay on the importance of communication and gives four thin lists has answered less.

The route therefore spends one step making the argument properly, one step showing that element 8 is supported by the rest of the Code, and then four substantial steps of measures. The four measure sets are where most of the marks are, and they are written as lists of measures because the printed word is "measures" - each bullet is a countable proposition.

blocks.h: The opening line that changes the answer

blocks.p: The first sentence of the question is ISM paragraph 8.3. Recognising and saying so does three things: it proves you know the Code rather than the topic, it tells you the examiner wants an ISM-based answer rather than a general management essay, and it gives you 8.1 and 8.2 free of charge as the surrounding structure.

Two words in 8.3 carry the whole question. "The Company's organization" - the paragraph is about the shore side. And "at any time" - which is why a 24-hour contact answered by a person is the single most important measure under item (i). If you quote nothing else, quote those.

blocks.h: Section 8 in full - it is three sentences

ul: 8.1 - identify potential emergency shipboard situations and establish procedures to respond to them
8.2 - establish programmes for drills and exercises
8.3 - the SMS provides measures ensuring the Company's organization can respond at any time

blocks.p: Three sentences is a very small amount of Code to memorise for a sixteen-mark question, and almost nobody does it. Note also, if it comes up in an oral, that 8.1 is the amended wording - the original 1993 text read "identify, describe and respond to" and was replaced by the 2008 amendment set. The current form is shorter.

blocks.h: Why the supporting sections matter

blocks.p: The Code is a system and element 8 leans on four other sections. Section 4 gives the Designated Person direct access to the highest level of management - that is what makes a 0300 call to a decision-maker possible. Section 5 gives the Master overriding authority and the express right to request the Company's assistance as may be necessary. Section 6 requires that people can communicate effectively and get SMS information in a working language they understand. Sections 9 and 12 turn a failure in a drill into a non-conformity that must be analysed and corrected.
Citing those four alongside element 8 is the difference between an answer about communication and an answer about the ISM Code.

blocks.h: What the Code does NOT say - and why saying so earns credit

blocks.p: The ISM Code requires that procedures exist. It says nothing whatever about press statements, next-of-kin contact or radio equipment specification. Those measures are good management practice, consistent with the Code but not prescribed by it. Making that distinction explicitly - "the Code requires the Company to establish procedures; what follows is what a competent procedure contains" - shows judgement, and it protects you from asserting as regulation something the examiner knows is not in the Code.

blocks.h: The two rules that connect items (iii) and (iv)

blocks.p: First: names are never released to the media before the next of kin have been informed. Second: one authorised spokesperson, and nobody else speaks. If you carry only two propositions across the external-communication half of this question, carry those - they are the two failures that turn a well-handled casualty into a reputational disaster, and both are entirely within the company's control.
The parallel rule inside item (iv) is that the family must hear it from the company, from a person, first, and accurately. Everything else in that list is a way of making that possible.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Not recognising that the stem is ISM 8.3, and answering with a general essay on communication.
Answering only the measures and never underlining the importance, when the stem prints both.
Giving four thin lists. The four items carry most of the marks and each needs real content.
Treating media handling as a job for the Master. It is a company function with a single authorised spokesperson.
Releasing names before the next of kin are informed - the one unforgivable error on this question.
Forgetting internal communications under item (ii). General alarm, public address, engine room telephones and portable sets are communication equipment, and most emergencies are lost internally.
Quoting GMDSS carriage requirements and sea areas instead of answering what measures are required - the question asks about management of the equipment, not the SOLAS table.
Presenting media and next-of-kin procedures as ISM requirements. They are not in the Code.
Omitting drills and exercises under 8.2, which are the only test that any of this works.
Forgetting the Master's overriding authority - the office supports; it does not command the response from ashore.
Making admissions of liability, to the press or to a family. Compassion and liability are separate.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Which paragraph of the ISM Code is the question quoting?" 8.3.
"What are the three paragraphs of element 8?" Identify situations and establish procedures; drills and exercises; the organisation can respond at any time.
"Whose organisation must respond, and when?" The Company's, at any time - it is about the shore side, round the clock.
"Who does the Master call, and why can he reach the top?" The Designated Person, who under section 4 has direct access to the highest level of management.
"Can the office order the Master to keep going?" No. Section 5 requires a clear statement of the Master's overriding authority for safety and pollution prevention.
"A reporter telephones the ship. What does the Master say?" Nothing. He refers them to the company spokesperson.
"When may a casualty's name be released?" Only after the next of kin have been informed.
"Is next-of-kin procedure required by the ISM Code?" Not expressly. The Code requires response procedures; this is what a competent procedure contains.
"What tests all of it?" The programme of drills and exercises under 8.2 - and a failure found in a drill is a non-conformity under section 9.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: State ISM paragraph 8.3. The SMS should provide for measures ensuring that the Company's organization can respond at any time to hazards, accidents and emergency situations involving its ships.

What must the initial report from the ship contain? Ship, position, time, nature of incident, casualties, pollution, damage and stability, weather, action taken, assistance required, and who is calling.
Why an agreed reporting interval? So the office need not interrupt the Master, and so silence is recognised as a signal.
Name the GMDSS functions. Distress alerting; SAR coordinating communications; on-scene communications; locating signals; maritime safety information; general communications.

What internal communications matter in an emergency? General alarm and public address; bridge to engine room and steering gear telephones independent of main power; portable intrinsically safe radios for teams.
Who speaks to the press? One named authorised spokesperson, and nobody else.

What goes in a holding statement? That an incident has occurred, that the company is responding, that the safety of those on board is the priority, and that more will follow. No cause, no quantities, no liability.
Who contacts the next of kin, and how quickly? Named, trained personnel, in the family's own language where possible, as soon as the facts are verified and before the names reach the press.
What support should the family be offered? Travel and accommodation, documents and visas, repatriation assistance, interpreters, counselling, and clear information on entitlements.
Where does the Designated Person fit? Section 4 - the link between Company and ship, with direct access to the highest level of management.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The Code first: IDENTIFY, DRILL, RESPOND ANY TIME - that is 8.1, 8.2, 8.3. Then the four supports: DP, MASTER, LANGUAGE, REVIEW - sections 4, 5, 6 and 12.

For the four printed items, note that they fall into two natural pairs. INWARD - the office and the equipment; OUTWARD - the press and the families. Inward is how the response is delivered; outward is how the company is judged.

Inside item (i): WHO, HOW, WHAT, HOW OFTEN - call-out list, multiple means, standard report format, agreed interval. Inside item (ii): WORKS, POWERED, PORTABLE, TESTED, MANNED, INTERNAL. Inside item (iii): ONE VOICE, FAST, FACTS ONLY, NO NAMES BEFORE FAMILIES. Inside item (iv): FROM US, FROM A PERSON, FIRST, AND TRUE.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the boundary between Code and practice

blocks.p: The Code half of this answer is primary verified. Section 8 was read directly in the ISM Code itself, paragraph 8.3 was confirmed word by word against the printed stem, and the amendment chain was checked rather than assumed: the 2008 amendment set replaces paragraph 8.1 and does not touch 8.2 or 8.3, and no later amendment set alters section 8 at all. Sections 3, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 12 were read in the same session.

The practice half is deliberately labelled as such. The ISM Code requires that procedures exist; it does not prescribe their content, and it says nothing whatever about media handling, next-of-kin contact or the specification of communication equipment. The four measure sets are therefore good management practice consistent with the Code, and the answer states that distinction openly rather than presenting management practice as regulation.

Three things are deliberately not asserted. No GMDSS carriage requirement, sea area or SOLAS chapter IV regulation number, because MIW holds no licensed SOLAS text - the equipment limb is answered by function and by management measure, which is what the question asks. No drill frequency or response-time target, because those come from SOLAS and company policy rather than from the ISM Code. And no legal advice on what may be said to press or family: the answer requires that legal and P&I advice be taken and that no admission be made, and goes no further.

The operative section 8 at this sitting is therefore 8.1 as amended, with 8.2 and 8.3 as originally adopted.

THE ISM CODE IS THE MOST TEMPORALLY STABLE INSTRUMENT ON THIS PAPER. The Code was adopted in 1993 and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX; the most recent amendment set relevant to any part of this answer entered force in JANUARY 2015, EIGHT YEARS before this sitting. Nothing on this question entered force, was amended or was superseded during 2023, and nothing could be back-ported from a later donor because no later instrument exists.

A.1184(33) WAS CHECKED AND IS OUT OF SCOPE. The corpus holds an ISM-related Assembly resolution adopted at the 33rd Assembly of 6 DECEMBER 2023 - SIX MONTHS AFTER this sitting. It is future here and is NOT used. Nothing in this answer depends on any 33rd Assembly instrument, and no guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations are cited at all, because none is needed for a question about what the Company's procedures must contain.
THE ONE SAME-YEAR FAMILY MEMBER RUNS THE RIGHT WAY. QP2302-Q5 is FEBRUARY 2023 - four months EARLIER than this sitting, in the same regime - and its ISM communication material required no adjustment.

THE FAMILY'S LATER MEMBERS WERE READ FOR ARGUMENT ONLY AND CARRY NO DATED CLAIM. QP2312-Q4(b) is December 2023, QP2509-Q6 September 2025, QP2601-Q2 January 2026 and QP2606-Q4(b) June 2026. All are about routine operational communication and none asserts a dated instrument, so none required reversing. The material taken from them - that communication failure is a recurring causal factor - is not date-dependent.

NO CLAIM DEPENDS ON THE EXAMINATION DAY WITHIN JUNE 2023. Nothing on this question moved during the sitting month, and neither of the two day-dependent June 2023 events recorded in the paper anchor touches the ISM Code.
MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 governs at this sitting; the 2025 Act is thirty-three months future. Neither is load-bearing here - the question is entirely about an IMO Code and about company procedure.

DONOR CONTAMINATION SWEEP: CLEAN, AND THE RISK WAS SUBJECT DRIFT RATHER THAN TIME. The five communication-family members are all about NORMAL operational communication - watchkeeping, engine resource management, multinational crews, a decarbonisation job. Carrying their content across would have produced an answer about communication in general and not about EMERGENCY communication, which is what the stem asks. The family was used for one step and the four measure sets were authored fresh from the Code.
