blocks.h: 1. What a repair contract is, and the one idea behind all five limbs

blocks.p: A ship repair contract is an agreement to carry out defined work on a defined vessel, in a defined time, for a defined price. The contract documents normally comprise the agreement, the general conditions, the repair specification, the yard's quotation, and any agreed clarifications - with an order of precedence clause saying which prevails if they conflict - together with the variation orders issued during the docking.

The command verb is illustrate, so each limb below is shown working. The organising idea is simple: the five printed issues are five allocations of the same four risks - cost, scope, time and defect - and each clause exists to answer one question: who carries this if it goes wrong? Two facts colour everything:

ul: The yard has the ship. Once she is docked, the owner's leverage is largely gone and the yard's is at its maximum. Every commercially important term must therefore be agreed before she arrives.

The owner's real exposure is time, not price. A ship in dock earns nothing. A dispute that adds a week may cost more than the item in dispute is worth - which is why the delay and variation machinery matters more than the headline price.

blocks.h: 2. A. Payment terms

ul: The pricing basis. A lump sum for the specified work gives price certainty and puts the productivity risk on the yard, but only for work that is fully specified. Because much dry-dock work is not, it is combined with a schedule of rates - steel renewal by weight, pipe by length, tank cleaning and coating by area, staging, gas-freeing, and day rates by trade - and provisional sums for open-and-inspect items.

Illustration. A tank top is specified as "open, inspect, renew wasted plate". Nobody knows the tonnage until it is opened. If a rate per tonne of renewed steel, fitted and coated, is agreed before the tender is accepted, the owner has price control over an unknown quantity. If it is not, he is negotiating that rate on the day, with the tank open and the ship immobilised - and he will pay a great deal more.

Stage payments tied to identifiable events - on arrival or docking, on undocking, and the balance on redelivery - so that neither side is far out of pocket at any point, with a retention held until the guarantee period expires so that there is money behind the guarantee.

Certification and disputed items. Invoices supported by measured quantities and signed variation orders, certified by the owner's superintendent. Disputed items should be severable, so that a disagreement over one item does not stop the whole payment - though note that yards commonly exclude the owner's right of set-off, which means paying first and arguing afterwards.

Currency, escalation, taxes and dues. The currency of account and who bears exchange movement; whether rates are firm for the contract period; and the allocation of port, dock and berth dues, tugs, waste disposal and local taxes - which is where a headline price and a final invoice most often diverge.
Security both ways. The yard wants payment security or an advance; the owner wants a refund or performance guarantee from a bank of standing, so that an advance is recoverable if the yard fails.

The lien, which dominates the limb. A repairer in possession will in practice assert a right to retain the ship until his account is settled. Whatever the position in the applicable law, the commercial reality is the same and the contract must deal with it: what is payable on redelivery, what security - a bank guarantee or a P&I letter of undertaking - the owner may offer instead of cash for a disputed sum, and on what terms the ship sails. Negotiate the exit before you dock, not after.

blocks.h: 3. B. Ambit of the specification and additional work

ul: The specification is the contract's definition of the work, and it is where cost is actually controlled. Everything the yard is obliged to do, and everything the price covers, is fixed by it. Every ambiguity is resolved on the day, in the yard's favour, at the yard's price.

Draft it to close gaps. State the standard of workmanship and the applicable class rules; state what is included by implication - staging, gas-freeing, cleaning, protection, removal of debris, reinstatement, cropping and refitting of insulation and pipework to get access; and state what the yard supplies as against what the owner supplies. A specification that says "renew valve" without saying who provides the valve, who lands it, who tests it and who reinstates the lagging has left four items to be charged as extras.
Open-and-inspect items are the standing problem of ship repair. Handle them by rate, as in limb A, and by defining the inspection standard and who determines it - usually class, attending.

The variation procedure is the heart of this limb. Additional work must be ordered in writing by a named owner's representative before it is performed, on a numbered variation order recording the work, the price, and - the part most often omitted - the effect on the delivery date.

Illustration. The ship is docked for a fifteen-day period. Opening a stern tube reveals bearing wear that must be dealt with. If the variation order records only the price, the owner has bought the work and inadvertently surrendered his delay remedy: the yard will say the extra work extended the docking and the liquidated damages clause is disapplied for that period. Agree the time and the money in the same document, or the delay clause in limb C is worth nothing.

Owner-supplied items and the owner's own subcontractors. Specialists - class-approved service suppliers, coating inspectors, makers' technicians - frequently work in the yard on the owner's account. Agree access, working hours, the yard's charge for facilities, the safety regime and the split of responsibility, or the two sides will each blame the other for delay.

Rework. State who bears the cost if class or the flag surveyor rejects work - the yard, where the workmanship or material is at fault - and distinguish that from a change of requirement, which is a variation.

blocks.h: 4. C. Contract period, liquidated damages and force majeure

blocks.p: The contract period runs from an agreed start - commonly arrival at the yard or docking - to redelivery, and is the yard's time to perform. It should also fix a date by which the owner must deliver the vessel, because a berth held empty is the yard's loss.
Liquidated damages are the agreed remedy for late redelivery:

ul: a pre-agreed sum per day of delay, usually after a short grace period;
capped at a proportion of the contract price - and the cap matters as much as the rate, because it is the yard's worst case;
normally the owner's sole and exclusive remedy for delay, excluding any claim for actual loss of earnings;
with a right to terminate once the cap is reached, which is what stops an indefinite delay becoming merely an expensive one.
Permissible delays must be listed and they extend the date rather than trigger damages: additional work ordered under limb B, the owner's own default, late owner-supplied items, and force majeure.

The legal caution, which is jurisdiction-dependent: the sum should be a genuine pre-estimate of the loss the owner would suffer. A figure fixed to punish rather than to compensate may be attacked as a penalty and be unenforceable, leaving the owner to prove his actual loss - so a rate loosely tied to prevailing charter earnings is defensible, and an arbitrary large number is not.

blocks.p: Force majeure relieves a party of liability for failure caused by events beyond its reasonable control. Four points, and the first is the one candidates miss:

ol: In common-law systems force majeure is a creature of contract. There is no general doctrine to fall back on; a party with no force majeure clause has only the very narrow doctrine of frustration. If it is not drafted, it does not exist.

The events must be defined, usually as a list - act of God, war and civil commotion, strikes and labour disputes, fire, flood and severe weather, epidemic, government or port authority action, and unavailability of essential materials - with the qualification that they be beyond the reasonable control of the affected party and not caused by its own default.

Procedure. Prompt written notice within a stated time, with particulars; a duty to mitigate and to resume as soon as possible; and notice when the event ends. Notice provisions are conditions and are commonly missed in practice.
Effect. An extension of time, not money - each side generally bears its own costs - and, if the event persists beyond a stated period, a right for either party to terminate.

blocks.p: Illustration. A yard-wide strike stops work for three weeks. Under the clause the yard gives notice, the redelivery date moves by three weeks, liquidated damages do not run for that period, and the owner recovers nothing for the lost earnings. If the strike ran for months and passed the stated period, either party could walk away - which is why the length of that period is negotiated as carefully as the daily rate.

blocks.h: 5. D. Guarantees and insurance

blocks.p: The guarantee, or defects liability period, is the owner's protection after redelivery:

ul: the yard makes good, at its own cost, defects due to defective workmanship or materials that appear within the period - commonly about a year from redelivery, though the length is negotiated and is not a rule;

the remedy is defined: usually the yard's option either to repair at its own yard, or to bear the reasonable cost of repair elsewhere on a quotation approved beforehand - because a ship that fails in another continent cannot practicably return;
notice of the defect within a stated period after discovery, and access for the yard to inspect;

exclusions, which are what the argument is always about: fair wear and tear, the owner's misuse, neglect or failure to maintain, owner-supplied materials and equipment, and - almost invariably - all consequential loss, including loss of time, hire and profit. So the yard replaces the failed component and the owner bears the off-hire, and an owner who has not understood that has misjudged his exposure;
supported commercially by the retention from limb A and, on larger contracts, a bank or parent company guarantee.

blocks.p: Insurance must be arranged on both sides, and the clause should say who carries what and require evidence:

rows: Cover continues during the docking, but underwriters must be notified of the port risk, the immobilisation, hot work and any layup - a docking is not the risk the policy was written for

Damage to the vessel while in the yard's care, custody and control - the yard's principal exposure. Agree a minimum limit adequate to the value of the vessel and require the certificate before docking
Injury to yard workers and damage to other property; port and dock risks
Crew remaining on board, and pollution from the vessel. Notify the club of the docking
Where any remain on board, and the tank condition required for hot work

ul: Include a waiver of subrogation between the two sides' insurers, or a knock-for-knock allocation, so that the yard's insurer does not sue the owner's and vice versa - circular claims consume the premium and delay the settlement.

Illustration. A fire starts during hot work in a pump room. Whether the owner's H&M or the yard's ship repairers' liability insurer ultimately pays turns on the care, custody and control wording, on the hot-work permit regime and on whether the parties waived subrogation. Fire during hot work is the classic repair-yard loss and it is worth naming as the illustration of why this limb exists.

blocks.h: 6. E. Termination events

blocks.p: Termination rights should be defined, mutual and consequential - that is, the contract must say not only when each party may terminate but what then happens to the ship, the money and the materials.

rows: The yard's insolvency, receivership, administration or winding-up · delay beyond the liquidated damages cap or beyond a long-stop date · abandonment of the work, or persistent failure to proceed with due diligence · material breach not remedied after written notice · a force majeure event continuing beyond the stated period
The owner's failure to pay a sum due after notice · the owner's insolvency · failure to deliver the vessel by the agreed date, or removal of her from the yard · the same prolonged force majeure

blocks.p: The consequences are where the value lies, and a clause that stops at "either party may terminate" is nearly useless:

ul: Valuation and payment for work actually done to the date of termination, and for materials already ordered or fabricated to the ship's specification.

Release of the vessel and security for the lien - on what terms she may leave, and what security the owner must provide for a disputed balance. This is the practical crux and it should be agreed before docking.

Condition on redelivery. A part-completed docking must be left in a seaworthy and towable state, with openings closed and systems reinstated so far as practicable - otherwise the owner terminates and finds he cannot move her.
Return of owner-supplied materials and equipment, and of drawings and technical information.
Repayment of advances, called under the refund guarantee where the yard has failed.
Removal and tow - who arranges and who pays.
Survival of the confidentiality, guarantee, insurance and dispute clauses, so that terminating the contract does not destroy the machinery for resolving the dispute that caused it.

blocks.h: 7. The two clauses the question does not name, but which decide all five

ol: Governing law and dispute resolution. The yard and the owner are usually in different countries, and the ship in a third. Every right in limbs A to E is worth exactly what it costs to enforce, so a clear governing law and a workable arbitration provision - seat, rules and language - is the clause that gives the others value. Consider also whether an expert determination or a short-form procedure is available for the sort of small, urgent technical dispute that actually arises mid-docking, when arbitration is far too slow to help.

Order of precedence. The specification, the general conditions, the quotation and the clarifications will conflict. Say which prevails. Without it the parties argue about which document governs before they can argue about the point in dispute.

blocks.p: Finally, note that widely used industry standard forms exist for ship repair, and their commercial value is precisely that these five issues are already allocated in a way both sides recognise. Starting from a known form and negotiating the schedule - rates, period, liquidated damages, guarantee and limits - is faster, cheaper and far safer than drafting each docking from scratch.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Five printed limbs, sixteen marks, no split anywhere, and the command verb is "illustrate". Two consequences follow and both are about discipline rather than knowledge. First, five does not divide into sixteen, so nothing can be written at length - roughly three marks a limb, and the candidate who writes a page on payment terms will not finish. Second, "illustrate" is not "list": each limb needs something shown working - a worked consequence, a scenario, a named failure mode - or it has not been illustrated.

The route therefore gives one step per printed limb, opens each with the commercial risk it allocates, and hangs a worked illustration inside four of the five. Step 1 supplies the organising idea in three lines, and step 7 adds the two clauses the examiner did not name - which is the cheapest way to show that the subject is understood as a whole rather than as five headings.

blocks.h: The idea that makes all five one subject

blocks.p: Every one of the five printed issues is an allocation of the same four risks - cost, scope, time and defect - and every clause answers one question: who carries this if it goes wrong? Payment allocates cost. Specification allocates scope. Period and liquidated damages allocate time. Guarantees and insurance allocate defect and damage. Termination decides what happens when the allocation fails altogether.
State that in your opening and the answer stops being five disconnected headings.

blocks.h: The two commercial facts that colour everything

blocks.p: First: the yard has the ship. Once she is docked the owner's leverage is gone and the yard's is at its maximum. Everything commercially important must be agreed before she arrives - which is why the exit terms, the rates for unknown quantities and the security for a disputed balance are all pre-docking negotiations, not mid-docking ones.

Second: the owner's exposure is time, not price. A ship in dock earns nothing, so a dispute that adds a week can cost more than the item in dispute. That is why the variation and delay machinery matters more than the headline figure, and it is the sentence that shows an examiner you have thought about this from the owner's side.

blocks.h: The single most valuable practical point on the question

blocks.p: A variation order must capture the TIME as well as the MONEY. If it records only the price, the owner has bought the extra work and inadvertently surrendered his delay remedy - the yard will say the additional work extended the docking, and liquidated damages are disapplied for that period.

This is the classic failure in real dockings, it links limb B directly to limb C, and it is exactly the sort of thing a Chief Engineer knows and a lawyer does not. Say it, and illustrate it with an open-and-inspect item such as a stern tube.

blocks.h: Force majeure is a creature of contract

blocks.p: The point most candidates miss entirely. In common-law systems there is no general doctrine of force majeure. If the clause is not drafted, the party has only the doctrine of frustration, which is narrow and rarely available. So force majeure is not a background legal protection - it is a negotiated list, with defined events, a notice obligation, a duty to mitigate, and a stated effect.
And note its effect precisely: an extension of time, not money. Each side generally bears its own costs. A candidate who says force majeure entitles the owner to compensation has it backwards.

blocks.h: Liquidated damages: the cap and the exclusivity matter more than the rate

blocks.p: Three features are usually more important than the daily figure. It is normally the owner's sole and exclusive remedy for delay, so he cannot claim his actual lost earnings instead. It is capped, so the yard's worst case is known. And reaching the cap should trigger a right to terminate - which is what prevents an indefinite delay from becoming merely an expensive one.
Add the jurisdiction-dependent legal caution: the sum should be a genuine pre-estimate of loss, or it may be attacked as a penalty and be unenforceable, leaving the owner to prove actual loss.

blocks.h: The exclusion that surprises owners

blocks.p: A repair guarantee almost always excludes consequential loss, including loss of time, hire and profit. So when a guarantee defect stops the ship, the yard replaces the component and the owner bears the off-hire. Knowing and stating that is worth a mark on its own, because it shows you understand what the guarantee is actually worth rather than merely that one exists.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Writing at length on one or two limbs and running out of time. Five limbs, sixteen marks - budget first.
Listing headings without illustrating anything, when the printed command verb is "illustrate".
Omitting the lien from the payment limb. It is the commercial fact that dominates the whole contract.
Treating the specification as a technical document rather than as the contract's definition of the work and the place cost is controlled.
Agreeing a variation on price alone and losing the delay remedy.
Saying force majeure is a general legal principle. In common-law systems it exists only if drafted.
Saying force majeure entitles a party to money. It gives an extension of time.
Giving liquidated damages figures or caps as percentages. They are negotiated and vary widely - quote none.
Forgetting that liquidated damages are usually exclusive and capped, and that the cap should trigger termination.
Omitting the consequential loss exclusion from the guarantee limb.
Forgetting ship repairers' liability insurance, which is the yard's central cover and the one to demand evidence of.
Writing termination as "either party may terminate" with no consequences - the consequences are the substance.
Omitting governing law and arbitration when the parties are in different countries.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "How do you price work whose quantity is unknown?" By an agreed schedule of rates and provisional sums, fixed before the tender is accepted - not negotiated with the tank open.

"The yard will not let the ship sail. What is your position?" He is asserting a repairer's possessory lien. Offer security - a bank guarantee or a club letter of undertaking - for the disputed sum, on terms agreed before docking.
"You order extra work. What have you just done to your delivery date?" Extended it, unless the variation order fixed the time impact.
"Is force majeure implied?" Not in common-law systems. If it is not drafted, it does not exist.
"What does force majeure give you?" Time, not money - and a right to terminate if it persists beyond the stated period.
"Why might your liquidated damages clause fail?" If it is a penalty rather than a genuine pre-estimate of loss.
"A guarantee defect puts the ship off hire for ten days. Who pays the hire?" The owner. Consequential loss is excluded.

"Whose insurance covers a fire started by the yard's hot work?" Turns on care, custody and control, on the ship repairers' liability wording, on the permit regime, and on whether subrogation was waived.
"You terminate mid-docking. What must the yard leave you?" A seaworthy and towable vessel, with openings closed and systems reinstated so far as practicable.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Name the contract documents and why an order of precedence clause is needed. Agreement, general conditions, specification, quotation, clarifications, variation orders - they will conflict.
How is a repair contract priced? Lump sum for specified work, schedule of rates for quantum-uncertain items, provisional sums for open-and-inspect.
What is retention for? To keep money behind the guarantee obligation until the guarantee period expires.
What must a variation order record? The work, the price, and the effect on the delivery date.
Who bears rework if class rejects the work? The yard, where its workmanship or material is at fault; a change of requirement is a variation.
What are permissible delays? Additional work ordered, owner default, late owner-supplied items, force majeure.
Name five force majeure events. Act of God; war or civil commotion; strikes; fire or flood; government or port authority action.
How long is a repair guarantee and what does it exclude? Commonly about a year, negotiated; excludes wear and tear, owner misuse, owner-supplied materials and all consequential loss.
What insurance must the yard carry? Ship repairers' liability for vessels in its care, custody and control, plus third-party and employer's liability.
Give three owner termination events. Yard insolvency; delay beyond the liquidated damages cap; abandonment or failure to proceed with due diligence.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The five limbs map onto four risks: COST · SCOPE · TIME · DEFECT, and then EXIT. Payment is cost, specification is scope, period and liquidated damages are time, guarantees and insurance are defect, termination is exit.

Inside each limb one hook. Payment - THE YARD HAS THE SHIP. Specification - EVERY GAP IS AN EXTRA. Time - THE VARIATION MUST BUY THE TIME TOO. Guarantees - THEY FIX THE PART, YOU PAY THE OFF-HIRE. Termination - SEAWORTHY AND TOWABLE.
And close with the two unnamed clauses: WHICH LAW, AND WHICH DOCUMENT WINS.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: There is no regulation on this question. A ship repair contract is a commercial contract and is governed by the law the parties choose, not by any IMO instrument or national maritime statute
Contract documents - agreement, general conditions, specification, quotation, clarifications, variation orders, with an order of precedence clause
Pricing - lump sum, schedule of rates, provisional sums, stage payments, retention
Security - owner's payment security; yard's refund or performance guarantee; the repairer's possessory lien
Delay - contract period, grace period, liquidated damages, cap, exclusivity, permissible delays, long-stop date
Force majeure - defined events, notice, mitigation, extension of time, termination on prolonged event
Guarantee - defects liability period, remedy and its location, notice of defect, exclusions including consequential loss
Insurance - owner's H&M and P&I; yard's ship repairers' liability, third party and employer's liability; waiver of subrogation
Termination - events for each party; valuation, release and security, seaworthy and towable condition, return of materials, repayment of advances, survival clauses
Governing law and arbitration; and the commercial value of a recognised industry standard form

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the evidential position on this question

blocks.p: This question is stated plainly to be the weakest-sourced on the paper alongside the marine insurance question, and for the same reason. The True Source corpus holds no ship repair contract standard form, no industry form of any kind, no shipbuilding or repair commentary and no contract law material, and no solved MIW question anywhere addresses this subject. This question therefore carries no primary source and none is claimed. Every proposition is industry guidance or commercial and engineering judgement.

Three disciplines follow, and they are what make the answer safe. No standard form is quoted and no clause of any form is reproduced; the existence of recognised industry forms is noted by identity only, to make a point about negotiation cost. No figure is asserted anywhere - no liquidated damages rate, no cap percentage, no retention percentage, no grace period, no guarantee period in months, no insurance limit - because every one of them is negotiated and varies by yard, region, vessel and market; where a common position is described, such as a guarantee of about a year, it is expressly stated as typical and negotiable. And no proposition of law is asserted for any named jurisdiction: the two legal points that do appear - that liquidated damages must be a genuine pre-estimate rather than a penalty, and that force majeure is a creature of contract - are both flagged as jurisdiction-dependent, and the repairer's lien is described as a commercial reality rather than as a rule of any stated law.

That is a deliberate choice rather than a gap. What the examiner asks for - the key issues, illustrated - is entirely answerable at the level of allocation and consequence, and an answer that quoted figures or asserted the law of an unnamed jurisdiction would be less reliable, not more.

notes: THIS QUESTION HAS NO REGULATORY CONTENT AT ALL, AND THAT IS ITSELF THE TEMPORAL FINDING. A ship repair contract is a commercial contract governed by whatever law the parties choose. No IMO instrument, no MARPOL or SOLAS provision, no Assembly resolution and no Indian maritime statute is engaged by any of the five printed limbs. There is accordingly nothing that could have entered into force, been amended or been superseded at or around this sitting, and nothing that a later donor could carry backwards.

THE ABSENCE OF A DONOR REMOVES THE ONLY VECTOR BY WHICH LATER LAW COULD HAVE REACHED THIS ANSWER. Every other question on this paper has at least a family relation to a later object; this one has none, so the standing 2023 warning that every donor runs backwards has nothing to bite on here.

NO CLAIM DEPENDS ON THE EXAMINATION DAY WITHIN JUNE 2023, and neither of the two day-dependent June 2023 events recorded in the paper anchor - the BBNJ adoption of 19 June and the Hong Kong Convention accessions of 26 June - touches commercial repair contracting.

MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 governs the paper at this sitting and the 2025 Act is thirty-three months future, but NEITHER IS ENGAGED. This is recorded explicitly because a sweep keyed to 'Indian statute at a 2023 sitting' would otherwise expect one to appear and find none. The correct position is that no national maritime statute governs the content of a repair contract; the parties' chosen law does.

THE TWO LEGAL PROPOSITIONS IN THE ANSWER ARE STABLE AND ARE FLAGGED AS JURISDICTION-DEPENDENT RATHER THAN DATED. The penalty-versus-liquidated-damages distinction and the proposition that force majeure is a creature of contract are long-settled features of common-law contracting and are not tied to any date. They are attributed to no statute and no decided case, so no citation can go stale.

NO PANDEMIC-ERA DRAFTING PRACTICE IS ASSERTED AS SETTLED. Epidemic and government action appear in the force majeure list as they routinely did before 2020, and no claim is made about how force majeure clauses were interpreted or renegotiated during or after the pandemic. That is a live commercial and legal debate at this sitting and asserting an outcome would be unsafe.
NO MARKET CONDITION IS DESCRIBED. Yard capacity, docking prices and lead times moved sharply in the years around this sitting; the answer asserts nothing about them, so nothing in it can date.

DONOR CONTAMINATION SWEEP: NOT APPLICABLE IN THE USUAL SENSE - THERE IS NO DONOR. The two 'dry dock' matches in the corpus were read and rejected as a different subject, and no content was taken from them. The insurance limb was authored from the exposures that arise in a repairer's custody and NOT from the marine insurance questions, because insuring a vessel in a yard is a different risk from insuring her trading.

regulations: No IMO instrument, national maritime statute or regulation governs this question - a ship repair contract is a commercial contract governed by the law the parties choose. This is stated rather than left implicit.
Contract documents and order of precedence - agreement, general conditions, specification, quotation, clarifications, variation orders
Liquidated damages must be a genuine pre-estimate of loss rather than a penalty - JURISDICTION-DEPENDENT, attributed to no statute or case
Force majeure is a creature of contract in common-law systems; frustration is the narrow fallback - JURISDICTION-DEPENDENT
The repairer's possessory lien - described as a commercial reality, not as a rule of any stated law

steps.title: What a repair contract is, and the one idea behind all five limbs
points: defined work, on a defined vessel, in a defined time, for a defined price
contract documents - agreement, general conditions, SPECIFICATION, quotation, clarifications, plus VARIATION ORDERS, with an ORDER OF PRECEDENCE clause
THE FIVE PRINTED ISSUES ARE FIVE ALLOCATIONS OF THE SAME FOUR RISKS - COST, SCOPE, TIME, DEFECT
every clause answers one question: WHO CARRIES THIS IF IT GOES WRONG?
FACT ONE - THE YARD HAS THE SHIP. Once docked, the owner's leverage is gone; agree everything commercially important BEFORE she arrives
FACT TWO - THE OWNER'S EXPOSURE IS TIME, NOT PRICE. A dispute that adds a week can cost more than the item in dispute
the command verb is ILLUSTRATE - each limb must be shown working

steps.title: A. Payment terms
points: LUMP SUM for fully specified work - price certainty, productivity risk on the yard
SCHEDULE OF RATES for quantum-uncertain work - steel by weight, pipe by length, coating by area, staging, gas-freeing, day rates by trade; PROVISIONAL SUMS for open-and-inspect
ILLUSTRATION - a tank top 'open, inspect, renew wasted plate'. Agree the rate per tonne BEFORE the tender is accepted, or negotiate it with the tank open and the ship immobilised
STAGE PAYMENTS on docking, undocking and redelivery; RETENTION held until the guarantee expires so there is money behind the guarantee

invoices supported by measured quantities and SIGNED VARIATION ORDERS, certified by the owner's superintendent; disputed items severable - but yards commonly EXCLUDE SET-OFF, so pay first and argue after
currency and exchange risk, escalation, taxes, port and dock dues - where headline price and final invoice diverge
SECURITY BOTH WAYS - owner's payment security; yard's REFUND OR PERFORMANCE GUARANTEE from a bank of standing
THE LIEN DOMINATES THE LIMB - a repairer in possession will assert a right to RETAIN THE SHIP until paid
so the contract must fix what is payable on redelivery and WHAT SECURITY may be offered instead of cash for a disputed sum. NEGOTIATE THE EXIT BEFORE YOU DOCK

steps.title: B. Ambit of the specification and additional work
points: THE SPECIFICATION IS THE CONTRACT'S DEFINITION OF THE WORK AND IS WHERE COST IS ACTUALLY CONTROLLED
EVERY AMBIGUITY IS RESOLVED ON THE DAY, IN THE YARD'S FAVOUR, AT THE YARD'S PRICE
draft to close gaps - workmanship standard and class rules; staging, gas-freeing, cleaning, protection, debris removal, reinstatement, access work; who supplies what
'renew valve' without saying who provides, lands, tests and re-lags it has left FOUR items to be charged as extras
OPEN-AND-INSPECT items handled by RATE, with a defined inspection standard and who determines it - usually class, attending
THE VARIATION PROCEDURE IS THE HEART OF THE LIMB - ordered IN WRITING by a NAMED owner's representative BEFORE the work is done
the variation order records the work, THE PRICE, and - most often omitted - THE EFFECT ON THE DELIVERY DATE

ILLUSTRATION - stern tube bearing wear found on opening. Record only the price and the yard will say the extra work extended the docking and liquidated damages are disapplied. AGREE TIME AND MONEY IN THE SAME DOCUMENT
owner-supplied items and OWNER'S OWN SUBCONTRACTORS - access, hours, yard's facility charge, safety regime, responsibility split
REWORK - the yard bears it where its workmanship or material is at fault; a change of requirement is a variation

steps.title: C. Contract period, liquidated damages and force majeure
points: the CONTRACT PERIOD runs from arrival or docking to redelivery; it should also fix a date by which the OWNER must deliver the vessel
LIQUIDATED DAMAGES - a pre-agreed sum PER DAY, usually after a GRACE PERIOD
CAPPED at a proportion of the contract price - the cap matters as much as the rate
normally the owner's SOLE AND EXCLUSIVE REMEDY for delay, excluding any claim for actual lost earnings
with a RIGHT TO TERMINATE once the cap is reached - what stops an indefinite delay being merely an expensive one
PERMISSIBLE DELAYS extend the date - additional work ordered, owner default, late owner-supplied items, force majeure
JURISDICTION-DEPENDENT CAUTION - the sum must be a GENUINE PRE-ESTIMATE OF LOSS; a figure fixed to punish may be attacked as a PENALTY and be unenforceable
FORCE MAJEURE IS A CREATURE OF CONTRACT - in common-law systems there is NO GENERAL DOCTRINE; without a clause there is only the narrow doctrine of FRUSTRATION

DEFINED EVENTS - act of God, war and civil commotion, strikes, fire, flood and severe weather, epidemic, government or port authority action, unavailability of essential materials; beyond reasonable control and not self-caused
PROCEDURE - prompt written notice within a stated time, duty to MITIGATE and resume, notice when it ends. Notice provisions are conditions and are commonly missed
EFFECT - AN EXTENSION OF TIME, NOT MONEY; each side bears its own costs; termination by EITHER party if it persists beyond a stated period
ILLUSTRATION - a three-week yard strike moves the date three weeks, suspends liquidated damages, and the owner recovers nothing for lost earnings

steps.title: D. Guarantees and insurance
points: GUARANTEE OR DEFECTS LIABILITY PERIOD - the yard makes good defects due to DEFECTIVE WORKMANSHIP OR MATERIALS appearing within the period from redelivery; commonly about a year, NEGOTIATED, not a rule
THE REMEDY IS DEFINED - the yard's option to repair at its own yard OR to bear the REASONABLE COST of repair elsewhere on a pre-approved quotation
notice of the defect within a stated period after discovery, and access for the yard to inspect
EXCLUSIONS ARE WHAT THE ARGUMENT IS ABOUT - fair wear and tear, owner's misuse or neglect, owner-supplied materials, and ALL CONSEQUENTIAL LOSS INCLUDING LOSS OF TIME, HIRE AND PROFIT
SO THE YARD REPLACES THE COMPONENT AND THE OWNER BEARS THE OFF-HIRE
supported by the RETENTION and, on larger contracts, a bank or parent company guarantee
INSURANCE - owner's H&M continues but underwriters must be NOTIFIED of port risk, immobilisation, hot work and layup
YARD'S SHIP REPAIRERS' LIABILITY for damage to the vessel in its CARE, CUSTODY AND CONTROL - agree a minimum limit and require the certificate BEFORE docking
yard's third-party and employer's liability; owner's P&I notified where crew remain on board
WAIVER OF SUBROGATION or knock-for-knock, so the two insurers do not sue each other
ILLUSTRATION - FIRE DURING HOT WORK is the classic repair-yard loss; who pays turns on care, custody and control, the permit regime and the subrogation waiver

steps.title: E. Termination events
points: termination rights must be DEFINED, MUTUAL AND CONSEQUENTIAL

OWNER MAY TERMINATE - yard's INSOLVENCY; DELAY BEYOND THE LIQUIDATED DAMAGES CAP or a long-stop date; ABANDONMENT or failure to proceed with due diligence; unremedied MATERIAL BREACH after notice; PROLONGED FORCE MAJEURE
YARD MAY TERMINATE - owner's FAILURE TO PAY after notice; owner's INSOLVENCY; failure to DELIVER THE VESSEL by the agreed date or removal of her; the same prolonged force majeure
CONSEQUENCES ARE WHERE THE VALUE LIES - a clause that stops at 'either party may terminate' is nearly useless
VALUATION AND PAYMENT for work done and materials ordered or fabricated to the ship's specification
RELEASE OF THE VESSEL AND SECURITY FOR THE LIEN - on what terms she may leave and what security covers a disputed balance. AGREE THIS BEFORE DOCKING
CONDITION ON REDELIVERY - SEAWORTHY AND TOWABLE, openings closed and systems reinstated so far as practicable
RETURN of owner-supplied materials, equipment, drawings and technical information
REPAYMENT OF ADVANCES called under the refund guarantee where the yard has failed
REMOVAL AND TOW - who arranges and who pays
SURVIVAL of confidentiality, guarantee, insurance and DISPUTE clauses

steps.title: The two clauses the question does not name, but which decide all five
points: GOVERNING LAW AND DISPUTE RESOLUTION - yard, owner and ship are usually in three different countries
every right in limbs A to E is worth what it costs to enforce, so a clear governing law and a workable ARBITRATION provision - seat, rules, language - is what gives the others value
consider EXPERT DETERMINATION or a short-form procedure for the small urgent technical dispute that actually arises mid-docking, when arbitration is far too slow
ORDER OF PRECEDENCE - the specification, general conditions, quotation and clarifications WILL conflict; say which prevails
without it the parties argue about which document governs before they can argue about the point in dispute
RECOGNISED INDUSTRY STANDARD FORMS EXIST FOR SHIP REPAIR and their value is that these five issues are already allocated in a way both sides recognise
starting from a known form and negotiating the schedule is faster, cheaper and safer than drafting each docking from scratch

questions.understand_first: A repair contract looks like five separate commercial topics and is really one. Somebody is going to spend a large sum of money on work whose full extent nobody can know until the ship is opened up, in a yard that may be on the other side of the world, while the ship earns nothing. Every clause in the agreement is an answer to the same question - if this goes wrong, whose problem is it? Who pays if the job costs more than expected; who pays if it turns out to include something the parties never wrote down; who pays if it takes longer; who pays if it fails afterwards; and what happens if the whole arrangement collapses. Two practical realities sit underneath all of it. The first is that once the ship is in the dock, the yard is holding the thing the owner needs back, so every term worth having must be settled before she arrives - including, specifically, the terms on which she is allowed to leave if there is an argument about the bill. The second is that for the owner the expensive risk is almost never the price of the work; it is the days. A ship in dock is earning nothing, so an extra week can cost more than the item being argued over, which is why the machinery for ordering extra work and for handling delay deserves more attention than the headline figure. Read the five headings that way and they stop being five topics: they are cost, scope, time, defect, and what happens when the arrangement fails.
questions.memory_cue: Map the five limbs to four risks and an exit: COST (2), SCOPE (3), TIME (4), DEFECT (5), EXIT (6). One hook inside each: payment is THE YARD HAS THE SHIP (2); specification is EVERY GAP IS AN EXTRA (3); delay is THE VARIATION MUST BUY THE TIME TOO (4); guarantees are THEY FIX THE PART, YOU PAY THE OFF-HIRE (5); termination is SEAWORTHY AND TOWABLE (6). Close on the two unnamed clauses - WHICH LAW, AND WHICH DOCUMENT WINS (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: FRAME. Defined work, defined ship, defined time, defined price. Documents: agreement, general conditions, specification, quotation, clarifications, variation orders, with an order of precedence clause. The five limbs are five allocations of four risks - COST, SCOPE, TIME, DEFECT - plus EXIT. Two facts: the yard has the ship (agree everything before docking), and the owner's exposure is time, not price. Command verb is illustrate. A. PAYMENT. Lump sum for specified work; schedule of rates for quantum-uncertain (steel by weight, pipe by length, coating by area, staging, gas-freeing, day rates); provisional sums for open-and-inspect. Stage payments on docking / undocking / redelivery; retention until guarantee expires. Invoices on measured quantities and signed variation orders; yards usually exclude set-off. Currency, escalation, taxes, dock dues. Security both ways - owner's payment security, yard's refund/performance guarantee. THE LIEN: a repairer in possession will retain the ship - so fix what is payable on redelivery and what security may be given instead of cash, before docking. B. SPECIFICATION. It is the contract's definition of the work and where cost is controlled - every ambiguity is resolved on the day, in the yard's favour. Close gaps: workmanship standard, class rules, staging, gas-freeing, cleaning, protection, reinstatement, access work, who supplies what. Open-and-inspect by rate, with a defined inspection standard. VARIATIONS: in writing, by a named representative, BEFORE the work - recording the work, THE PRICE AND THE TIME EFFECT. Record price alone and you have surrendered the delay remedy. Owner's subcontractors: access, hours, facility charge, safety, responsibility. Rework at the yard's cost where its workmanship is at fault. C. TIME. Period from arrival/docking to redelivery; fix the owner's delivery date too. Liquidated damages: per day, after a grace period, capped, normally the sole and exclusive remedy, with a right to terminate at the cap. Permissible delays: extra work, owner default, late owner items, force majeure. Must be a genuine pre-estimate of loss or attacked as a penalty (jurisdiction-dependent). FORCE MAJEURE IS A CREATURE OF CONTRACT - no general doctrine; without it, only frustration. Defined events; notice, mitigation; effect is time, not money; termination if prolonged. D. GUARANTEE AND INSURANCE. Defects due to defective workmanship or materials within the period from redelivery (commonly about a year, negotiated); remedy at the yard or the reasonable cost elsewhere; notice and access; excludes wear and tear, owner misuse, owner-supplied materials and ALL CONSEQUENTIAL LOSS - they fix the part, you pay the off-hire. Insurance: owner's H&M notified of port risk, immobilisation and hot work; yard's ship repairers' liability for the vessel in its care, custody and control with an agreed limit and certificate before docking; yard's third-party and employer's liability; P&I for crew aboard; waiver of subrogation. Classic loss: fire during hot work. E. TERMINATION. Owner: yard insolvency, delay beyond the cap or long-stop, abandonment or lack of due diligence, unremedied material breach, prolonged force majeure. Yard: non-payment after notice, owner insolvency, failure to deliver the vessel, prolonged force majeure. Consequences: valuation and payment for work done and materials, release of the vessel and security for the lien, seaworthy and towable condition, return of owner materials and drawings, repayment of advances under the refund guarantee, removal and tow, survival of dispute clauses. CLOSE: governing law and arbitration, and order of precedence.
keywords: five allocations of cost, scope, time, defect - plus exit
the yard has the ship
the owner's exposure is time, not price
every ambiguity in the specification is charged as an extra
a variation must record the time as well as the money
liquidated damages are capped and usually exclusive
force majeure is a creature of contract - time, not money
the guarantee excludes consequential loss
ship repairers' liability - care, custody and control
seaworthy and towable on termination
governing law, arbitration, and order of precedence
critical_numbers: NO figure is asserted anywhere on this question - no liquidated damages rate, no cap percentage, no retention percentage, no grace period, no guarantee period in months, no insurance limit, no interest rate. All are negotiated and vary by yard, region, vessel and market
A guarantee period of about a year from redelivery is described as TYPICAL AND NEGOTIABLE, not as a rule
The five printed limbs do not divide evenly into sixteen marks; the paper does not divide them and no split is invented
quick_revision.critical_regulation: There is no regulation on this question, and saying so is itself a point. A ship repair contract is a commercial contract governed by the law the parties choose; no IMO instrument and no national maritime statute determines its content. Two general propositions apply and both are jurisdiction-dependent: a stipulated sum for delay is enforceable as liquidated damages where it is a genuine pre-estimate of the loss and may be unenforceable as a penalty where it is not; and in common-law systems force majeure is a creature of contract, with only the narrow doctrine of frustration behind it if no clause is drafted.
quick_revision.major_trap: Budgeting, first of all: five printed limbs against sixteen marks with no split, so nothing can be written at length and nothing may be omitted - and the command verb is illustrate, so a bare list of headings has not answered the question. The substantive traps are: omitting the repairer's lien from the payment limb, when it is the commercial fact that dominates the whole contract; agreeing a variation on price alone and thereby surrendering the delay remedy, which is the classic real-world failure and the point that links limbs B and C; asserting that force majeure is a general legal principle when in common-law systems it exists only if drafted, and that it gives money when it gives an extension of time; forgetting that the guarantee excludes consequential loss, so the yard replaces the part and the owner bears the off-hire; and writing termination as a bare right with no consequences, when the consequences - valuation, release of the ship against security, seaworthy and towable condition, return of materials - are the substance of the limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the ship repair contract question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the contract is and the one idea - five allocations of cost, scope, time and defect. 2 A payment terms. 3 B specification and additional work. 4 C period, liquidated damages and force majeure. 5 D guarantees and insurance. 6 E termination. 7 The two unnamed clauses - governing law and arbitration, and order of precedence.
retrieval_cards.why: Five limbs into sixteen marks with no split; the route fixes the budget and step 7 shows the subject is understood as a whole.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the organising idea behind the five printed limbs?
retrieval_cards.answer: Each is an allocation of the same four risks - cost, scope, time and defect - and every clause answers one question: who carries this if it goes wrong? Payment allocates cost, the specification allocates scope, period and liquidated damages allocate time, guarantees and insurance allocate defect, and termination decides what happens when the allocation fails altogether.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating it in the opening turns five disconnected headings into one argument.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why must the commercially important terms be agreed before the ship arrives at the yard?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the yard has the ship. Once she is docked the owner's leverage is largely gone and the yard's is at its maximum, and a repairer in possession will in practice assert a right to retain her until his account is settled. So the rates for unknown quantities, the exit terms and the security that may be offered instead of cash for a disputed sum must all be settled in advance.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the commercial fact that dominates the whole contract and the payment limb in particular.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is work of unknown quantity priced in a repair contract?
retrieval_cards.answer: By an agreed schedule of rates - steel renewal by weight, pipework by length, tank cleaning and coating by area, staging, gas-freeing and day rates by trade - together with provisional sums for open-and-inspect items, all fixed before the tender is accepted. The alternative is negotiating the rate on the day with the tank open and the ship immobilised.
retrieval_cards.why: It is where an owner actually keeps control of cost on a docking.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must a variation order record, and what happens if it records only the price?
retrieval_cards.answer: The work, the price, and the effect on the delivery date. If it records only the price, the owner has bought the extra work and inadvertently surrendered his delay remedy - the yard will say the additional work extended the docking and the liquidated damages clause is disapplied for that period.
retrieval_cards.why: The classic real-world failure, and the point that links the specification limb to the delay limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the four features of a liquidated damages provision that matter most?
retrieval_cards.answer: A pre-agreed daily sum after a grace period; a cap expressed as a proportion of the contract price; exclusivity, so it is normally the owner's sole remedy for delay in place of actual lost earnings; and a right to terminate once the cap is reached. Permissible delays - extra work ordered, owner default, late owner-supplied items and force majeure - extend the date instead of triggering damages.
retrieval_cards.why: The cap and the exclusivity are usually more important commercially than the daily rate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why might a liquidated damages clause be unenforceable?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the sum stipulated must be a genuine pre-estimate of the loss the owner would suffer. A figure fixed to punish rather than to compensate may be attacked as a penalty and struck down, leaving the owner to prove his actual loss. This is jurisdiction-dependent.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why the rate is tied to prevailing earnings rather than set arbitrarily high.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is force majeure implied into a contract, and what does it give you?
retrieval_cards.answer: In common-law systems it is not implied. Force majeure is a creature of contract - if it is not drafted, it does not exist, and the party is left with the narrow doctrine of frustration. Where drafted, it gives an extension of time and not money, each side generally bearing its own costs, with a right for either party to terminate if the event persists beyond a stated period.
retrieval_cards.why: Both halves are commonly stated backwards, and both are worth a mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a force majeure clause need besides a list of events?
retrieval_cards.answer: That the events be beyond the reasonable control of the affected party and not caused by its own default; prompt written notice within a stated time with particulars; a duty to mitigate and to resume as soon as possible; notice when the event ends; and a stated period after which either party may terminate. Notice provisions are conditions and are commonly missed in practice.
retrieval_cards.why: The procedure is where force majeure claims actually fail.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A guarantee defect puts the ship off hire for ten days. Who bears the hire?
retrieval_cards.answer: The owner. A repair guarantee almost always excludes consequential loss, including loss of time, hire and profit. The yard makes good the defect due to its defective workmanship or materials - at its own yard, or by bearing the reasonable cost of repair elsewhere on a pre-approved quotation - but the commercial loss stays with the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: It shows what the guarantee is actually worth rather than merely that one exists.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What insurance must be in place while a ship is in a repair yard?
retrieval_cards.answer: The owner's hull and machinery cover continuing, with underwriters notified of the port risk, immobilisation and hot work; the owner's P&I where crew remain on board. The yard must carry ship repairers' liability cover for damage to vessels in its care, custody and control, with an agreed minimum limit and a certificate produced before docking, plus third-party and employer's liability. A waiver of subrogation between the two sides' insurers avoids circular claims.
retrieval_cards.why: Ship repairers' liability is the yard's central cover and the one an owner should demand evidence of.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You terminate mid-docking. What must the termination clause provide for?
retrieval_cards.answer: Valuation and payment for work actually done and materials ordered or fabricated to the ship's specification; release of the vessel and what security must be given for a disputed balance; a seaworthy and towable condition with openings closed and systems reinstated so far as practicable; return of owner-supplied materials, drawings and technical information; repayment of advances under the refund guarantee; who arranges and pays for removal and tow; and survival of the confidentiality, guarantee, insurance and dispute clauses.
retrieval_cards.why: A clause that stops at 'either party may terminate' is nearly useless - the consequences are the substance.

Every proposition is industry guidance or commercial and engineering judgement, and the answer states this openly. If contract material is ever acquired, this question should be re-verified against it; the absence is recorded as an accepted limitation and not as a defect.

reverify_before_publication.why: Standard forms are copyright commercial documents and MIW holds none. Their existence is noted solely to make the point that starting from a known form reduces negotiation cost. No provision is attributed to any form, and a later editor must not attach one.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No figure is asserted anywhere - no liquidated damages rate, no cap percentage, no retention percentage, no grace period, no guarantee period in months, no insurance limit, no interest rate
reverify_before_publication.why: Every one is negotiated and varies by yard, region, vessel type and market conditions. Where a common commercial position is described - such as a guarantee of about a year - it is expressly stated as typical and negotiable. If a figure is ever added it must be sourced and must be stated as a market norm rather than a rule.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No proposition of law is asserted for any named jurisdiction, and the repairer's lien is described as a commercial reality rather than a rule of any stated law
reverify_before_publication.why: The two general legal points - penalty versus liquidated damages, and force majeure as a creature of contract - are flagged as jurisdiction-dependent and are attributed to no statute and no decided case. The existence and extent of a repairer's possessory lien differ between jurisdictions and MIW holds material on none of them; what is asserted is the practical consequence, which is jurisdiction-independent.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No pandemic-era force majeure drafting or interpretation practice is asserted as settled, and no market condition is described
reverify_before_publication.why: How force majeure clauses were interpreted and renegotiated during and after the pandemic was a live legal and commercial debate at this sitting, and asserting an outcome would be unsafe. Yard capacity, docking prices and lead times also moved sharply in the years around this sitting; asserting nothing about them means nothing in the answer can date.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Five printed limbs, sixteen marks, no split anywhere, and the command verb is ILLUSTRATE - which is neither 'list' nor 'discuss'. The examiner wants each of the five issues shown working: what risk it allocates, how the clause does it, and what goes wrong when it is drafted badly. He is testing commercial judgement of the kind a Chief Engineer contributes to a docking - where the money actually leaks, and what a superintendent must settle before the ship arrives - rather than legal drafting skill.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks across five limbs with no printed split, and none invented. Roughly three marks a limb, with limb C allowed slightly more because it carries three named sub-topics where the others carry one or two, and one or two marks for the framing and the closing observation. The binding constraint is that NOTHING can be written at length; a candidate who writes a page on payment terms will not finish the question.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate knows where the commercial risk actually sits: that the specification, not the price, is where cost is controlled; that a variation must capture the time as well as the money; that the yard's possession of the ship is the dominant bargaining fact; that a guarantee excludes consequential loss so the owner bears the off-hire; and that force majeure exists only because it is drafted. A candidate who also names governing law and order of precedence - clauses the question does not list - has shown he understands the contract as a whole.
primary_source_plan: ESTABLISH FIRST WHETHER ANY DONOR OR ANY HELD MATERIAL EXISTS - run targeted searches on repair contract, shipyard, force majeure, liquidated damages, termination and tender before assuming the subject is unbuilt
Search the corpus directly for any standard form, contract commentary or contract law material, and set the evidence class on the result rather than on expectation
Read the two 'dry dock' matches in the corpus and decide explicitly whether they are the same subject - they are not
Decide, before drafting, which figures may appear at all, given that no form is held and every figure is negotiated
Decide, before drafting, how the two general legal propositions will be flagged, given that no jurisdiction is named in the question
Identify for each limb the one worked illustration that will satisfy the command verb, rather than adding examples afterwards
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - and unusually, for a structural reason rather than a fortunate one. This question has no regulatory content at all: no IMO instrument, no national maritime statute and no dated legal proposition is engaged, so there is nothing that could have entered force, been amended or been superseded at this sitting. The two legal propositions used are long-settled features of common-law contracting and are attributed to no statute or case, so no citation can go stale. The only freshness discipline required is negative - assert no market condition and no post-pandemic drafting practice as settled.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: HIGH, and it is managed by asserting nothing. A repair contract is governed by the law the parties choose, and the yard, the owner and the ship are typically in three different countries. No proposition of law is therefore asserted for any named jurisdiction; the two general points that do appear are expressly flagged as jurisdiction-dependent, and the repairer's lien is described by its practical consequence rather than as a rule of any stated law. That is why the closing step names the governing law clause as the one that gives the other five their value.
technical_ambiguities: Whether the specification is a technical or a contractual document - it is both, and treating it as only technical is how cost is lost
Whether a variation is complete when the price is agreed - it is not; the time effect must be captured in the same document
Whether force majeure operates without a clause - not in common-law systems
Whether force majeure gives money or time - time
Whether liquidated damages are always enforceable - not if they are a penalty rather than a genuine pre-estimate
Whether a guarantee covers the owner's lost earnings - no; consequential loss is excluded
Whether the owner's hull policy simply continues unchanged in the yard - not without notifying underwriters of the port risk, immobilisation and hot work
Whether a termination right is worth anything without stated consequences - it is not
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Three lines of framing that state the organising idea and the two commercial facts, then one compact block per printed limb in the printed order, each opening with the risk it allocates and each carrying a worked illustration - a rate for an open-and-inspect item, a stern-tube variation, a yard strike, a fire during hot work. Bullets rather than prose throughout, because five limbs in sixteen marks leaves no room for paragraphs, with two small tables where the material is genuinely two-sided - the insurance allocation and the termination events. Close on the two clauses the question does not name, and on why a recognised standard form is commercially valuable.
