blocks.h: 1. What the SEEMP is, and where the four steps live

blocks.p: The Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) is required by regulation 26 of MARPOL Annex VI. It is a ship-specific, operational management document kept on board, developed and reviewed taking into account the guidelines adopted by the Organization. The guidelines operative at this examination are the 2022 Guidelines, resolution MEPC.346(78), adopted on 10 June 2022, which revoked the 2016 Guidelines, MEPC.282(70).

Note the numbering, because it is where most marks are quietly lost. The SEEMP sits at regulation 26, not regulation 22: chapter 4 of Annex VI was renumbered by MEPC.328(76), which entered into force on 1 November 2022 - seven months before this examination. Within chapter 4, the goal is stated at regulation 20, the fuel oil data collection system at regulation 27, and the operational carbon intensity indicator at regulation 28.
The plan has three Parts, and it matters for this question that the four steps belong to Part I:

ul: Part I - Ship Management Plan to Improve Energy Efficiency, required by regulation 26.1, applying to any ship of 400 GT and above. This is the part built on the four-step cycle.

Part II - Ship Fuel Oil Consumption Data Collection Plan, required by regulation 26.2, applying to any ship of 5,000 GT and above. It describes the methodology for collecting the data required by regulation 27 and reporting it to the Administration.

Part III - Ship Operational Carbon Intensity Plan, required by regulations 26.3 and 28.8 for ships of 5,000 GT and above in the listed categories. It carries the attained annual operational CII methodology, the required CII for the next three years, a three-year implementation plan, a procedure for self-evaluation, and - for a ship rated D for three consecutive years or E in a single year - a plan of corrective actions.

blocks.p: Section 3.6 states the cycle directly: Part I should be developed as a ship-specific plan by the company and should reflect efforts to improve energy efficiency and reduce carbon intensity through four steps - planning, implementation, monitoring, and self-evaluation and improvement - and "these components play a critical role in the continuous cycle". It adds that with each iteration some elements of Part I will necessarily change while others may remain. Section 3.7 carries the standing qualification that safety considerations are paramount at all times, and that the trade a ship is engaged in may determine which measures are feasible.

Two further permissions are worth a line each, because they show the plan is meant to be absorbed rather than added: a company already running an ISO 14001 environmental management system should treat efficiency monitoring within it (3.3), and Part I may form part of the ship's safety management system (3.4).

blocks.h: 2. Step 1 - Planning

blocks.p: The Guidelines are unusually emphatic here. Section 4.1.1: planning is the most crucial stage of Part I, because it primarily determines both the ship's current status of energy usage and carbon intensity and the expected improvement - so sufficient time should be devoted to it. Planning has four components:

ol: Ship-specific measures. Establish the ship's present status; identify measures already undertaken and how effective they have actually been; identify what further can be adopted. The Guidelines warn (4.1.3) that not all measures can be applied to all ships, or even to the same ship under different operating conditions, and that SOME OF THEM ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE - and add the practical point that initial savings can be reinvested in more difficult or expensive upgrades.

Company-specific measures. Efficiency does not depend on single-ship management alone (4.1.5): repair yards, owners, operators, charterers, cargo owners, fuel suppliers, ports and traffic management services all bear on it. The Guidelines' own example is "just in time" arrival, which requires good early communication among operators, ports and traffic management services. A company-level plan and coordination is therefore recommended.
Human resource development. Awareness-raising and training for personnel ashore and on board (4.1.6) - which the Guidelines call both a planning component and a critical element of implementation.

Goal setting (4.1.7). For a ship subject to regulation 28, the goal should be consistent with the continuous CII improvement that regulation requires. For a ship or company not subject to regulation 28 the Guidelines say expressly that there is no requirement to define a goal, to communicate it publicly, or to be subject to external inspection, survey or audit in respect of the SEEMP - though a meaningful goal should still be set as a signal of commitment, using indicators such as annual fuel consumption, AER, cgDIST, EEOI or another CII. In all cases the goal should be measurable and easy to understand.

blocks.p: Examples. Ship-specific: speed optimisation; weather routeing; hull and propeller condition management with a coating and polishing regime; trim optimisation; and confirming berth availability and arrival time with the destination port, so the ship is not steaming hard in order to wait at anchor. Company-specific: negotiating just-in-time arrival with terminals, which cannot be delivered from the bridge and needs the operator, the port and traffic management talking early. Mutually exclusive: a fixed-pitch propeller re-pitched for a lower service speed forecloses later gains from increasing speed, and slow steaming interacts with waste-heat recovery output. Goal: "reduce AER by a stated percentage year on year, consistent with the required CII" - measurable, and tied to the regulation.

blocks.h: 3. Step 2 - Implementation

blocks.p: Section 4.2.1: once measures are identified it is essential to establish a system for implementing them. That means developing procedures for energy management, defining the tasks associated with them and assigning those tasks to responsible personnel, with defined levels of authority and lines of communication, and procedures for internal audit and management review where relevant. Part I should state how each measure is to be implemented, who is responsible, and the start and end dates of each. The Guidelines note that building this system can be treated as part of planning and completed there.
Section 4.2.2 adds record-keeping, and two duties that are easy marks because they are counter-intuitive:

ul: if an identified measure cannot be implemented for any reason, the reason should be recorded for internal use - a plan that quietly drops a measure has destroyed the evidence its own next self-evaluation needs;

events and operational conditions outside the control of the ship's crew - the Guidelines instance waiting for berths, extended port dwell times and operation in severe adverse weather - should be documented, because they may affect the ship's rating and cannot be reconstructed afterwards.

blocks.p: Examples. The Chief Engineer is named as responsible for the hull and propeller condition regime, with inspection at each dry-docking and in-water polishing at defined fouling thresholds; the Master for trim and speed compliance against the passage plan; the shore superintendent for retrofit scheduling. A shaft generator retrofit deferred because the yard slot moved is recorded with the reason, so that the next evaluation does not read it as a failure of the measure itself.

blocks.h: 4. Step 3 - Monitoring

blocks.p: Section 4.3.1: energy efficiency should be monitored quantitatively, by an established method and preferably by an international standard. The monitoring tool should target the goal indicator set at planning - AER, cgDIST, EEOI or another CII - and a ship subject to regulation 28 is likely to use the CII itself, calculated in accordance with the guidelines developed by the Organization.

ul: 4.3.4 - monitor at regular intervals, for consistency of data and to assist verification; fuel oil consumption monitored using daily reporting, such as noon reports, or at higher frequency.

4.3.5 - continuous, consistent and reliable data collection is the foundation of monitoring, so a monitoring system with data-collection procedures and assigned personnel must be developed - and, again, completed at the planning stage.

4.3.6 - to avoid unnecessary administrative burden on ships' staff, monitoring should be carried out as much as possible by shore staff where data can be transferred automatically, using existing required records such as the official and engineering logbooks and the oil record books.
4.3.7 - where a ship diverts to engage in search and rescue, the data obtained during those operations should not be used in energy efficiency monitoring and should be recorded separately.

blocks.p: Examples. Noon reports feeding a performance system that separates hull-fouling degradation from weather effect; a shaft power meter and mass flow meters giving consumption independent of tank soundings; the attained CII tracked monthly against the required value, so that corrective action is taken in month seven rather than discovered in the annual return.

blocks.h: 5. Step 4 - Self-evaluation and improvement

blocks.p: Section 4.4.1: this is the final phase of the management cycle, and its purpose is to produce meaningful feedback for the coming first stage - the planning stage of the next improvement cycle. Section 4.4.2 gives four purposes:

ol: evaluate the effectiveness of the planned measures and of their implementation;
deepen the understanding of the overall characteristics of the ship's operation - what types of measure can or cannot function effectively, and how and why;
comprehend the trend of the efficiency improvement of that ship; and
develop the improved management plan for the next cycle by identifying further opportunities.

blocks.p: Note the second and third. The Guidelines do not ask only "did it work?" but "why did it work, and what is the trend" - and section 4.4.3 makes that explicit by requiring that time be invested in identifying the cause and effect of the performance during the evaluated period, so lessons learned are taken into account in revising the plan. That is what converts a year of data into a better plan rather than into a score.

Examples. Evaluation shows weather routeing delivered most of its claimed saving on ocean legs and almost none on short coastal legs, so the next cycle applies it selectively and reinvests the effort in trim optimisation. Hull coating performance is found to degrade faster on a trade with long idle periods in warm water, so the next cycle shortens the polishing interval rather than blaming the coating. And for a ship subject to regulation 28, Part III carries this further with a statutory consequence: rated D for three consecutive years or E in a single year, a plan of corrective actions must be developed and included in the SEEMP.

blocks.h: 6. Why the cycle is critical, not merely administrative

blocks.p: The printed command asks for the critical role of each component, so the answer must show why removing any one of them breaks the whole:

rows: Establishes the baseline and selects measures that suit this ship and this trade
Measures are adopted by fashion rather than by fit, and no saving can be claimed because there is no baseline to claim it against
Converts intention into assigned, dated, auditable action
The plan becomes a document carried for inspection rather than a way the ship is run
Effectiveness becomes a matter of opinion; the return is unverifiable, and adverse weather cannot be distinguished from poor operation
Turns the data into a better plan, and explains why measures worked
The cycle does not close - the same plan is re-issued each year and improvement stops

blocks.p: The cycle is also what keeps the plan ship-specific and living rather than generic: section 3.6 says that with each iteration some elements of Part I will necessarily change while others may remain. And it is what connects an operational management document to a regulatory outcome, because the same four beats reappear in Part III - planning becomes the required CII for the next three years and the three-year implementation plan, monitoring becomes the attained annual operational CII, and self-evaluation becomes the plan of corrective actions.

Two closing observations fix the answer to this examination. First, note what the SEEMP is not: it is operational, not technical. The EEDI and EEXI fix what the ship is, once; the SEEMP governs how she is operated, continuously - which is why it is a cycle and they are not. Second, the timing gives the cycle unusual force just now: the CII entered into force on 1 January 2023, so this is the first year in which data is being collected against it and no ship has yet been rated. Every ship is presently inside her first monitoring period, which is precisely the point at which the planning and implementation steps determine what the first rating will be. The Committee has also undertaken to keep these Guidelines under review, noting that under regulations 25.3 and 28.11 a review of the technical and operational measures shall be completed by 1 January 2026.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks, one limb, and the question names its own four sections. That is a gift and a trap. The gift is that the structure is handed to you. The trap is that four equal paragraphs of description will not score sixteen marks, because the printed command is "describe with suitable examples, the critical role of each of these components" - three separate demands. You must (i) describe each step, (ii) give examples, and (iii) say why each is critical. An answer that does only the first has answered roughly a third of the question.

The route therefore spends one step per component, attaches the examples inside each step, and then adds a dedicated criticality step - the table at step 6 - which is where the "critical role" marks are actually banked. The framing at step 1 is worth the space because it lets you say something most candidates cannot: that the four steps are the framework of Part I specifically, not of the whole plan.

blocks.h: Which guidelines - and why this is the whole currency test

blocks.p: The SEEMP Guidelines are re-adopted periodically and each edition revokes the last. At this examination the operative edition is MEPC.346(78), the 2022 Guidelines, adopted 10 June 2022 - a year old - which revoked MEPC.282(70), the 2016 Guidelines.

This is the single most valuable thing to get right, and it is also the easiest to get wrong from later material. If you are revising from a 2024 or 2025 paper you will find a different resolution number, and it is wrong here. The 2022 Guidelines are the operative edition for the whole of 2023 and beyond into 2024; anything adopted later belongs to a later paper. Equally, an answer citing the 2016 Guidelines is a year out of date at this sitting, and quite a lot of circulating material still does.

blocks.h: The regulation number is the other easy mark to lose

blocks.p: A great deal of older material - textbooks, circulars and notes written before 2023 - cites the SEEMP as MARPOL Annex VI regulation 22. That was correct until chapter 4 was renumbered by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022. Since then the SEEMP is regulation 26, with Part I at 26.1, Part II at 26.2 and Part III at 26.3 read with 28.8.

At this sitting the renumbering is only about seven months old, so a candidate working from anything written before late 2022 will have the old number. Getting it right, and being able to say why the old number exists, is a visible sign of current reading. Carry the neighbours too: regulation 20 the goal of chapter 4, regulation 27 the data collection system, regulation 28 the CII.

blocks.h: Where the decarbonisation position actually stood in June 2023

blocks.p: If the answer reaches for context it must be the context of this sitting, and this is where the traps cluster:

ul: EEXI and CII entered into force on 1 January 2023, so at this examination the CII is five months old, 2023 is the first data year and it is still running, and no ship has yet been rated. Do not describe rating experience, rating distributions or how the fleet performed - none exists yet.

The operative strategy is the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018. The 2023 Strategy was adopted at MEPC 80 on 7 July 2023 - after this examination. Citing it here is future contamination and is the commonest single error a candidate revising from a later paper will make.

MEPC 80 has not yet met, so nothing from it exists. The only forward-looking statement legitimately available is the one in the Guidelines themselves: operative paragraph 4 records that under regulations 25.3 and 28.11 a review of the technical and operational measures shall be completed by 1 January 2026. That is a requirement with a deadline, not a process with a result.
Do not import any mid-term measure as adopted. None was, at this sitting.

blocks.h: The five facts from section 4 that most answers miss

ul: Planning is expressly the "most crucial stage" (4.1.1). Say so and attribute it - it converts a generic opening into a cited one.
Some measures are mutually exclusive (4.1.3). Almost nobody says this, and it demonstrates real engineering understanding rather than a list of green measures.
Reasons for non-implementation must be recorded (4.2.2). Counter-intuitive, and precise.
Conditions outside the crew's control should be documented (4.2.2) - waiting for berths, extended port dwell, severe adverse weather - because they may affect the rating.
Search and rescue data is excluded from monitoring and recorded separately (4.3.7). A small, exact, memorable point that proves the Guidelines were opened.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Citing the SEEMP as regulation 22. It has been regulation 26 since 1 November 2022.
Citing a 2024 guidelines edition. At this sitting the operative edition is MEPC.346(78), the 2022 Guidelines - anything later does not exist yet.
Citing the 2016 Guidelines, MEPC.282(70). They were revoked by MEPC.346(78) in June 2022.
Citing the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy. It was adopted on 7 July 2023 - one month after this examination. The operative strategy here is the Initial Strategy of 2018.
Describing CII rating experience or a rating distribution. 2023 is the first data year, it is still running, and no ship has been rated.
Presenting the four steps as the structure of the whole SEEMP. They are the framework of Part I.
Describing the steps without giving examples, when the question prints "with suitable examples".
Describing the steps without saying why each is critical, when the question prints "the critical role of each".
Confusing the SEEMP with the EEDI or EEXI. Those are technical and one-off; the SEEMP is operational and continuous.
Writing that Part I applies to ships of 5,000 GT and above. That is Part II; Part I is 400 GT and above.
Treating monitoring as something done only for the annual return. The Guidelines require regular intervals and daily fuel reporting.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Whose plan is it?" Part I is developed as a ship-specific plan by the company (3.6) - not written on board, though implemented on board.

"Is the SEEMP audited?" The answer splits. For a ship not subject to regulation 28 the Guidelines say expressly there is no requirement to define a goal, publish it, or be subject to external inspection, survey or audit in respect of the SEEMP (4.1.7.2). For a ship subject to regulation 28 the position differs, because Part III is verified. Knowing that the answer splits is worth a mark.

"What happens if the ship rates badly?" D for three consecutive years, or E in one year, triggers a plan of corrective actions in the SEEMP. Note that at this sitting that is a requirement, not yet an experience.
"Why must adverse weather be recorded?" Because it may affect the rating and cannot be reconstructed afterwards - 4.2.2.
"Where does safety come in?" Section 3.7 - safety considerations are paramount at all times, and the trade may determine which measures are feasible.
"Can the SEEMP sit inside another system?" Yes - ISO 14001 (3.3), and Part I may form part of the safety management system (3.4).
"Which GHG strategy applies?" The Initial Strategy of 2018. The 2023 Strategy is one month future at this sitting.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which regulation requires the SEEMP, and which guidelines are current? Regulation 26 of MARPOL Annex VI; the 2022 Guidelines, MEPC.346(78).
What did those guidelines revoke? The 2016 Guidelines, MEPC.282(70).
What are the three Parts and their thresholds? Part I 400 GT and above; Part II 5,000 GT and above; Part III for ships of 5,000 GT and above in the listed categories, under regulations 26.3 and 28.8.
Name the four steps. Planning, implementation, monitoring, self-evaluation and improvement.
Which step do the Guidelines call the most crucial, and why? Planning - it determines the current status and the achievable improvement.
Give two ship-specific and one company-specific measure. Speed optimisation and hull condition management; just-in-time arrival negotiated with the terminal.
What must be recorded when a measure is not implemented? The reason, for internal use.
What data is excluded from energy efficiency monitoring? Data from search and rescue diversions, recorded separately.
How does Part III mirror the cycle? Required CII and three-year implementation plan; attained annual CII; plan of corrective actions.
When must the review of the technical and operational measures be completed? By 1 January 2026, under regulations 25.3 and 28.11.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: PIMS - Plan, Implement, Monitor, Self-evaluate. It is a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle wearing IMO clothes, which is exactly why section 3.3 says a company already running ISO 14001 should treat efficiency monitoring as part of its existing management system, and section 3.4 allows Part I to form part of the safety management system.

For the four sub-parts of planning: SHIP, COMPANY, PEOPLE, GOAL - ship-specific measures, company-specific measures, human resource development, goal setting. For implementation: WHO, WHAT, BY WHEN. For monitoring: QUANTITATIVE, CONTINUOUS, SHORE-SIDE. For the four purposes of self-evaluation: did it work, why, what is the trend, what next.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: The four steps, their content and every section number in this answer are taken from MEPC.346(78) read directly. Three limitations are recorded. MIW holds no licensed consolidated MARPOL Annex VI, so the numbering and content of regulations 20, 25, 26, 27 and 28 are established from the recitals and cross-references inside MEPC.346(78) rather than from a licensed Annex text, and no regulation is quoted verbatim. No CII rating, distribution or fleet statistic is asserted, and none could be - 2023 is the first data year and it is still running at this sitting. And the Initial GHG Strategy of 2018 is cited by identity and by its levels of ambition; MIW holds no text of it and it is not quoted.

One currency instruction for any later editor, and it is the most important on this paper. MEPC.346(78) is the correct edition here and must not be advanced. This question recurs verbatim at later sittings where a different guidelines edition, a different GHG strategy and real rating experience all apply. Every one of those is future at June 2023. Do not update the resolution number, do not substitute the 2023 GHG Strategy for the Initial Strategy, and do not add rating experience. The one thing that does not need reversing is the regulation 26 numbering, which had already taken effect seven months before this examination.

notes: THIS QUESTION CARRIES THE LARGEST TEMPORAL REVERSAL ON THE PAPER AND IS THE CLEAREST DEMONSTRATION IN THE BATCH THAT AN EXACT QUESTION IS NOT AN EXACT ANSWER. The stem is verbatim identical to QP2412-Q8, one of the most thoroughly built objects in the corpus, and ALMOST EVERY REGULATORY STATEMENT IN THAT OBJECT IS WRONG FOR JUNE 2023. Four separate reversals were performed and each was re-derived from primary source.

REVERSAL 1 - THE GUIDELINES EDITION. The operative edition at this sitting is MEPC.346(78), the 2022 Guidelines, ADOPTED 10 JUNE 2022 and read directly this session. The donor cites MEPC.395(82), which was not adopted until 4 OCTOBER 2024 - SIXTEEN MONTHS AFTER this examination - and it records MEPC.388(81) as an intermediate 2024 amendment. NEITHER INSTRUMENT EXISTS AT THIS SITTING. The correct revocation chain here runs backwards, not forwards: MEPC.346(78) operative paragraph 5 revokes MEPC.282(70), the 2016 Guidelines.

REVERSAL 2 - THE GHG STRATEGY, AND IT IS THE SHARPEST ON THE WHOLE PAPER. The donor cites the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, MEPC.377(80), adopted 7 JULY 2023 at MEPC 80. THIS SITTING IS JUNE 2023 - MEPC 80 HAS NOT YET MET AND THE 2023 STRATEGY IS ONE MONTH FUTURE. The operative strategy is the INITIAL IMO GHG STRATEGY OF 2018. This is the paper-level boundary recorded in the anchor and it bites here more directly than anywhere else on the paper.

THE ONE-MONTH BOUNDARY IS DAY-INDEPENDENT AND THAT WAS CHECKED. The paper prints JUNE 2023 with no day. MEPC 80 sat 3 to 7 July 2023, so EVERY possible sitting day in June falls before it. Unlike the July 2023 paper, which straddles this boundary irresolvably, June 2023 is unambiguous and no reasoning about the examination day is required.

REVERSAL 3 - CII RATING EXPERIENCE. The donor correctly records that 2023 was the first full CII data year and that the first ratings were issued during 2024. AT THIS SITTING 2023 IS THE FIRST DATA YEAR AND IT IS STILL RUNNING; NO SHIP HAS BEEN RATED AT ALL. The answer therefore states the D-three-years-or-E trigger for a plan of corrective actions as a REQUIREMENT and asserts no experience of it, no rating distribution and no fleet statistic - and none could be asserted.

REVERSAL 4 - THE REVIEW OF THE SHORT-TERM MEASURES. The donor records the MEPC 82 review as in progress. That has no counterpart here; MEPC 82 is sixteen months future. The only forward-looking statement legitimately available at this sitting is MEPC.346(78) OPERATIVE PARAGRAPH 4, which records that under regulations 25.3 and 28.11 a review of the technical and operational measures SHALL BE COMPLETED BY 1 JANUARY 2026. That is stated as a requirement with a deadline, not as a process with a result.

ONE ELEMENT TRANSFERS UNCHANGED, AND IT WAS VERIFIED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. The SEEMP is required by MARPOL ANNEX VI REGULATION 26, not regulation 22. Chapter 4 was renumbered by MEPC.328(76) with effect from 1 NOVEMBER 2022 - SEVEN MONTHS before this sitting. The renumbering had therefore already taken effect and the donor's numbering is correct here.

TSCR-3 IS ENGAGED BY THIS QUESTION AND IS DECLINED, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT TRUE SOURCE FINDING ON THE PAPER. The corpus amendment register for MARPOL Annex VI records the entry into force of MEPC.328(76) as 2023-11-01. THAT IS WRONG; THE CORRECT DATE IS 1 NOVEMBER 2022, and this paper sits INSIDE the window the error corrupts. Consuming the corpus date would place a June 2023 sitting BEFORE the revised Annex VI entered into force, and the answer would then have to say that the SEEMP is required by regulation 22, that chapter 4 had not been renumbered, and that EEXI and CII were not yet applicable - three wrong statements, one of which inverts the substance of this very question. THE CORPUS FIGURE IS DECLINED. It is refuted from INSIDE the corpus by primary source: the preamble of MEPC.346(78), read directly this session, states that MEPC.328(76) 'will enter into force on 1 November 2022'. No corpus file was touched; TSCR-3 remains OPEN and is re-reported, not repaired.
TSCR-4 IS NOT ENGAGED. It concerns MEPC.376(80) being presented as current. MEPC.376(80) is a July 2023 instrument and is FUTURE at this sitting, so no question on this paper consumes it.

A FURTHER FUTURE-CONTAMINATION CHECK WAS RUN AND IS CLEAN. No 33rd Assembly instrument appears (6 December 2023, six months future); no MEPC 81, 82 or 83 material appears; no IMO Net-Zero Framework or GFI material appears (October 2025); no EU ETS or FuelEU Maritime material appears, both being future at this sitting and in any event outside the SEEMP framework.
MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958 governs the paper at this sitting; the 2025 Act is thirty-three months future. Neither is engaged - MARPOL Annex VI applies internationally and India is a Party.

DONOR CONTAMINATION SWEEP: THE HIGHEST-RISK SWEEP ON THE PAPER, AND CLEAN ON INSPECTION. The donor was read IN FULL EXPRESSLY TO IDENTIFY WHAT HAD TO BE REVERSED rather than to supply content, and the entire regulatory layer was re-derived from MEPC.346(78) read at source. What was taken from the donor is the six-step route, which is a correct decomposition of the printed command and carries no dated claim.

questions.understand_first: This question hands you its own structure, which is why it is easier to answer adequately than to answer well. The four steps are printed in the stem, so describing them earns only part of the marks; the printed command asks for the critical role of each, with examples. So the real task is to show that the four steps form a closed loop in which each stage is load-bearing - plan without monitoring and you cannot prove a saving; monitor without evaluating and the loop never closes; implement without naming who does what by when and the plan becomes a document carried for inspection rather than a way the ship is run. Two framing facts separate a current answer from a stale one. The four steps are the framework of one part of the plan and not of the whole thing, because the plan also carries a data-collection part and a carbon-intensity part that apply to bigger ships. And the requirement moved recently to a different regulation number, so a great deal of circulating material cites the old one. The timing also gives the cycle unusual force just now: the carbon-intensity rules took effect at the start of this year, so every ship is in the middle of the first period of data collection, with no ratings issued to anybody yet - which means the planning and implementing that is being done right now is what will determine the first result anyone sees.
questions.memory_cue: PIMS - Plan, Implement, Monitor, Self-evaluate. It is Plan-Do-Check-Act in IMO clothes. Inside planning: SHIP, COMPANY, PEOPLE, GOAL (2). Implementation is WHO, WHAT, BY WHEN (3). Monitoring is QUANTITATIVE, CONTINUOUS, SHORE-SIDE (4). Self-evaluation asks did it work, why, what trend, what next (5). Then close with BREAK ONE LINK AND THE LOOP FAILS (6).

quick_revision.recall_15s: SEEMP = MARPOL Annex VI regulation 26 (NOT reg 22 - renumbered by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 Nov 2022, seven months before this sitting). Ship-specific, operational, kept on board. Guidelines at this sitting: MEPC.346(78), the 2022 Guidelines, adopted 10 June 2022, REVOKING MEPC.282(70) (2016). Chapter 4: reg 20 goal, reg 27 data collection, reg 28 CII; regs 25.3 and 28.11 - review to be completed by 1 January 2026. Three Parts: Part I (reg 26.1, 400 GT+) - the four-step cycle; Part II (reg 26.2, 5,000 GT+) - fuel oil data collection plan; Part III (regs 26.3 and 28.8, 5,000 GT+ in listed categories) - operational carbon intensity plan with required CII for three years, a three-year implementation plan, self-evaluation, and a plan of corrective actions for D three years running or E once. 3.6 states the four steps and calls them critical to the continuous cycle, with some elements changing each iteration; 3.7 safety paramount; 3.3 ISO 14001; 3.4 may form part of the SMS. 1 PLANNING (4.1) - the MOST CRUCIAL stage; ship-specific measures (some mutually exclusive), company-specific measures (just in time needs early communication), human resource development, goal setting - measurable and easy to understand; ships not subject to reg 28 need no goal, no publication, no external audit of the SEEMP. 2 IMPLEMENTATION (4.2) - establish a system: procedures, defined tasks, responsible personnel, levels of authority, lines of communication, start and end dates; record the reason if a measure cannot be implemented; document conditions outside the crew's control - berth waiting, port dwell, severe weather - because they may affect the rating. 3 MONITORING (4.3) - quantitative, established method, preferably an international standard; targets the goal indicator (AER, cgDIST, EEOI, CII); regular intervals, fuel by noon reports; continuous consistent reliable data is the foundation; shore-side where possible using logbooks and oil record books; SAR data excluded and recorded separately. 4 SELF-EVALUATION (4.4) - final phase, feeds the next planning stage; four purposes: effectiveness, understanding how and why, the trend, the improved plan; 4.4.3 invest time in cause and effect. WHY CRITICAL: no baseline means no provable saving; no assignment means a document not a practice; no consistent data means opinion; no evaluation means the loop never closes. Part III mirrors it. Contrast: EEDI/EEXI technical and one-off; SEEMP operational and continuous. AT THIS SITTING: CII in force 1 Jan 2023 - first data year, still running, NO ship rated yet; operative strategy is the Initial GHG Strategy of 2018 - the 2023 Strategy is 7 July 2023, ONE MONTH FUTURE.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 26 requires each ship to keep on board a Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan, developed and reviewed taking into account the guidelines adopted by the Organization - which at this sitting are the 2022 Guidelines, resolution MEPC.346(78) of 10 June 2022, revoking the 2016 Guidelines MEPC.282(70). Section 3.6 of those Guidelines states that Part I should be developed as a ship-specific plan by the company and should reflect efforts to improve energy efficiency and reduce carbon intensity through four steps - planning, implementation, monitoring, and self-evaluation and improvement - and that these components play a critical role in the continuous cycle.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering the question as a description of four steps when the printed command asks for the critical role of each, with suitable examples - three demands, of which description is only one. Alongside it sit the currency traps, and on this question they are unusually dangerous because the identical stem recurs at later sittings where the answers differ. At this sitting the guidelines are MEPC.346(78), the 2022 edition; the strategy is the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018, because the 2023 Strategy was adopted on 7 July 2023, one month after this examination; and no ship has yet been rated under the CII, because 2023 is the first data year and it is still running. The regulation number is the one thing that does not reverse: the SEEMP is regulation 26, not 22, the renumbering having taken effect on 1 November 2022. Finally, the four steps are the framework of Part I only.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the SEEMP four-step question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What the SEEMP is and where the four steps live. 2 Planning. 3 Implementation. 4 Monitoring. 5 Self-evaluation and improvement. 6 Why the cycle is critical rather than administrative.
retrieval_cards.why: Step 6 is where the 'critical role' marks are banked; steps 2 to 5 carry the examples inside them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which regulation requires the SEEMP, and which guidelines are operative at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 26. The operative guidelines are the 2022 Guidelines, resolution MEPC.346(78), adopted 10 June 2022, which revoke the 2016 Guidelines, MEPC.282(70).
retrieval_cards.why: Two citation traps in one card - the old regulation 22 numbering, and a later guidelines edition carried back from a 2024 or 2025 paper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why do many sources cite the SEEMP as MARPOL Annex VI regulation 22?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because that was the numbering before MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 was renumbered by resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022. Since then the SEEMP is regulation 26, with Part I at 26.1, Part II at 26.2 and Part III at 26.3 read with 28.8.
retrieval_cards.why: The renumbering is only about seven months old at this sitting, so most circulating material still carries the old number.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three Parts of the SEEMP and the ships each applies to.
retrieval_cards.answer: Part I, Ship Management Plan to Improve Energy Efficiency - any ship of 400 GT and above. Part II, Ship Fuel Oil Consumption Data Collection Plan - any ship of 5,000 GT and above. Part III, Ship Operational Carbon Intensity Plan - required by regulations 26.3 and 28.8 for ships of 5,000 GT and above in the listed categories.
retrieval_cards.why: The four steps belong to Part I only, and the two tonnage thresholds are commonly transposed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the planning stage consist of, and what do the Guidelines say about its importance?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 4.1.1 calls it the most crucial stage, because it primarily determines both the current status of energy usage and carbon intensity and the expected improvement. It has four components: ship-specific measures, company-specific measures, human resource development, and goal setting - the goal to be measurable and easy to understand.
retrieval_cards.why: Attributing 'most crucial stage' to the Guidelines converts a generic opening into a cited one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does section 4.1.3 say about combining efficiency measures?
retrieval_cards.answer: That not all measures can be applied to all ships, or even to the same ship under different operating conditions, and that some of them are mutually exclusive. It adds that initial savings can be reinvested in more difficult or expensive upgrades.
retrieval_cards.why: Almost no candidate says this, and it demonstrates engineering judgement rather than a list of green measures.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must the implementation system contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: Procedures for energy management; defined tasks assigned to responsible personnel; defined levels of authority and lines of communication; procedures for internal audit and management review where relevant; and, for each measure, how it is to be implemented, who is responsible and the start and end dates. The system may be developed at the planning stage.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Who, what, by when' is the whole of step 2 and is what makes the plan auditable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Two things must be recorded under section 4.2.2 that candidates rarely mention. What are they?
retrieval_cards.answer: First, if an identified measure cannot be implemented for any reason, the reason should be recorded for internal use. Second, events and operational conditions outside the control of the ship's crew - waiting for berths, extended port dwell times, operation in severe adverse weather - should be documented, because they may affect the ship's rating.
retrieval_cards.why: Both are counter-intuitive and precise, and the second links implementation to the CII outcome.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does monitoring require, and what data is expressly excluded?
retrieval_cards.answer: Quantitative monitoring by an established method, preferably an international standard, using a tool targeting the goal indicator - AER, cgDIST, EEOI or another CII; at regular intervals, with fuel oil consumption monitored by daily reporting such as noon reports; supported by a monitoring system established at the planning stage and carried out as far as possible by shore staff using existing records. Data obtained during a search and rescue diversion is excluded and recorded separately.
retrieval_cards.why: The search and rescue exclusion is small, exact and memorable, and proves the Guidelines were opened.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the four purposes of self-evaluation under section 4.4.2?
retrieval_cards.answer: To evaluate the effectiveness of the planned measures and their implementation; to deepen the understanding of the ship's operation - what works, how and why; to comprehend the trend of efficiency improvement; and to develop the improved management plan for the next cycle. Section 4.4.3 adds that time should be invested in identifying cause and effect during the evaluated period.
retrieval_cards.why: The middle two are what convert data into a better plan rather than a score.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the SEEMP from the EEDI and EEXI.
retrieval_cards.answer: EEDI and EEXI are technical indices fixing what the ship is - design efficiency, assessed once. The SEEMP is an operational management plan governing how the ship is run, continuously, through a repeating four-step cycle.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why the SEEMP is a cycle and the indices are not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where did the decarbonisation position stand at this sitting, and what must not be imported?
retrieval_cards.answer: EEXI and CII entered into force on 1 January 2023, so this is the first CII data year, it is still running, and no ship has yet been rated. The operative strategy is the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018 - the 2023 Strategy was adopted on 7 July 2023, one month after this examination, and must not be cited. The only forward-looking statement available is that a review of the technical and operational measures is to be completed by 1 January 2026 under regulations 25.3 and 28.11.
retrieval_cards.why: This identical question recurs at later sittings with different answers to every one of these, and material revised from a later paper carries all of them backwards.

reverify_before_publication.claim: Resolution MEPC.346(78) of 10 June 2022 is the operative SEEMP guidelines edition at this sitting, having revoked MEPC.282(70)
reverify_before_publication.why: DO NOT ADVANCE THIS. The SEEMP guidelines are re-adopted periodically and this identical question recurs at later sittings where a different edition applies. MEPC.388(81) and MEPC.395(82) are 2024 instruments and DO NOT EXIST at June 2023. Equally, do not revert to MEPC.282(70), which was revoked a year before this examination.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The operative GHG strategy at this sitting is the Initial IMO Strategy of 2018, NOT the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy
reverify_before_publication.why: THE SHARPEST REVERSAL ON THE PAPER. The 2023 Strategy, MEPC.377(80), was adopted at MEPC 80 on 7 JULY 2023 - ONE MONTH AFTER this examination. MEPC 80 sat 3 to 7 July, so every possible sitting day in June falls before it and the boundary is day-independent. Any donor or revision source from a later sitting carries the 2023 Strategy and it must not be back-read.

reverify_before_publication.claim: No CII rating, rating distribution or fleet statistic is asserted, because 2023 is the first data year and it is still running at this sitting
reverify_before_publication.why: No ship has been rated at all. The D-three-years-or-E trigger is stated as a REQUIREMENT and not as an experience. A later editor working from a 2024 or 2025 object would find rating experience described and must not add it here.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The SEEMP is required by MARPOL Annex VI regulation 26, not regulation 22, and THIS ELEMENT DOES NOT REVERSE
reverify_before_publication.why: Established from the preamble and section 1.3 of MEPC.346(78), read directly. The renumbering took effect 1 November 2022 under MEPC.328(76), seven months before this sitting. Recorded so that an editor performing the other three reversals does not over-correct and revert the numbering as well - and so that a corpus entry recording the entry into force of MEPC.328(76) as 1 November 2023 is not consumed. See the anchor: that entry is the subject of an open True Source correction request and is DECLINED here.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The regulation numbering and content of MARPOL Annex VI regulations 20, 25, 26, 27 and 28
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW holds no licensed consolidated MARPOL Annex VI. These rest on the recitals and cross-references inside MEPC.346(78), which was read directly. No regulation is quoted verbatim anywhere in the answer.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The worked examples are engineering judgement consistent with the Guidelines, not resolution content
reverify_before_publication.why: Section 4.1.2 lists measures but does not work them through, and the printed command requires suitable examples. Where an example goes beyond the listed measures it is engineering judgement, and the distinction is preserved in the answer. No fuel-saving or efficiency-gain percentage is asserted for any of them.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: One limb, sixteen marks printed, and the stem names its own four sections. The printed command is 'describe with suitable examples, the critical role of each of these components in improving energy efficiency of ships' - THREE demands: describe, exemplify, and justify criticality. Description alone answers about a third of it. Because the stem is verbatim identical to a much later paper, the second intent of this question at THIS sitting is a currency test: which guidelines edition, which strategy, and what CII experience actually existed in June 2023.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks, undivided. Roughly three marks per step for description plus examples, and four for the criticality argument together with the framing that locates the cycle in Part I and fixes the two citations. An answer that gives four equal descriptive paragraphs and stops will not reach the upper band.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate has read the SEEMP guidelines rather than a summary of them. The tell-tales are: knowing the four steps are the framework of Part I; that planning is expressly called the most crucial stage; that some measures are mutually exclusive; that reasons for non-implementation and conditions outside the crew's control must be recorded; and that search and rescue data is excluded from monitoring. Correct citation of regulation 26 and of the CURRENT guidelines edition is the currency test, and at this sitting so is knowing that the 2023 GHG Strategy does not yet exist.
primary_source_plan: ESTABLISH WHICH EDITION OF THE SEEMP GUIDELINES WAS OPERATIVE IN JUNE 2023 BEFORE READING ANY OF IT, because the verbatim donor is eighteen months later and cites a different edition

Read section 1.3 for the three Parts and their tonnage thresholds

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - the risk runs in both directions. Forward: the verbatim donor is eighteen months later and carries a guidelines edition, a GHG strategy and rating experience that are all future here - four separate reversals. Backward: the underlying regulation 26 requirement is itself stable, but its numbering changed only seven months before this sitting and most circulating material still carries the old number, so an answer built from older material is stale in the opposite direction. Both were handled by reading the operative resolution at source.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. MARPOL Annex VI applies internationally and India is a Party. No Indian statute is load-bearing and the Merchant Shipping Act is not engaged.

reuse_evidence: PRINTED STEMS COMPARED IN FULL, BOTH READ. The only difference in the entire stem is the spelling of 'defense' against 'defence'. Both papers print (8) on each limb. The similarity score of 0.948 is entirely accounted for by that one word.

THE PRINTED SPELLING IS PRESERVED. This paper prints 'defense' and the transcription records it. It is not normalised to the December 2024 printing, and the difference is recorded because two printings of an identical stem differing in one word is exactly the sort of evidence that establishes how these papers are set.

sources: P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (via MIW verification record verification/QP2412/Q7.md, read in full, where the provisions were set out) - Hague Rules, Article I(e): 'carriage of goods' covers the period from the time when the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship. Article I(b): 'contract of carriage' applies only to contracts covered by a bill of lading or similar document of title. Article I(c): 'goods' excludes live animals and deck cargo stated as carried on deck and so carried.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (same record) - Hague Rules Article II: the carrier's responsibilities and liabilities, and rights and immunities, in relation to the loading, handling, stowage, carriage, custody, care and discharge of the goods.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (same record) - Article III rule 1: the carrier shall be bound, before and at the beginning of the voyage, to exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy, to properly man, equip and supply her, and to make the holds and all other parts in which goods are carried fit and safe for their reception, carriage and preservation.
P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (same record) - Article III rule 2: the carrier shall properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods carried.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (same record) - Article III rules 3 and 4: the bill of lading as prima facie evidence of receipt of the goods as described, and conclusive evidence in the hands of a third party who has taken it in good faith. Article III rule 6: notice of loss or damage in writing at or before removal, or within three days where the loss is not apparent, and discharge from all liability unless suit is brought within one year. Article III rule 8: any clause relieving the carrier otherwise than as provided in the Rules is null and void.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (same record) - Article IV rule 1: neither carrier nor ship is liable for loss or damage arising from unseaworthiness unless caused by want of due diligence, and the burden of proving the exercise of due diligence is on the carrier. Article IV rule 2(a) to (q): the catalogue of excepted perils, including (a) act, neglect or default of the master, mariner, pilot or servants of the carrier in the navigation or in the management of the ship; (b) fire unless caused by the actual fault or privity of the carrier; (c) perils, dangers and accidents of the sea; (i) act or omission of the shipper or owner of the goods; (m) wastage in bulk or weight or any other loss or damage arising from inherent defect, quality or vice of the goods; (n) insufficiency of packing; (o) insufficiency or inadequacy of marks; (p) latent defects not discoverable by due diligence; and (q) any other cause arising without the actual fault or privity of the carrier and without the fault or neglect of his agents or servants, the burden of proof being on the person claiming the benefit.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (same record) - Article IV rule 4: deviation in saving or attempting to save life or property at sea, or any reasonable deviation, is not an infringement of the Rules. Article IV rule 5: the package or unit limitation, expressed under the Visby and SDR Protocols in Special Drawing Rights per package or unit, or per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is the higher - the figures are not asserted here.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (same record) - Hague-Visby: the Hague Rules as amended by the Visby Protocol 1968 and the SDR Protocol 1979 - the conclusive-evidence rule for third parties, the container clause, the extension of the defences to servants and agents, and the loss of the limitation right for intentional or reckless conduct with knowledge.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (same record) - Hamburg Rules 1978, in force since 1992: the carrier is responsible for the goods during the period in which he is in charge of them at the port of loading, during the carriage and at the port of discharge; liability is founded on presumed fault - the carrier is liable unless he proves that he, his servants and agents took all measures that could reasonably be required to avoid the occurrence and its consequences; the nautical fault exception is abolished; fire liability is recast; deck cargo and live animals are brought within the regime; and the time bar is two years.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY (same record) - Rotterdam Rules 2008: a door-to-door period of responsibility running from receipt to delivery, capable of covering a carriage that includes an inland leg; extended obligations of seaworthiness throughout the voyage rather than only before and at its beginning; and the abolition of the nautical fault exception. NOT IN FORCE AT THIS SITTING AND NEVER HAS BEEN.

blocks.h: 1. Why the duration of responsibility matters

blocks.p: The period of responsibility is not a technicality. It decides whether a loss falls inside the convention regime at all - and therefore whether the carrier is answerable under it, whether his exceptions and his limitation of liability apply, and whether the claimant is instead thrown back on the general law of bailment or on the terms of the contract.

Damage occurring outside the period is not covered by the Rules in either direction: the carrier does not get the benefit of the exceptions or the limits, and the cargo owner does not get the benefit of the mandatory obligations. The three regimes in force draw that period in three different places, and the fourth would draw it wider still.

blocks.h: 2. Hague and Hague-Visby - tackle to tackle

ul: The Hague Rules define 'carriage of goods' as covering the period from the time when the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship - the classic "tackle to tackle" period.

The Hague-Visby Rules are the same Rules as amended by the Visby Protocol 1968 and the SDR Protocol 1979. They do not change the period of responsibility; they change the evidential effect of the bill in third-party hands, the limitation figures and their basis, the treatment of containers, and the extension of the defences to servants and agents.

Two further limits on scope matter as much as the period. The Rules apply only to a contract covered by a bill of lading or similar document of title, so a pure charterparty relationship is outside them; and 'goods' excludes live animals and deck cargo stated as carried on deck and so carried.

Example. Steel coils are damaged in a shore warehouse before loading, or in a stack on the quay after discharge. Neither loss is within the Hague-Visby period, and the claimant must look to the terms of the contract or to the general law. Damage caused by rough handling as the sling is landed on the deck is within it.
The consequence to state. Tackle to tackle leaves two uncovered gaps, one at each end, filled - or not - by the contract.

blocks.h: 3. Hamburg - port to port

ul: The Hamburg Rules make the carrier responsible for the goods during the period in which he is in charge of them at the port of loading, during the carriage, and at the port of discharge. That is "port to port", and it deliberately closes the two gaps the Hague regime leaves.

The change of period comes with a change of basis. Liability rests on presumed fault: the carrier is liable for loss, damage or delay unless he proves that he, his servants and agents took all measures that could reasonably be required to avoid the occurrence and its consequences. There is no catalogue of excepted perils to shelter behind.

The nautical fault exception is abolished, fire liability is recast, deck cargo and live animals are brought within the regime, delay is expressly covered, and the time bar is two years rather than one.

Example. Bagged cargo received into the carrier's custody in a port shed two days before loading and damaged by a shed roof leak is outside Hague-Visby and inside Hamburg, because the carrier was in charge of it at the port of loading.

blocks.h: 4. Rotterdam - door to door, and not in force

ul: The Rotterdam Rules would run the period of responsibility from receipt to delivery - "door to door" - so that a single carriage contract including an inland leg falls under one regime rather than being split between a sea convention and a road or rail one.
They would also extend the seaworthiness obligation to a continuing one, throughout the voyage, rather than only before and at its beginning, and would abolish the nautical fault exception.

They are NOT in force at this examination and never have been. That must be stated plainly. The Rules are relevant to this question as the intended direction of travel and as the sharpest illustration of how far a period of responsibility can be extended - not as applicable law.

Example. A container collected from an inland factory, railed to the port, shipped and delivered to a consignee's inland warehouse is a single door-to-door contract. Under Rotterdam it would be governed throughout by one regime; today it is not.

blocks.h: 5. The comparison, and the Indian position

rows: Port to port - in charge at the load port, carriage, discharge port
Duty to care, with a catalogue of excepted perils
Presumed fault - carrier must prove all reasonable measures were taken
Due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage
In force, but with limited commercial reach

blocks.p: India applies the Hague-Visby regime. The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925, as amended in 1993 to give effect to the Visby and SDR Protocols, is the operative statute at this sitting. India is not a party to the Hamburg Rules and has not ratified the Rotterdam Rules. So the answer to limb b) is worked under Hague-Visby, and the general merchant shipping statute in force is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

blocks.h: 6. The grain claim - how it is framed, and who must prove what

blocks.p: Limb b) is best answered as a sequence of burdens, not as a list of defences. Setting the sequence out is worth more than any single exception.

ol: The consignee establishes a prima facie case. He produces a clean bill of lading - prima facie evidence that the grain was shipped in apparent good order and condition, and conclusive evidence in his hands if he took it in good faith as a third party - and an outturn showing damaged cargo. Good in, bad out.

The carrier must then bring himself within an exception under Article IV rule 2, and the burden of proving it is on him. It is not enough to say the cause is unknown - although the residual exception at rule 2(q) exists precisely for the case where he can show the loss arose without actual fault or privity on his part and without fault or neglect of his agents or servants.

The claimant may then defeat the exception by showing a breach of the overriding obligations: want of due diligence to make the ship seaworthy and the holds fit, or a failure to care properly for the cargo.

Before any of that, two contract questions must be answered, because they may dispose of the claim entirely: what does the bill of lading actually say - is it clean, is it shipped or received-for-shipment, does it carry a weight or quality qualification - and who contracted to do the loading, stowage and discharge. Where those operations were transferred to the shipper or charterer, responsibility for damage caused by them may go with them.

blocks.h: 7. The excepted perils that answer a grain claim

blocks.p: Article IV rule 2 gives a catalogue; these are the heads that actually arise on a grain cargo:

ul: (m) Wastage in bulk or weight, and inherent defect, quality or vice of the goods. The most important defence on this facts. Grain is hygroscopic: shipped above its safe moisture content it will self-heat, sweat, cake and mould without any fault of the ship. Short-delivery claims on a bulk grain cargo are also commonly answered by natural moisture loss and by the inherent inaccuracy of draught survey - trade allowance.

(i) Act or omission of the shipper or owner of the goods. Grain loaded wet, hot, or already infested; loading in rain against the ship's protest; a false or inadequate declaration of moisture content.
(n) Insufficiency of packing and (o) insufficiency or inadequacy of marks, where any part of the parcel was bagged.
(c) Perils, dangers and accidents of the sea. Heavy weather of a severity the ship could not reasonably guard against, causing water ingress despite properly maintained and tested closing appliances.

(a) Act, neglect or default of the master or crew in the navigation or in the MANAGEMENT of the ship. Available under Hague-Visby and abolished under Hamburg - a difference worth naming. But it is confined to the management of the ship; an act done for the care of the cargo, such as mishandling ventilation, is not within it and is a breach of Article III rule 2.
(b) Fire, unless caused by the actual fault or privity of the carrier - relevant where self-heating has progressed to a hold fire.
(p) Latent defects not discoverable by due diligence - a hidden crack in a ballast line or a hatch coaming defect not findable on proper inspection.
(q) The residual exception, where the carrier can show the loss arose without his actual fault or privity and without the fault or neglect of his servants or agents.

blocks.h: 8. The overriding obligations that can defeat every one of those defences

blocks.p: This is the half of the answer that separates a good script. The exceptions do not operate if the carrier is in breach of Article III.

ul: Article III rule 1 - due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage to make the ship seaworthy, to properly man, equip and supply her, and to make the holds fit and safe for the reception, carriage and preservation of the cargo. On grain that means hold cleanliness, dryness and freedom from infestation and residues; hatch covers weathertight and pressure- or hose-tested; bilge wells, strums, sounding pipes and non-return valves proved clear and operable; ventilators and air pipes sound and closing appliances working; and ballast and fuel lines through the holds tested for tightness. Article IV rule 1 puts the burden of proving due diligence squarely on the carrier.

Article III rule 2 - properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods. On grain the live issue is almost always ventilation: whether the ship followed a defensible rule based on dew-point comparison between hold and outside air, whether the record shows what was actually done and why, and whether ventilation was correctly stopped in conditions that would have introduced moist air.
Article III rule 8 - any clause purporting to relieve the carrier otherwise than as the Rules provide is null and void, so the defences cannot be enlarged by contract.

The practical consequence, and the one that decides real cases: a carrier who cannot produce hold-preparation records, hatch-cover test results and a proper ventilation log will very often lose an inherent-vice defence that was factually correct, because he cannot discharge the burden the Rules place on him.

blocks.h: 9. Procedural and quantum defences, and the evidence

ul: Notice of loss or damage under Article III rule 6 - in writing at or before removal of the goods, or within three days where the damage is not apparent. Absence of notice is not fatal, but it is prima facie evidence that the goods were delivered as described.

The one-year time bar. Under Hague-Visby the carrier is discharged from all liability unless suit is brought within one year of delivery or of the date when the goods should have been delivered. It is a complete answer and it is the first thing to check.
Title to sue. Whether the claimant actually holds the bill of lading and has the right to sue on it.

Limitation of liability under Article IV rule 5 - a figure per package or unit, or per kilogramme of gross weight, whichever is the higher. Not a defence to liability but a cap on it, and on a bulk cargo the weight basis is the operative one. The right to limit is lost where the damage resulted from an act or omission done with intent to cause damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result.

Quantum. Damaged grain is rarely a total loss: it is usually sound-arrived-value less damaged-arrived-value, and the claimant is under a duty to mitigate - by segregation, reconditioning or sale of the damaged parcel.

The evidence, without which none of the above works. Hold-preparation and cleaning records with photographs; hatch-cover ultrasonic or hose test certificates; the loading survey, draught survey and moisture-content certificates; the ventilation log with hold and ambient dew points; deck and engine log entries for the weather; the pre-loading survey and any protest at loading; and prompt appointment of surveyors on both sides, with a joint survey at discharge wherever it can be arranged.

blocks.p: Close with the point that ties the two limbs together: the defences in limb b) are available only because the loss fell inside the period of responsibility examined in limb a). Move the damage to the quay before loading, and the Hague-Visby exceptions - and its limits - do not apply at all.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Eight and eight, printed - so unlike most of this paper the budget is fixed. Limb a) asks for a comparison across conventions with examples, and the marks are for the differences, not for a description of each regime in turn. Limb b) is a scenario, and the marks are for a defence strategy, not for a recitation of Article IV rule 2.

The route reflects that. Limb a) runs the three in-force regimes in ascending order of period - tackle to tackle, port to port, then the door-to-door regime that is not in force - and finishes with a comparison table and the Indian position, because the paper is an Indian one and the second limb has to be worked under some particular law. Limb b) is built as a burden-of-proof sequence rather than a list, and the exceptions are only the second of its four beats.

blocks.h: The three phrases that carry limb a)

blocks.p: Tackle to tackle. Port to port. Door to door. If you can write those three and attach the right convention to each, you have the spine of the limb. Then attach one consequence to each: tackle to tackle leaves a gap at each end; port to port closes both; door to door would cover the inland legs as well.

And remember the negative that is worth a mark by itself: the Visby and SDR Protocols do not change the period. They change limitation, evidence, containers and the position of servants and agents. A candidate who says Hague-Visby extended the period has misunderstood what the Protocols did.

blocks.h: The Rotterdam Rules are not in force - say it plainly

blocks.p: They must be discussed, because the question asks about the different conventions and the door-to-door period is the sharpest illustration of the point. But they must be labelled. They are not in force at this sitting and never have been. Presenting them as applicable law is the single most damaging error available on limb a), and it is easy to make because they are extensively written about.

blocks.h: Limb b) is a sequence of burdens, not a list

blocks.p: Almost every weak answer to a cargo-claim question produces the Article IV rule 2 catalogue and stops. The examiner is asking what defence is available, which requires knowing who has to prove what:

ol: Claimant: clean bill in, damaged cargo out. Prima facie case made.
Carrier: bring yourself within an exception - and the burden is on you.
Claimant: defeat the exception by proving a breach of Article III - unseaworthiness through want of due diligence, or failure to care for the cargo.
Carrier, throughout: Article IV rule 1 puts the burden of proving due diligence on him.

blocks.p: State that sequence and the exceptions then fall into place as the second beat rather than as the whole answer.

blocks.h: Why grain is the cargo the examiner chose

blocks.p: Grain is hygroscopic and it is the classic inherent vice cargo. Loaded above its safe moisture content it will self-heat, sweat, cake and mould with no fault on the part of the ship at all, which makes Article IV rule 2(m) - wastage in bulk or weight, and inherent defect, quality or vice - the natural defence. Add (i), act or omission of the shipper, where the grain was loaded wet or hot or was mis-declared.

But the same facts make the counter-attack obvious, and it is where cases are actually decided: the cargo interest will say the ship ventilated badly. That is a failure to care for the cargo under Article III rule 2, it is not within the management-of-the-ship exception, and it defeats the inherent-vice defence. Which is why the ventilation log with hold and ambient dew points is the most valuable single document on a wet-damage grain claim.

blocks.h: Management of the ship versus care of the cargo

blocks.p: A distinction worth having ready. Article IV rule 2(a) excuses act, neglect or default of the master or crew in the navigation or in the MANAGEMENT OF THE SHIP. It does not excuse acts done for the care of the cargo. Mishandling ballast in a way that affects the ship is management of the ship; mishandling ventilation, which exists to protect the cargo, is not - it is a breach of Article III rule 2.
Add that the exception is abolished under the Hamburg Rules, which connects the two limbs neatly and shows the comparison in limb a) was not merely descriptive.

blocks.h: Check the time bar first

blocks.p: Under Hague-Visby the carrier is discharged from all liability unless suit is brought within one year. It is a complete answer, it costs nothing to check, and it is the first thing a practitioner looks at. Contrast the two-year bar under Hamburg. Notice of damage under Article III rule 6 - at or before removal, or within three days if the damage is not apparent - is not a bar, but its absence is prima facie evidence of good delivery.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Describing the three regimes in turn without comparing them. The marks are in the differences.
Saying the Visby Protocol extended the period of responsibility. It did not.
Treating the Rotterdam Rules as in force. They are not, and never have been.
Forgetting that Hague-Visby excludes live animals and deck cargo stated as carried on deck, and that Hamburg includes them.
Omitting that the Rules apply only to a contract covered by a bill of lading or similar document of title.
Answering limb b) with the Article IV rule 2 list and no burden of proof.
Missing inherent vice under rule 2(m), which is the natural defence to a grain claim.
Failing to see that bad ventilation defeats the inherent-vice defence, because it is a breach of Article III rule 2.
Putting ventilation inside the management-of-the-ship exception. It is care of the cargo.
Forgetting the one-year time bar, which is a complete defence.
Quoting SDR limitation figures. They are amended over time and a stale number is worse than none.
Working limb b) under the wrong law. India applies Hague-Visby, through the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Cargo is damaged in the port shed before loading. Which regime covers it?" Not Hague-Visby - outside tackle to tackle. Hamburg would, if it applied.
"Did the Visby Protocol change the period of responsibility?" No.
"Are the Rotterdam Rules in force?" No.
"Which regime abolishes nautical fault?" Hamburg - and Rotterdam would.
"Is deck cargo covered?" Not under Hague-Visby where it is stated as carried on deck and so carried. It is under Hamburg.
"Who proves due diligence?" The carrier - Article IV rule 1.
"Is bad ventilation management of the ship?" No. It is care of the cargo under Article III rule 2, and the exception does not cover it.

"The grain was wet when loaded. Is that a defence?" Yes in principle - inherent vice, and act or omission of the shipper. But only if you can prove the condition at loading and prove your own due diligence.
"How long has the consignee to sue?" One year under Hague-Visby; two under Hamburg.
"What single document decides most wet-damage grain claims?" The ventilation log, with hold and ambient dew points.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Define the Hague period of responsibility. From the time the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship.
And the Hamburg period? While the carrier is in charge of the goods at the port of loading, during carriage, and at the port of discharge.
What is the basis of liability under Hamburg? Presumed fault - the carrier is liable unless he proves he and his servants took all measures that could reasonably be required.
What would Rotterdam change? Receipt-to-delivery period, continuing seaworthiness throughout the voyage, no nautical fault exception. Not in force.
Which regime does India apply and under what statute? Hague-Visby, under the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993.

State Article III rule 1 and Article III rule 2. Due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage to make the ship seaworthy and the holds fit; and properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods.
Name four excepted perils relevant to grain. Inherent vice and wastage in bulk; act or omission of the shipper; perils of the sea; latent defects not discoverable by due diligence.
What defeats an inherent-vice defence? Proof that the carrier failed to exercise due diligence to make the holds fit, or failed to care for the cargo - typically ventilation.

What records would you produce to defend the claim? Hold preparation and cleaning records with photographs; hatch-cover test certificates; loading and draught surveys and moisture certificates; ventilation log with dew points; weather log; any protest at loading.
What is the time bar and what is the notice requirement? Suit within one year; notice in writing at or before removal, or within three days if the damage is not apparent.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb a) is three phrases and a status: TACKLE TO TACKLE (Hague / Hague-Visby, in force) · PORT TO PORT (Hamburg, in force) · DOOR TO DOOR (Rotterdam, NOT in force). Then four axes of comparison: PERIOD · BASIS · NAUTICAL FAULT · TIME BAR. And the Indian anchor: Hague-Visby, by the 1925 Act as amended in 1993.

Limb b) is four beats: GOOD IN, BAD OUT · FIND AN EXCEPTION · SURVIVE ARTICLE III · CHECK THE CLOCK. Inside the exceptions, for grain: VICE, SHIPPER, SEA, LATENT. Inside Article III: HOLDS FIT, CARGO CARED FOR. And the practical rule that decides real cases: NO RECORDS, NO DEFENCE.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: MIW holds no licensed consolidated text of the Hague, Hague-Visby, Hamburg or Rotterdam Rules, nor of the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925. Every Article relied on is established from MIW's own verification record for an earlier sitting of this identical question, where the provisions were set out, and is given in substance. No Article is quoted verbatim anywhere in this answer.

Three things are therefore deliberately not asserted. No package or weight limitation figure - the Article IV rule 5 limits are expressed in Special Drawing Rights and have been amended over time, so the mechanism is described and no number is given. No number of ratifications or States party for any of the four conventions, because those figures move continuously; what is asserted about the Rotterdam Rules - that they are not in force - is certain and needs no count. And no case law in any jurisdiction: the burden-of-proof sequence is stated as it follows from the Articles themselves.

Both are left open and identified as questions the carrier must answer before choosing his defence, rather than assumed either way.
