EXAMPLE - steel coils damaged in a shore warehouse before loading, or stacked on the quay after discharge, are OUTSIDE the period
TACKLE TO TACKLE LEAVES TWO UNCOVERED GAPS, ONE AT EACH END

steps.title: Hamburg - port to port
points: the carrier is responsible DURING THE PERIOD IN WHICH HE IS IN CHARGE OF THE GOODS AT THE PORT OF LOADING, DURING THE CARRIAGE, AND AT THE PORT OF DISCHARGE
it deliberately CLOSES THE TWO GAPS the Hague regime leaves
the basis changes too - PRESUMED FAULT: liable unless he proves he and his servants and agents TOOK ALL MEASURES THAT COULD REASONABLY BE REQUIRED to avoid the occurrence and its consequences
NO CATALOGUE OF EXCEPTED PERILS to shelter behind
NAUTICAL FAULT ABOLISHED; fire recast; DECK CARGO AND LIVE ANIMALS INCLUDED; DELAY expressly covered; time bar TWO YEARS
EXAMPLE - bagged cargo received into the carrier's custody in a port shed two days before loading and damaged by a roof leak is OUTSIDE Hague-Visby and INSIDE Hamburg

steps.title: Rotterdam - door to door, and not in force
points: the period would run FROM RECEIPT TO DELIVERY, so a single contract including an INLAND LEG falls under one regime
SEAWORTHINESS WOULD BECOME A CONTINUING OBLIGATION THROUGHOUT THE VOYAGE, not only before and at its beginning
NAUTICAL FAULT ABOLISHED
THEY ARE NOT IN FORCE AT THIS EXAMINATION AND NEVER HAVE BEEN - state it plainly
relevant as the direction of travel and as the sharpest illustration of period extension - NOT AS APPLICABLE LAW
EXAMPLE - a container collected from an inland factory, railed, shipped and delivered to an inland warehouse

steps.title: The comparison, and the Indian position
points: compare on four axes - PERIOD, BASIS OF LIABILITY, NAUTICAL FAULT, TIME BAR - plus deck cargo and status
Hague/Hague-Visby - tackle to tackle, excepted perils, nautical fault A DEFENCE, one year, deck cargo excluded, IN FORCE and dominant
Hamburg - port to port, presumed fault, nautical fault ABOLISHED, two years, deck cargo included, IN FORCE but limited reach
Rotterdam - door to door, continuing seaworthiness, nautical fault abolished, NOT IN FORCE
INDIA APPLIES HAGUE-VISBY through the CARRIAGE OF GOODS BY SEA ACT, 1925 AS AMENDED IN 1993 giving effect to the Visby and SDR Protocols
India is NOT a party to the Hamburg Rules and has not ratified Rotterdam
the general merchant shipping statute at this sitting is the MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958
SO LIMB B IS WORKED UNDER HAGUE-VISBY

steps.title: The grain claim - how it is framed, and who must prove what
points: ANSWER AS A SEQUENCE OF BURDENS, NOT A LIST OF DEFENCES
1 - the consignee produces a CLEAN BILL (prima facie, and CONCLUSIVE in a good-faith third party's hands) and a damaged OUTTURN. GOOD IN, BAD OUT
2 - THE CARRIER MUST BRING HIMSELF WITHIN AN EXCEPTION and THE BURDEN IS ON HIM
3 - the claimant may DEFEAT THE EXCEPTION by proving breach of the OVERRIDING OBLIGATIONS - want of due diligence, or failure to care for the cargo
BEFORE ANY OF THAT, TWO CONTRACT QUESTIONS - what does the bill actually say (clean? shipped or received-for-shipment? weight or quality qualification?)
and WHO CONTRACTED TO DO THE LOADING, STOWAGE AND DISCHARGE - where transferred to shipper or charterer, responsibility may go with them

steps.title: The excepted perils that answer a grain claim
points: (m) WASTAGE IN BULK OR WEIGHT, AND INHERENT DEFECT, QUALITY OR VICE - the principal defence. Grain is hygroscopic; above its safe moisture content it self-heats, sweats, cakes and moulds without fault of the ship
(m) also answers short-delivery by natural moisture loss and draught-survey inaccuracy - TRADE ALLOWANCE
(i) ACT OR OMISSION OF THE SHIPPER - grain loaded wet, hot or infested; loading in rain against protest; a false moisture declaration
(n) insufficiency of PACKING and (o) insufficiency of MARKS where any part was bagged
(c) PERILS OF THE SEA - heavy weather beyond what the ship could reasonably guard against, with properly maintained closing appliances
(a) NAUTICAL FAULT AND MANAGEMENT OF THE SHIP - available under Hague-Visby, ABOLISHED under Hamburg. But CONFINED TO MANAGEMENT OF THE SHIP; ventilation is care of the CARGO and is NOT within it
(b) FIRE unless the actual fault or privity of the carrier - relevant where self-heating has become a hold fire
(p) LATENT DEFECTS not discoverable by due diligence; (q) the RESIDUAL exception, loss without actual fault or privity and without fault of servants or agents

steps.title: The overriding obligations that can defeat every one of those defences
points: THE EXCEPTIONS DO NOT OPERATE IF THE CARRIER IS IN BREACH OF ARTICLE III
ARTICLE III RULE 1 - due diligence BEFORE AND AT THE BEGINNING OF THE VOYAGE: seaworthy, properly manned equipped and supplied, and HOLDS FIT AND SAFE for reception, carriage and preservation

on grain that means HOLD CLEANLINESS, DRYNESS AND FREEDOM FROM INFESTATION; HATCH COVERS WEATHERTIGHT AND TESTED; BILGES, STRUMS, SOUNDING PIPES AND NON-RETURN VALVES CLEAR; VENTILATORS AND CLOSING APPLIANCES SOUND; BALLAST AND FUEL LINES THROUGH THE HOLDS TESTED
ARTICLE IV RULE 1 PUTS THE BURDEN OF PROVING DUE DILIGENCE ON THE CARRIER
ARTICLE III RULE 2 - properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, CARE FOR and discharge

on grain the live issue is VENTILATION - a defensible rule based on DEW-POINT COMPARISON between hold and outside air, a record of what was done and why, and ventilation correctly STOPPED when it would introduce moist air
ARTICLE III RULE 8 - contracting out of the Rules is NULL AND VOID, so the defences cannot be enlarged by contract

THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: a carrier who cannot produce hold-preparation records, hatch-cover tests and a proper ventilation log OFTEN LOSES A FACTUALLY CORRECT INHERENT-VICE DEFENCE, because he cannot discharge his burden

steps.title: Procedural and quantum defences, and the evidence
points: ARTICLE III RULE 6 NOTICE - in writing AT OR BEFORE REMOVAL, or WITHIN THREE DAYS where the damage is not apparent. Absence is not fatal but is prima facie evidence of good delivery
THE ONE-YEAR TIME BAR - discharged from all liability unless SUIT IS BROUGHT WITHIN ONE YEAR. A complete answer, and the FIRST THING TO CHECK. Two years under Hamburg
TITLE TO SUE - does the claimant hold the bill and have the right to sue on it
ARTICLE IV RULE 5 LIMITATION - per package or unit, or PER KILOGRAMME OF GROSS WEIGHT, WHICHEVER IS THE HIGHER; on a bulk cargo the weight basis operates. NO FIGURE ASSERTED
the right to limit is LOST for an act or omission done with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result
QUANTUM - sound arrived value less damaged arrived value; the claimant must MITIGATE by segregation, reconditioning or sale

THE EVIDENCE, WITHOUT WHICH NONE OF THE ABOVE WORKS - hold preparation records and photographs; hatch-cover ultrasonic or hose test certificates; loading and draught surveys and moisture certificates; VENTILATION LOG WITH HOLD AND AMBIENT DEW POINTS; weather logs; protest at loading; prompt surveyors and a JOINT SURVEY at discharge
CLOSE - the defences exist only because the loss fell INSIDE the period examined in limb a)

questions.understand_first: Both halves of this question turn on the same hinge: when does the carrier's responsibility begin and end. That sounds like housekeeping and it is actually decisive, because the international rules that govern a sea carriage only bite during a defined window. Damage that happens outside that window is not governed by them at all - which cuts both ways, since the carrier loses his special defences and his financial cap, and the cargo owner loses the protections the rules impose. The oldest and still the most widely used scheme draws the window very tightly, from the moment the cargo comes aboard to the moment it leaves the ship, leaving a gap at each end that has to be filled, if at all, by whatever the parties agreed. A later scheme widens it to cover the whole time the carrier has the goods in the port, and in exchange takes away the long list of excuses and simply asks whether he did everything that could reasonably be expected. A third would widen it further still, to the whole journey from the shipper's premises to the receiver's, but it never came into effect. The second half then works a real claim inside the narrowest of those windows, and the thing to grasp is that it is a contest about who has to prove what rather than a list of excuses. The receiver only has to show the cargo went aboard sound and came off damaged. The ship then has to point to a recognised reason it is not answerable - and for a cargo like grain, which spoils itself if it is loaded too wet, there is a very good one. But that reason evaporates if the ship cannot show it prepared the holds properly and looked after the cargo during the passage, and it is almost always the paperwork, not the physics, that decides which way that goes.
questions.memory_cue: Limb a) is three phrases and a status - TACKLE TO TACKLE (2), PORT TO PORT (3), DOOR TO DOOR (4), the last NOT IN FORCE - compared on four axes at (5): PERIOD, BASIS, NAUTICAL FAULT, TIME BAR, with India on HAGUE-VISBY (5). Limb b) is four beats - GOOD IN BAD OUT (6), FIND AN EXCEPTION (7), SURVIVE ARTICLE III (8), CHECK THE CLOCK (9). For grain the exceptions are VICE, SHIPPER, SEA, LATENT (7); the counter-attack is HOLDS FIT, CARGO CARED FOR (8); and the rule that decides real cases is NO RECORDS, NO DEFENCE (9).

quick_revision.recall_15s: LIMB A. Why it matters: the period decides whether the loss is inside the regime at all - and therefore whether the carrier's exceptions and limits apply. Outside it, neither side gets the benefit. HAGUE / HAGUE-VISBY - TACKLE TO TACKLE: Art I(e), from loading on to discharge from the ship. The Visby and SDR Protocols do NOT change the period - they change limitation, evidence in third-party hands, containers, servants and agents. Applies only to a contract covered by a bill of lading or similar document of title (I(b)); 'goods' excludes live animals and deck cargo stated as carried on deck (I(c)). Leaves a gap at each end. HAMBURG - PORT TO PORT: responsible while in charge at the load port, during carriage, and at the discharge port. Presumed fault - liable unless he proves he and his servants took all measures that could reasonably be required. No catalogue of exceptions. Nautical fault abolished. Deck cargo and live animals in. Delay covered. Two-year bar. ROTTERDAM - DOOR TO DOOR: receipt to delivery, continuing seaworthiness throughout the voyage, nautical fault abolished. NOT IN FORCE - say so. INDIA: Hague-Visby, by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended 1993; not a party to Hamburg; general statute Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. LIMB B - four beats. (1) Good in, bad out: clean bill (prima facie; conclusive for a good-faith third party) plus damaged outturn. First check the bill and who contracted to load, stow and discharge. (2) Find an exception - burden on the carrier: (m) inherent vice / wastage in bulk - grain is hygroscopic and self-heats, sweats, cakes and moulds if loaded wet; also natural moisture loss and draught-survey inaccuracy on short delivery. (i) act or omission of the shipper - loaded wet, hot, infested, mis-declared. (c) perils of the sea. (a) nautical fault / management of the ship - but ventilation is care of the CARGO, not management of the ship. (b) fire, (n) packing, (p) latent defect, (q) residual. (3) Survive Article III: rule 1 due diligence before and at the beginning - holds clean, dry, free of infestation; hatch covers weathertight and tested; bilges, strums, sounding pipes and non-return valves clear; ventilators sound; ballast and fuel lines tested. Art IV r 1 puts the burden of proving due diligence on the carrier. Rule 2 properly and carefully care for the cargo - on grain that is ventilation on a dew-point rule, logged. Rule 8 - no contracting out. (4) Check the clock: notice at or before removal, or within three days if not apparent; suit within ONE YEAR - a complete defence. Limitation per package or per kg of gross weight, whichever higher (no figure); lost for intent or recklessness with knowledge. Quantum = sound less damaged value, claimant must mitigate. Evidence: hold prep records and photos, hatch-cover tests, loading and draught surveys, moisture certificates, VENTILATION LOG WITH DEW POINTS, weather log, protest at loading, joint survey. NO RECORDS, NO DEFENCE.

critical_numbers: Hague Rules Article I(e) - the period runs from loading on to discharge from the ship
Article III rule 1 - due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage
Article III rule 6 - notice at or before removal, or within three days if not apparent; suit within ONE YEAR
Article IV rule 2(a) to (q) - the excepted perils; (m) inherent vice, (i) act of the shipper, (c) perils of the sea

quick_revision.critical_regulation: Hague Rules Article I(e) defines carriage of goods as covering the period from the time when the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship - the tackle-to-tackle period, unchanged by the Visby and SDR Protocols. Article III rule 1 binds the carrier, before and at the beginning of the voyage, to exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy and to make the holds fit and safe for the reception, carriage and preservation of the goods; Article III rule 2 requires him properly and carefully to load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge them. Article IV rule 1 places the burden of proving the exercise of due diligence on the carrier, and Article IV rule 2 gives the catalogue of excepted perils, of which rule 2(m) - wastage in bulk or weight and inherent defect, quality or vice - is the natural answer to a grain claim.
quick_revision.major_trap: In limb a), describing the three regimes in turn instead of comparing them - the marks are in the differences - and two specific errors: saying the Visby Protocol extended the period of responsibility, which it did not, and treating the Rotterdam Rules as in force, which they are not and never have been. In limb b), producing the Article IV rule 2 catalogue with no burden of proof, when the question is really a sequence: clean bill in and damaged cargo out makes the prima facie case, the carrier must then bring himself within an exception and Article IV rule 1 puts the burden on him, and the claimant defeats it by proving breach of Article III. The sharpest technical trap is putting ventilation inside the management-of-the-ship exception: ventilation is care of the cargo under Article III rule 2, and bad ventilation is precisely what destroys an otherwise correct inherent-vice defence. Finally, check the one-year time bar first, and quote no SDR figure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the carrier's period of responsibility and grain claim question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Why the period matters. 2 Hague and Hague-Visby, tackle to tackle. 3 Hamburg, port to port. 4 Rotterdam, door to door and not in force. 5 The comparison and the Indian position. 6 How the grain claim is framed and who proves what. 7 The excepted perils. 8 The overriding Article III obligations. 9 Procedure, quantum and the evidence.
retrieval_cards.why: Eight and eight printed; limb a) is a comparison and limb b) is a burden-of-proof sequence, not a list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the period of responsibility under each of the three carriage regimes.
retrieval_cards.answer: Hague and Hague-Visby: from the time the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship - tackle to tackle. Hamburg: while the carrier is in charge of the goods at the port of loading, during the carriage, and at the port of discharge - port to port. Rotterdam: from receipt to delivery - door to door, and not in force.
retrieval_cards.why: Three phrases carry the whole of limb a); everything else hangs off them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Did the Visby Protocol change the carrier's period of responsibility?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The Hague-Visby Rules are the Hague Rules as amended by the Visby Protocol 1968 and the SDR Protocol 1979, and those Protocols changed limitation figures and their basis, the evidential effect of the bill in a good-faith third party's hands, the treatment of containers and the extension of defences to servants and agents. The tackle-to-tackle period is unchanged.
retrieval_cards.why: A very common misstatement, and correcting it shows you know what the Protocols actually did.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the status of the Rotterdam Rules, and why must they still be discussed?
retrieval_cards.answer: They are not in force and never have been. They must still be discussed because the question asks about the different conventions and the door-to-door period is the sharpest illustration of how far a period of responsibility can extend - together with continuing seaworthiness throughout the voyage and the abolition of nautical fault. But they must be labelled as not applicable law.
retrieval_cards.why: Presenting them as in force is the most damaging single error available on limb a).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Compare Hague-Visby and Hamburg on four axes.
retrieval_cards.answer: Period - tackle to tackle against port to port. Basis of liability - a duty of care with a catalogue of excepted perils, against presumed fault where the carrier must prove all reasonable measures were taken. Nautical fault - a defence, against abolished. Time bar - one year against two. Add that deck cargo and live animals are excluded from Hague-Visby 'goods' and included under Hamburg.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb a)'s marks are in the differences, and four axes make them countable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which regime applies in India, and under what statute?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Hague-Visby regime, under the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 as amended in 1993 to give effect to the Visby and SDR Protocols. India is not a party to the Hamburg Rules and has not ratified the Rotterdam Rules. The general merchant shipping statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
retrieval_cards.why: The second limb has to be worked under some particular law, and this is it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Set out the burden-of-proof sequence in a cargo claim.
retrieval_cards.answer: The claimant establishes a prima facie case with a clean bill of lading - prima facie evidence of good order, conclusive in a good-faith third party's hands - and a damaged outturn. The carrier must then bring himself within an excepted peril, and the burden is on him. The claimant may then defeat it by proving breach of the overriding obligations - want of due diligence, or failure to care for the cargo. Article IV rule 1 keeps the burden of proving due diligence on the carrier.
retrieval_cards.why: Answering limb b) with a list of exceptions and no sequence misses what the question actually asks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is inherent vice the natural defence to a grain claim, and what destroys it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Grain is hygroscopic; loaded above its safe moisture content it will self-heat, sweat, cake and mould without any fault of the ship, which is Article IV rule 2(m) - wastage in bulk or weight and inherent defect, quality or vice. It is destroyed by proof that the carrier failed to exercise due diligence to make the holds fit under Article III rule 1, or failed to care properly for the cargo under Article III rule 2 - in practice, by bad or unrecorded ventilation.
retrieval_cards.why: The defence and its counter-attack are the two halves of the same question, and the case turns on the second.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is bad ventilation within the management-of-the-ship exception?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Article IV rule 2(a) excuses act, neglect or default of the master or crew in the navigation or in the management of the ship. Ventilation is done for the care of the cargo, so it falls under Article III rule 2 and is a breach, not an excepted peril. Note also that the exception is abolished altogether under the Hamburg Rules.
retrieval_cards.why: The management-of-the-ship line is the classic dividing question in cargo claims and this is its clearest instance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must the carrier be able to prove about hold preparation on a grain cargo?
retrieval_cards.answer: Due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage under Article III rule 1: holds clean, dry and free of infestation and previous residues; hatch covers weathertight and ultrasonically or hose tested; bilge wells, strums, sounding pipes and non-return valves clear and operable; ventilators, air pipes and closing appliances sound; and ballast and fuel lines passing through the holds tested for tightness. Article IV rule 1 puts the burden of proving that diligence on him.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the concrete engineering content of an otherwise abstract legal obligation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the notice and time-bar provisions, and why check the bar first?
retrieval_cards.answer: Notice of loss or damage in writing at or before removal of the goods, or within three days where the damage is not apparent; absence of notice is not fatal but is prima facie evidence that the goods were delivered as described. The carrier is discharged from all liability unless suit is brought within one year under Hague-Visby, or two years under Hamburg. The bar is checked first because it is a complete answer and costs nothing to establish.
retrieval_cards.why: A complete defence that many candidates never mention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What evidence decides most wet-damage grain claims?
retrieval_cards.answer: The ventilation log, showing hold and ambient dew points and what was done and why - together with hold preparation records and photographs, hatch-cover test certificates, the loading and draught surveys and moisture-content certificates, weather log entries, any protest at loading, and a joint survey at discharge. A carrier who cannot produce them will often lose a factually correct inherent-vice defence because he cannot discharge his burden.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most practical point on the question - no records, no defence.

Explain various skin friction reduction methods currently under consideration, with special mention on the following: a) Hull Air Cavity Systems b) Hull Surface Texturing c) Micro bubbles

subparts.text: Hull Air Cavity Systems.
Hull Surface Texturing.
Micro bubbles. PRINTED AS TWO WORDS, 'Micro bubbles'. Preserved as printed.

P3 INDUSTRY GUIDANCE - Hull Air Cavity Systems: recesses or cavities formed in the flat of bottom, into which air is injected at low pressure and retained by the cavity geometry - a step at the leading edge and a closing beach aft - so that a stable gas pocket displaces water from part of the wetted surface. P3 INDUSTRY GUIDANCE - the constraints on air cavity systems: hull structural modification at design or major conversion; loss of internal volume and added structural weight; the cavity must be maintained across the ship's range of draught and trim; motion in a seaway disturbs or collapses the cavity; escaping air may reach the propeller and cause thrust loss, cavitation and vibration; and the geometry suits flat-bottomed full-form vessels rather than fine forms.

P3 INDUSTRY GUIDANCE - Hull Surface Texturing: the engineering of surface micro-geometry rather than the addition of gas. Riblets - streamwise micro-grooves of shark-skin type, applied as film or as a moulded coating - which restrain the spanwise motion of the near-wall vortices and so reduce turbulent momentum transfer to the wall. Superhydrophobic surfaces, combining micro and nano roughness with low surface energy to hold a retained air film giving partial slip. Lubricant-infused textured surfaces.

P3 INDUSTRY GUIDANCE - the constraints on texturing: the riblet dimension must be matched to the local boundary-layer thickness, which varies along the hull and with speed, so a single texture cannot be optimal everywhere; the texture is vulnerable to fouling and mechanical damage, and a fouled or damaged texture performs worse than a plain smooth surface; application quality control over a very large area is demanding; and compatibility with the anti-fouling scheme must be resolved, since the two occupy the same surface.

P3 INDUSTRY GUIDANCE - Microbubble drag reduction: air injected through porous plates or nozzle arrays in the flat of bottom, forming a cloud of small bubbles entrained within the turbulent boundary layer, which reduces the effective density near the wall and modifies the turbulence structure so as to reduce the Reynolds shear stress. The related air layer regime, in which at higher air flux the bubbles coalesce into a continuous film giving a larger reduction over a smaller area.

blocks.h: 1. What viscous resistance is, and why it is the target

blocks.p: Total resistance divides into frictional (viscous) resistance and residuary resistance, the latter comprising wave-making and eddy or form resistance. Frictional resistance is the tangential drag of water on the hull surface, and it depends on:

ul: Wetted surface area - the area actually in contact with water;
Speed, raised to a power slightly below two;
Reynolds number, through the skin friction coefficient; and
Surface roughness, which adds a further allowance and which fouling and coating condition control.

blocks.p: Two facts make it the right target. First, at ship scale the boundary layer is turbulent over essentially the whole hull - there is no laminar flow worth preserving - and turbulent friction is an order of magnitude greater than laminar. Second, on a full-form, moderate-speed merchant ship such as a tanker or bulk carrier the frictional component dominates total resistance; on a fine, fast form the residuary share is much larger. So on the ships that carry most of the world's cargo, friction is where the power actually goes, which is exactly why the examiner calls it "a major component".

The mechanism worth stating, because all three named technologies interfere with it: immediately at the wall there is a thin viscous sublayer; above it, streamwise vortex structures continually sweep fast fluid toward the wall and eject slow fluid away from it, and that exchange of momentum is the wall shear stress. Reduce or disrupt that exchange and you reduce friction.

blocks.h: 2. The logically distinct ways of attacking skin friction

blocks.p: There are only four, and placing the named technologies among them turns a list into an argument:

ol: Reduce the wetted area - hull form optimisation, constrained by the displacement the ship must carry.
Reduce the roughness of the surface that is wetted - smooth coatings, fouling control, hull cleaning and propeller polishing, fair plating and flush appendages.

Put a gas between the hull and the water, so that part of the surface is in contact with a fluid of far lower density and viscosity. Air cavity systems and microbubbles are both in this family, and they differ in how the gas is held.
Change the nature of the surface itself, so that the near-wall turbulence transfers less momentum to it. Surface texturing is in this family, along with polymer and compliant-coating approaches.

blocks.p: Note the consequence at once: two of the three named technologies are active - they consume power to supply air - and one is passive. That distinction decides most of the comparison at step 6.

blocks.h: 3. a) Hull Air Cavity Systems

rows: Recesses or cavities are built into the flat of bottom and air is injected into them at low pressure. The cavity geometry - a step at the leading edge and a closing beach aft - traps and retains a stable gas pocket, so that over that area the hull is in contact with air rather than water. Water is displaced from part of the wetted surface rather than merely aerated

Structural modification of the hull, at the design stage or in a major conversion; low-pressure blowers; a control system holding the cavity across the operating range. Air demand is set by leakage from the cavity edges, not by the area covered - which is why the blower power is comparatively modest

The largest and most stable gas coverage of the air-based methods, and the lowest parasitic power for a given covered area. Effective at moderate and low speeds. Well suited to flat-bottomed, full-form vessels - tankers, bulk carriers, barges and inland craft - which is exactly the tonnage where friction dominates

It is a hull modification, so retrofit is a structural job and there is a penalty in internal volume and added weight. The cavity must be maintained across the ship's range of draught and trim, and is disturbed or collapsed by motion in a seaway, so the benefit falls away in the conditions where power is most needed. Escaping air may reach the propeller, causing thrust loss, cavitation and vibration. The recesses complicate hull inspection, coating and cleaning. And the geometry does not suit fine forms

blocks.h: 4. b) Hull Surface Texturing

blocks.p: This is the one passive method of the three. Nothing is injected and no power is consumed; the micro-geometry of the surface itself is engineered so that the near-wall turbulence transfers less momentum to the wall.

ul: Riblets are the principal form - very fine streamwise grooves, of shark-skin type, applied as an adhesive film or as a moulded coating. They do not make the surface smoother; they restrain the spanwise motion of the near-wall vortices and lift them slightly clear of the wall, reducing the momentum exchange that constitutes wall shear stress. A riblet surface is measurably rougher than a smooth one and yet has lower drag, which is the counter-intuitive point worth making.

Superhydrophobic surfaces combine micro and nano roughness with low surface energy so that a retained air film is held in the texture, giving partial slip at the wall - conceptually a bridge between texturing and air lubrication.
Lubricant-infused textured surfaces hold a liquid within the texture to present a slippery interface.

blocks.p: Merits. Entirely passive - no machinery, no air supply, no parasitic power, and therefore no net-benefit calculation to argue about. No hull structural change, so it is a coating operation rather than a conversion. It can in principle be combined with fouling control, since both occupy the same surface.

Limits, and they are severe at present. The riblet dimension must be matched to the local boundary-layer thickness, which varies along the hull and with speed and draught, so one texture cannot be optimal everywhere and the benefit is lost outside the design condition. Durability is the central problem: the texture is vulnerable to mechanical damage and, far more importantly, to fouling - and a fouled or damaged texture performs worse than a plain smooth surface, so the technology can turn from a benefit into a penalty in service. Applying a controlled micro-texture over tens of thousands of square metres to a consistent standard is demanding, and its compatibility with the anti-fouling scheme must be resolved because the two compete for the same surface.

blocks.h: 5. c) Micro bubbles

rows: Air is injected through porous plates or nozzle arrays set in the flat of bottom, producing a cloud of small bubbles entrained within the turbulent boundary layer. The bubbles reduce the effective density in the near-wall region and modify the turbulence structure, reducing the Reynolds shear stress and hence the wall friction. Unlike a cavity, the water is not displaced - it is aerated

As the air flux is increased the bubbles coalesce into a continuous air layer, which gives a substantially larger reduction. Microbubble, transitional and air layer regimes are points on one scale, selected by air flow rate - and the air layer regime needs a great deal more air

A continuous supply of compressed air from blowers or compressors, injectors in the shell, and a control system. No change to the hull form beyond the injector fittings, which makes it far more retrofittable than a cavity system
Retrofittable without structural modification. Coverage can be distributed across the flat of bottom. It works with the existing hull and can be combined with a good coating

The parasitic power decides everything. The net benefit is the friction saving less the compressor power, and that power rises with the hydrostatic head at the injection point - so a deep-draught ship pays more air power for the same coverage, which is precisely the ship where friction dominates. The bubble cloud is swept aft and disperses, so the effect decays with distance from the injectors and several injection stations are needed. Bubble persistence depends on salinity and surface-active contaminants in the water. Air reaching the propeller risks thrust loss, cavitation and vibration. The benefit falls away in a seaway. And injectors and porous plates require maintenance and are liable to fouling

blocks.h: 6. Comparing the three named technologies

rows: Gas between hull and water - water displaced
Gas between hull and water - water aerated
Durability and fouling; benefit lost outside the design condition
Net benefit after compressor power; decay aft of injection

blocks.p: Three conclusions worth stating explicitly:

ol: For the two air-based methods the decisive question is never the gross drag reduction but the NET benefit after the air supply power - and for microbubbles that penalty grows with draught, which works directly against the ships that would gain most.
For texturing the decisive question is durability, not physics. The mechanism is sound; the difficulty is holding a micro-texture in service on a fouling, abrading surface for years.

All three degrade in a seaway and none is a substitute for a clean, smooth hull. Hull and propeller condition management remains the largest and cheapest single lever on frictional resistance, and any of these technologies is applied on top of it, not instead of it.

blocks.h: 7. The other methods currently under consideration

ul: Hull roughness and fouling control - low-friction and fouling-release coatings, planned hull cleaning and propeller polishing, condition monitoring of performance, and attention to weld seams, plate unfairness, appendages, overboard openings and flush sea-chest gratings. Unglamorous and by far the most effective.
Reduction of wetted surface through hull form optimisation, within the displacement and stability the ship must have.
Air layer drag reduction as a distinct operating regime rather than a distinct technology, discussed at step 5.

Polymer and surfactant drag reduction - the Toms effect, in which minute quantities of long-chain polymer released into the boundary layer suppress turbulent bursting and sharply reduce friction. The mechanism is well established; the obstacles are continuous consumption, storage and cost, and above all the environmental objection to discharging the additive to the sea, which is why it remains a research route rather than a shipboard one.
Compliant or elastic coatings, intended to deform in response to the near-wall pressure fluctuations and damp the turbulence - long studied and not yet commercially established.

blocks.h: 8. Where this stands at present

ul: Maturity differs sharply across the three. Air lubrication in its cavity and air-layer forms is in commercial service on a limited number of ships, most of them flat-bottomed full-form vessels. Microbubble injection is closely related and less separable in practice, since a system designed for one regime often operates across the scale. Surface texturing remains at trial and early-application stage, held back by durability rather than by principle. No claim is made here about how many ships are fitted, because that figure moves and no verified figure is held.

Verification is the practical difficulty. A saving of this order is hard to demonstrate on a working ship: it must be separated from weather, sea state, loading condition, hull and propeller fouling, and the natural scatter of noon-report data. Credible assessment needs a performance monitoring system with correction for weather and displacement, and preferably shaft power measurement. That is why an owner should require the same evidential standard from a friction-reduction retrofit as from any other efficiency measure.

The regulatory driver is why these are under active consideration now. EEXI and the CII entered into force on 1 January 2023 - five months before this examination - so a technical index and an operational rating now bear on the same hull. This is the first CII data year and it is still running, so no ship has yet been rated, and every ship's present operation is what her first rating will reflect. The operative strategy is the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018.

There is also a route to credit. IMO guidance exists on the treatment of innovative energy efficiency technologies for the calculation and verification of the attained EEDI, under which a technology that reduces the propulsion power required - which is precisely what air lubrication does - may be credited, subject to verification. That is what turns these from interesting experiments into commercial propositions.

The engineering conclusion to close on. Skin friction is the largest single component of resistance on the ships that move most of the world's cargo, and there is no single technology that removes it. What is under consideration is a set of partial measures, each with a different cost, a different parasitic penalty and a different failure mode - and the sound approach is to secure the clean, smooth, well-maintained hull first, and then to apply whichever of these suits the hull form, the draught range, the trade and the seaway the ship actually works in.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem asks two things and the second is easy to miss. It asks for "various skin friction reduction methods currently under consideration" - a survey - and for "special mention" of three named technologies. A candidate who writes only about air cavities, texturing and microbubbles has answered the second half; one who surveys the field and treats the three thinly has answered the first. The route carries a survey step at 7 alongside the three limb steps, and that is deliberate.

Sixteen marks with no printed split, and three named limbs that do not divide evenly. Each named technology gets the same four-heading treatment - principle, what it needs, merits, limits - which makes the answer visibly systematic and makes the comparison at step 6 possible. Step 1 is not throat-clearing: you cannot say why these technologies are worth having until you have said what fraction of the problem friction is and how wall friction actually arises.

blocks.h: The classification that turns a list into an argument

blocks.p: There are only four ways to reduce skin friction: reduce the wetted area · reduce the roughness · put gas between the hull and the water · change the surface itself. Place the three named technologies among them in your opening and the rest of the answer has a spine.

The immediate payoff is that air cavities and microbubbles are the same family - both interpose gas - and they differ only in how the gas is held: a cavity displaces the water and holds a stable pocket by its geometry; microbubbles aerate the boundary layer and the cloud is swept away. Everything else about them follows from that one difference. Texturing is a different family altogether, and it is the only passive one of the three.

blocks.h: The single most important practical point

blocks.p: For an air-based system the number that matters is not the drag reduction but the NET saving after the air supply power. A system that cuts friction impressively and consumes a large blower or compressor load may deliver very little. And for microbubbles the penalty scales with the hydrostatic head at the injection point - meaning a deep-draught ship pays more air power for the same coverage, which is exactly the ship on which friction dominates.

That is why the air cavity is attractive despite being a structural job: its air demand is set by leakage from the cavity edges, not by the area covered, so it holds a large gas area for comparatively little power.

blocks.h: The counter-intuitive fact about riblets

blocks.p: A riblet surface is measurably rougher than a smooth one and yet has lower drag. That is worth saying because it shows you know the mechanism rather than the label: riblets do not smooth the surface, they restrain the spanwise motion of the near-wall vortices and lift them slightly clear of the wall, cutting the momentum exchange that constitutes wall shear stress.

And the corollary is the technology's weakness: because it works by a micro-geometry matched to the boundary layer, a fouled or damaged texture performs worse than a plain smooth surface. The physics is sound; the problem is holding the geometry in service for years on an abrading, fouling hull. Durability, not principle, is what holds texturing back.

blocks.h: The sentence that should close the answer

blocks.p: None of the three is a substitute for a clean, smooth, well-maintained hull. Hull roughness and fouling control - coatings, cleaning, propeller polishing, fair plating, flush openings - remains the largest and cheapest single lever on frictional resistance, and any of these technologies is applied on top of it, not instead of it. An examiner reading a page of enthusiasm for air lubrication will be looking for exactly that qualification.

blocks.h: Where the regulation comes in at this sitting

blocks.p: This is what makes it a live question rather than a technical curiosity. EEXI and the CII entered into force on 1 January 2023, five months before this examination, so a technical index and an operational rating now both bear on the same hull. 2023 is the first CII data year and it is still running, so no ship has yet been rated - do not describe rating experience. The operative strategy is the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018; the 2023 Strategy was adopted at MEPC 80 on 7 July 2023, one month after this sitting.

There is also a route to credit: IMO guidance exists on the treatment of innovative energy efficiency technologies for the calculation and verification of the attained EEDI, under which a technology reducing the required propulsion power may be credited subject to verification. That is what converts these from experiments into commercial propositions.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Answering only the three named technologies and ignoring the printed request for various methods.
Describing the three without comparing them. With sixteen marks and no split, the comparison is where the upper band is.
Treating air cavities and microbubbles as the same thing. One displaces water and holds a stable pocket; the other aerates the boundary layer with a cloud that is swept aft.
Quoting drag-reduction or fuel-saving percentages. They vary enormously with hull, speed, draught and method of measurement.
Ignoring the parasitic power of the air supply, which is what actually decides whether an air system is worth fitting.
Saying riblets work by making the hull smoother. They do not - a riblet surface is rougher and still has lower drag.
Omitting the durability and fouling problem with texturing, which is the reason it is not in general service.
Forgetting propeller air ingestion as a risk of both air-based systems.
Forgetting that all three degrade in a seaway.
Presenting any of these as a substitute for hull cleaning and good coatings.
Citing the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, which is one month future at this sitting, or describing CII rating experience, of which there is none yet.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: "Which resistance component dominates on a loaded VLCC?" The frictional component - full form, moderate speed.
"Is the boundary layer laminar anywhere on a ship?" Effectively not at ship scale - it is turbulent over essentially the whole hull.
"What is the difference between an air cavity and microbubbles?" The cavity displaces water and holds a stable gas pocket by geometry; microbubbles aerate the boundary layer and disperse aft.
"Why does a deep-draught ship pay more for microbubbles?" The compressor works against the hydrostatic head at the injection point.
"Why do you need several injection stations?" Because the bubble cloud is swept aft and disperses, so the effect decays with distance from the injectors.
"Do riblets make the hull smoother?" No - rougher, and yet lower drag, because they restrain the near-wall vortices.
"When does a riblet surface become a penalty?" When it fouls or is damaged - it then performs worse than a plain smooth surface.
"What is the risk to the propeller?" Air ingestion, causing thrust loss, cavitation and vibration.
"What happens to all three in heavy weather?" The benefit falls away - cavities are disturbed, bubble layers dispersed.
"What is the cheapest way to reduce skin friction?" Keep the hull clean, smooth and well coated, and the propeller polished.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: What does frictional resistance depend on? Wetted surface area, speed to a power slightly below two, Reynolds number, and surface roughness.
How does wall friction actually arise? Turbulent structures above the viscous sublayer exchange momentum with the wall; that exchange is the wall shear stress.
Name the four ways of reducing it. Reduce wetted area; reduce roughness; interpose gas; change the surface itself.
How is the air held in a cavity system? By the cavity geometry - a step forward and a closing beach aft - so air demand is set by leakage, not by area.
What does a cavity system cost you structurally? Hull modification, internal volume and added weight, plus sensitivity to draught, trim and seaway.
How do microbubbles reduce drag? By reducing effective near-wall density and modifying the turbulence structure, lowering the Reynolds shear stress.
What is air layer drag reduction? The same system at higher air flux, where bubbles coalesce into a continuous film for a larger reduction.
How do riblets work? Streamwise micro-grooves that restrain spanwise vortex motion and lift the vortices clear of the wall.

What is the Toms effect and why is it not used? Long-chain polymers suppress turbulent bursting; the obstacles are continuous consumption and the environmental objection to discharging additive to the sea.
How would you verify a claimed saving? Performance monitoring corrected for weather, sea state and displacement, preferably with shaft power measurement.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Start from the four families: AREA · ROUGHNESS · GAS · SURFACE. The three named technologies then sort themselves - two GAS, one SURFACE.

For the two gas methods, one word each: CAVITY DISPLACES · BUBBLES AERATE. And one consequence each: cavity = structure, low air power; bubbles = retrofit, high air power. For texturing: ROUGHER YET SLIPPERIER - AND IT WEARS OUT.
Treat each under the same four headings - PRINCIPLE, NEEDS, MERITS, LIMITS - and close on the qualification that carries the marks: NONE OF THEM BEATS A CLEAN HULL.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the evidential position on this question

blocks.p: The True Source corpus holds no naval architecture or ship resistance material whatever - no resistance and propulsion reference, no towing-tank or trials material, and no guidance on innovative energy efficiency technologies. Nor does any solved MIW question address any of the three named technologies. This question therefore carries no primary source and none is claimed. The technology content is engineering judgement and industry guidance and is labelled as such.

The discipline that follows is that no quantitative claim is asserted anywhere. No percentage of total resistance attributable to friction for any hull form; no drag-reduction percentage for any of the three technologies; no net fuel saving; no air flow rate, injection pressure or blower power; no riblet dimension; no payback period. All are highly configuration-, speed-, draught- and hull-specific, and published figures vary by a wide margin between full-scale trials, model tests and computational studies. No correlation line, extrapolation method or roughness allowance is cited by name, no ship, supplier or trial is named, and no claim is made about fleet uptake.

The regulatory frame was re-anchored to this sitting rather than inherited from the energy-efficiency family, whose members all sit between 2024 and 2026 and therefore carry a later strategy and real rating experience. And the IMO guidance on innovative technologies is referred to by description and not by circular number, because MIW holds no copy: what is asserted is that such guidance exists and that a power-reducing technology may be credited under it subject to verification, and no clause or category is quoted.

steps.title: What viscous resistance is, and why it is the target
points: total resistance = FRICTIONAL (VISCOUS) + RESIDUARY (wave-making plus eddy or form)
frictional resistance depends on WETTED SURFACE AREA, SPEED to a power slightly below two, REYNOLDS NUMBER, and SURFACE ROUGHNESS
at ship scale the boundary layer is TURBULENT OVER ESSENTIALLY THE WHOLE HULL - there is no laminar flow worth preserving
on a FULL-FORM, MODERATE-SPEED merchant ship the frictional component DOMINATES; on a fine fast form the residuary share is much larger
SO ON THE SHIPS THAT CARRY MOST OF THE WORLD'S CARGO, FRICTION IS WHERE THE POWER GOES
THE MECHANISM ALL THREE TECHNOLOGIES ATTACK - a thin VISCOUS SUBLAYER at the wall, streamwise vortex structures above it exchanging momentum with the wall, and THAT EXCHANGE IS THE WALL SHEAR STRESS

steps.title: The logically distinct ways of attacking skin friction
points: THERE ARE ONLY FOUR, and placing the named technologies among them turns a list into an argument
1 REDUCE THE WETTED AREA - hull form optimisation, constrained by the displacement the ship must carry
2 REDUCE THE ROUGHNESS of the surface that is wetted - coatings, fouling control, cleaning, fair plating, flush appendages
3 PUT A GAS BETWEEN HULL AND WATER - AIR CAVITIES AND MICROBUBBLES ARE BOTH HERE, differing in HOW THE GAS IS HELD
4 CHANGE THE SURFACE ITSELF so the near-wall turbulence transfers less momentum - TEXTURING is here, with polymer and compliant approaches
CONSEQUENCE - two of the three named technologies are ACTIVE and consume power for air; one is PASSIVE. That decides most of the comparison

steps.title: a) Hull Air Cavity Systems
points: PRINCIPLE - RECESSES OR CAVITIES BUILT INTO THE FLAT OF BOTTOM, air injected at low pressure
the geometry - A STEP FORWARD AND A CLOSING BEACH AFT - TRAPS AND RETAINS A STABLE GAS POCKET
WATER IS DISPLACED from part of the wetted surface, not merely aerated
NEEDS - STRUCTURAL MODIFICATION at design or major conversion; low-pressure blowers; control across the operating range
AIR DEMAND IS SET BY LEAKAGE FROM THE CAVITY EDGES, NOT BY THE AREA COVERED - hence comparatively modest blower power

MERITS - the LARGEST AND MOST STABLE gas coverage and the LOWEST PARASITIC POWER for a given area; effective at moderate and low speed; suits FLAT-BOTTOMED FULL-FORM vessels, which is where friction dominates
LIMITS - a HULL MODIFICATION, so retrofit is structural; loss of internal volume and added weight
LIMITS - the cavity must hold across the range of DRAUGHT AND TRIM, and is DISTURBED OR COLLAPSED BY MOTION IN A SEAWAY
LIMITS - ESCAPING AIR MAY REACH THE PROPELLER causing thrust loss, cavitation and vibration; recesses complicate inspection, coating and cleaning; unsuited to fine forms

steps.title: b) Hull Surface Texturing
points: THE ONE PASSIVE METHOD OF THE THREE - nothing injected, no power consumed
PRINCIPLE - ENGINEER THE MICRO-GEOMETRY OF THE SURFACE so near-wall turbulence transfers less momentum to the wall
RIBLETS - very fine STREAMWISE GROOVES of shark-skin type, as film or moulded coating
they RESTRAIN THE SPANWISE MOTION of the near-wall vortices and lift them slightly clear of the wall
A RIBLET SURFACE IS MEASURABLY ROUGHER THAN A SMOOTH ONE AND YET HAS LOWER DRAG - the counter-intuitive point
SUPERHYDROPHOBIC surfaces - micro and nano roughness plus low surface energy holding a RETAINED AIR FILM for partial slip; a bridge to air lubrication
LUBRICANT-INFUSED textured surfaces holding a liquid within the texture
MERITS - entirely PASSIVE, no machinery, no air, NO PARASITIC POWER and no net-benefit argument; no structural change; combinable in principle with fouling control
LIMITS - the riblet dimension must MATCH THE LOCAL BOUNDARY-LAYER THICKNESS, which varies along the hull and with speed and draught
LIMITS - DURABILITY IS THE CENTRAL PROBLEM. A FOULED OR DAMAGED TEXTURE PERFORMS WORSE THAN A PLAIN SMOOTH SURFACE
LIMITS - application quality control over tens of thousands of square metres; compatibility with the anti-fouling scheme, since both occupy the same surface

steps.title: c) Micro bubbles
points: PRINCIPLE - air injected through POROUS PLATES OR NOZZLE ARRAYS in the flat of bottom
a cloud of small bubbles ENTRAINED WITHIN THE TURBULENT BOUNDARY LAYER, reducing effective near-wall density and MODIFYING THE TURBULENCE STRUCTURE, lowering the Reynolds shear stress
UNLIKE A CAVITY, THE WATER IS NOT DISPLACED - IT IS AERATED

THE RELATED REGIME - at higher air flux the bubbles COALESCE INTO A CONTINUOUS AIR LAYER for a larger reduction; microbubble, transitional and air layer are points on ONE SCALE selected by air flow rate
NEEDS - a CONTINUOUS SUPPLY OF COMPRESSED AIR, injectors in the shell, control system. NO HULL FORM CHANGE beyond the injectors, so far more RETROFITTABLE
MERITS - retrofittable without structural work; coverage distributed across the flat of bottom; works with the existing hull and a good coating
LIMITS - THE PARASITIC POWER DECIDES EVERYTHING. Net benefit = friction saving LESS COMPRESSOR POWER
LIMITS - that power RISES WITH THE HYDROSTATIC HEAD AT THE INJECTION POINT, so a DEEP-DRAUGHT SHIP PAYS MORE for the same coverage - exactly the ship where friction dominates
LIMITS - the cloud is SWEPT AFT AND DISPERSES, so the effect DECAYS WITH DISTANCE from the injectors and several stations are needed

LIMITS - bubble persistence depends on SALINITY AND SURFACE-ACTIVE CONTAMINANTS; AIR REACHING THE PROPELLER is a real risk; benefit falls away IN A SEAWAY; injectors and porous plates foul and need maintenance

steps.title: Comparing the three named technologies
points: FAMILY - cavity: gas, WATER DISPLACED. Texturing: SURFACE CHANGED. Microbubbles: gas, WATER AERATED
ACTIVE OR PASSIVE - blowers / none / compressors
PARASITIC POWER - LOW (set by leakage) / NONE / HIGH AND DRAUGHT-DEPENDENT
HULL CHANGE - STRUCTURAL / a coating operation / INJECTORS ONLY, retrofittable
PRINCIPAL WEAKNESS - seaway and draught/trim sensitivity / DURABILITY AND FOULING / NET BENEFIT AFTER COMPRESSOR POWER and decay aft of injection
PROPELLER AIR INGESTION - a real risk for both gas methods
CONCLUSION 1 - for the air methods the decisive question is never gross drag reduction but NET BENEFIT after air power, and for microbubbles that penalty GROWS WITH DRAUGHT
CONCLUSION 2 - for texturing the decisive question is DURABILITY, NOT PHYSICS
CONCLUSION 3 - ALL THREE DEGRADE IN A SEAWAY AND NONE IS A SUBSTITUTE FOR A CLEAN, SMOOTH HULL

steps.title: The other methods currently under consideration
points: HULL ROUGHNESS AND FOULING CONTROL - low-friction and fouling-release coatings, planned hull cleaning and propeller polishing, performance monitoring, and attention to WELD SEAMS, PLATE UNFAIRNESS, APPENDAGES, OPENINGS AND FLUSH SEA-CHEST GRATINGS. Unglamorous and by far the most effective
REDUCTION OF WETTED SURFACE through hull form optimisation, within the displacement and stability required
AIR LAYER DRAG REDUCTION as a distinct operating regime rather than a distinct technology
POLYMER AND SURFACTANT DRAG REDUCTION - the TOMS EFFECT: minute quantities of long-chain polymer suppress turbulent bursting
the obstacles are CONTINUOUS CONSUMPTION, storage and cost, and above all the ENVIRONMENTAL OBJECTION TO DISCHARGING THE ADDITIVE TO THE SEA - which is why it remains a research route
COMPLIANT OR ELASTIC COATINGS deforming in response to near-wall pressure fluctuations - long studied, not commercially established

steps.title: Where this stands at present
points: MATURITY DIFFERS SHARPLY - air lubrication in cavity and air-layer forms is IN COMMERCIAL SERVICE on a limited number of ships, mostly flat-bottomed full-form vessels
microbubble injection is closely related and less separable in practice; SURFACE TEXTURING REMAINS AT TRIAL AND EARLY-APPLICATION STAGE, held back by DURABILITY rather than principle
NO CLAIM IS MADE ABOUT HOW MANY SHIPS ARE FITTED
VERIFICATION IS THE PRACTICAL DIFFICULTY - a saving must be separated from weather, sea state, loading condition, fouling and noon-report scatter
credible assessment needs PERFORMANCE MONITORING CORRECTED FOR WEATHER AND DISPLACEMENT, preferably with SHAFT POWER MEASUREMENT
THE REGULATORY DRIVER - EEXI AND CII IN FORCE 1 JANUARY 2023, five months before this examination; a technical index and an operational rating now bear on the same hull

THIS IS THE FIRST CII DATA YEAR AND IT IS STILL RUNNING, SO NO SHIP HAS YET BEEN RATED; present operation is what the first rating will reflect. Operative strategy is the INITIAL IMO GHG STRATEGY OF 2018

A ROUTE TO CREDIT EXISTS - IMO guidance on the treatment of INNOVATIVE ENERGY EFFICIENCY TECHNOLOGIES for the attained EEDI, under which a power-reducing technology may be credited subject to verification

CLOSING ENGINEERING CONCLUSION - there is no single technology that removes friction; SECURE THE CLEAN, SMOOTH, WELL-MAINTAINED HULL FIRST, then apply whichever suits the hull form, draught range, trade and seaway

questions.understand_first: A ship pushing through water pays for it twice: once for shoving the water aside and making waves, and once for dragging it along the skin of the hull. On the big, slow, full-bodied ships that carry most of the world's cargo, the second of those is the larger bill by a wide margin, which is why so much effort now goes into it. The drag itself comes from a very thin region right against the plating, where swirling motions in the water keep carrying fast-moving fluid down onto the surface and slow fluid away from it; that constant exchange is what the hull feels as friction. So there are only a few honest ways to reduce it. You can wet less of the ship, which the hull designer does but only so far, because she still has to carry her cargo. You can make the wetted part smoother and keep it that way, which is what coatings and cleaning are for and which remains the biggest and cheapest gain of all. You can put a gas in between, so that some of the hull is touching air instead of water - and the two ways of doing that differ in whether you trap the air in a shaped pocket built into the bottom, or blow it out as a cloud of bubbles that the flow carries away aft. Or you can change the texture of the surface itself so that the swirls near the wall are held back, which sounds like making it rougher and in a sense is, yet gives less drag. Each has a catch. Blowing air costs power, and the deeper the ship the more it costs, so the saving has to be counted net. A shaped pocket is a structural alteration and stops working when the ship starts moving in a seaway. And a clever texture only works while it survives, which on a fouling, scraping hull is the whole problem.

One word each for the gas pair: CAVITY DISPLACES (3), BUBBLES AERATE (5); one consequence each: structure but low air power against retrofit but high air power. Texturing is ROUGHER YET SLIPPERIER - AND IT WEARS OUT (4). Treat all three under PRINCIPLE, NEEDS, MERITS, LIMITS, compare at (6), survey the rest at (7), and close on NONE OF THEM BEATS A CLEAN HULL (6, 8).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the skin friction reduction question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What viscous resistance is and why it is the target. 2 The four ways of attacking it. 3 Hull air cavity systems. 4 Hull surface texturing. 5 Micro bubbles. 6 Comparison. 7 The other methods under consideration. 8 Maturity, verification and the regulatory driver.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for a survey AND for three special mentions, so step 7 is compulsory, not optional.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does frictional resistance depend on, and how does wall friction arise?
retrieval_cards.answer: On wetted surface area, on speed raised to a power slightly below two, on Reynolds number through the friction coefficient, and on surface roughness. It arises because above a thin viscous sublayer at the wall, streamwise vortex structures continually sweep fast fluid toward the wall and eject slow fluid away from it; that momentum exchange is the wall shear stress.
retrieval_cards.why: Every one of the three named technologies interferes with that exchange, so stating it makes them comparable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the four logically distinct ways of reducing skin friction?
retrieval_cards.answer: Reduce the wetted area, by hull form optimisation within the displacement required. Reduce the roughness of the wetted surface, by coatings, fouling control and cleaning. Put a gas between the hull and the water - air cavities and microbubbles. Change the nature of the surface itself - texturing, polymer and compliant approaches.
retrieval_cards.why: Placing the three named technologies among four families turns a list into an argument.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between an air cavity system and microbubble injection?
retrieval_cards.answer: A cavity displaces the water: recesses built into the flat of bottom, with a step forward and a closing beach aft, trap a stable gas pocket so the hull is in contact with air over that area. Microbubbles aerate: air injected through porous plates or nozzles forms a cloud entrained within the boundary layer, reducing effective near-wall density and modifying the turbulence, and the cloud is swept aft and disperses.
retrieval_cards.why: Everything else about the two - air demand, hull change, retrofittability, seaway behaviour - follows from that one difference.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the air demand of a cavity system comparatively modest?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the cavity geometry retains the gas, so air need only be supplied to make up the leakage from the cavity edges - the demand is set by leakage rather than by the area covered. That is what gives a cavity system the lowest parasitic power of the air-based methods, despite the structural cost of building it.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the reason a structural modification can still be the better commercial choice.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does a deep-draught ship pay more for microbubble drag reduction?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the compressor must work against the hydrostatic head at the injection point, so the parasitic power rises with draught. The net benefit is the friction saving less that compressor power - and the penalty grows on exactly the ships where frictional resistance dominates.
retrieval_cards.why: The decisive commercial fact about the technology, and the one most candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do riblets reduce drag, and what is counter-intuitive about them?
retrieval_cards.answer: They are fine streamwise micro-grooves that restrain the spanwise motion of the near-wall vortices and lift them slightly clear of the wall, reducing the momentum exchange that constitutes wall shear stress. The counter-intuitive point is that a riblet surface is measurably rougher than a smooth one and still has lower drag.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying it proves you know the mechanism rather than the label.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What holds surface texturing back, and when does it become a penalty?
retrieval_cards.answer: Durability, not physics. The riblet dimension must match the local boundary-layer thickness, which varies along the hull and with speed and draught, so one texture cannot be optimal everywhere. More seriously the texture is vulnerable to fouling and mechanical damage, and a fouled or damaged texture performs worse than a plain smooth surface - so it can turn from a benefit into a penalty in service.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why a mechanism that works in the laboratory is not in general service.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is air layer drag reduction and how does it relate to microbubbles?
retrieval_cards.answer: The same injection system operated at higher air flux, at which the bubbles coalesce into a continuous air film rather than remaining a dispersed cloud, giving a substantially larger drag reduction. Microbubble, transitional and air layer regimes are points on a single scale selected by air flow rate - the air layer regime requiring considerably more air.
retrieval_cards.why: It shows the two named technologies are less separable in practice than the question implies.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What risk do both air-based systems share, and what happens to all three in heavy weather?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both risk air reaching the propeller, causing thrust loss, cavitation and vibration. All three degrade in a seaway - cavities are disturbed or collapsed by the ship's motion, and bubble clouds and air layers are dispersed - so the benefit falls away in exactly the conditions where the power is most needed.
retrieval_cards.why: Two limitations examiners reliably ask about, and both are easy to omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Toms effect, and why is it not used at sea?
retrieval_cards.answer: Polymer drag reduction: minute quantities of long-chain polymer released into the boundary layer suppress turbulent bursting and sharply reduce friction. The mechanism is well established, but it requires continuous consumption with the associated storage and cost, and above all it discharges the additive to the sea, which is environmentally objectionable - so it remains a research route rather than a shipboard one.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the strongest of the 'other methods' the stem asks for, and its failure mode is not technical.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the qualification that should close this answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: That none of these is a substitute for a clean, smooth, well-maintained hull. Hull roughness and fouling control - good coatings, planned hull cleaning, propeller polishing, fair plating and flush openings - remains the largest and cheapest single lever on frictional resistance, and any of these technologies is applied on top of it rather than instead of it.
retrieval_cards.why: An examiner reading a page of enthusiasm for air lubrication is looking for exactly this qualification.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Sixteen marks, no printed split, and TWO printed demands: 'explain various skin friction reduction methods currently under consideration' AND 'with special mention on the following' three named technologies. Both must be answered. The examiner is testing whether the candidate understands the MECHANISM of wall friction well enough to explain why three quite different interventions all reduce it, and whether he can weigh them practically - which for the two air methods means the parasitic power, and for the third means durability. The words 'currently under consideration' additionally fix the answer to the state of the art at this sitting.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 marks, undivided, and the three named limbs carry no split so none is invented. Roughly three marks on the framing at steps 1 and 2 - which is not preamble, because the four-family classification is what makes the rest coherent - about eight spread evenly across the three named technologies, two on the comparison, and the remainder on the survey of other methods and on maturity and verification. A candidate who omits the survey step has forfeited the marks attached to the word 'various'.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can state the mechanism of turbulent wall friction and then show that air cavities, microbubbles and texturing attack it in two quite different ways. Specifically: that a cavity DISPLACES water and a bubble cloud AERATES it; that the air demand of a cavity is set by leakage while a microbubble system's compressor power rises with draught; that riblets are rougher and yet lower-drag; and that a fouled texture is worse than a plain surface. The qualification that none of these substitutes for a clean hull is what an examiner will be waiting for.
primary_source_plan: ESTABLISH FIRST WHETHER ANY DONOR OR HELD MATERIAL EXISTS - run targeted searches on air cavity, microbubble, air lubrication, skin friction and texturing before assuming the subject is unbuilt
Search the corpus directly for any resistance, propulsion or naval architecture material, and set the evidence class on the result
Read the energy-efficiency family for the resistance FRAMEWORK only, and discard its regulatory context, which is 2024 to 2026
RE-ANCHOR THE REGULATORY FRAME TO JUNE 2023 EXPLICITLY - which strategy, how old the CII is, and whether any ship has been rated
Decide before drafting that no quantitative claim will appear, given that published figures vary by a wide margin
Decide how the IMO innovative-technology guidance will be referred to, given that no copy is held
Manage the overlap with Q5 on the same paper deliberately, since both concern the same wetted surface
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - and it sits entirely in the regulatory tail rather than in the physics. Boundary-layer behaviour, cavity geometry, the riblet mechanism and microbubble physics carry no dated instrument and did not move. But every family member that informed the framework is a 2024 to 2026 object carrying the 2023 GHG Strategy and post-2023 CII rating experience in its closing paragraphs, and both are future here. The printed words 'currently under consideration' add a second freshness obligation, met by stating maturity relatively and asserting no uptake figure.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The question is entirely technical. No Indian statute is load-bearing; the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs the paper at this sitting but is not engaged.
technical_ambiguities: Whether air cavities and microbubbles are the same technology - they are the same family but differ in whether water is displaced or aerated
Whether the gross drag reduction is the relevant figure for an air system - it is not; the net saving after air supply power is
Whether microbubble parasitic power is independent of draught - it is not; it rises with the hydrostatic head at the injector
Whether riblets work by smoothing the surface - they do not; they restrain the near-wall vortices, and the surface is rougher
Whether a textured surface is always better than a smooth one - no; fouled or damaged, it is worse
Whether air lubrication works in a seaway - the benefit falls away for all three
Whether any of these replaces hull cleaning and coating - none does
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Open with the resistance decomposition and the wall-friction mechanism, briefly but properly, because the mechanism is what makes the three technologies comparable. Then the four-family classification in a numbered list, which places the named technologies and generates the active-versus-passive distinction that runs through the rest. Then each named technology in its own tabulated or bulleted block under the same four headings - principle, what it needs, merits, limits - so the reader can compare across them. Then a single comparison table with the three as columns, followed by three explicit conclusions. Then the survey of other methods, which the printed word 'various' requires. Close on maturity, the practical difficulty of verifying a saving, the regulatory driver as it stood at this sitting, and the qualification that none of this beats a clean hull.
